text:
An Iowa man who alleges federal bureaucracy has left him stranded in Canada for a year, with no way to return to the United States, is now suing the federal government.

Haider Raza, a citizen and national of Pakistan, is suing the U.S. Department of State in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Iowa for alleged delays in processing his visa-related application to remain in the United States.

Raza, 32, of Ames, works for Kingland Systems at the company’s headquarters in Clear Lake. In his lawsuit, he indicates he first arrived in America 11 years ago through a student visa, then attended Iowa State University where he received both a bachelor’s and master’s degree.

After graduating, Raza was granted “H-1B status” — a temporary, employer-sponsored classification that allows foreign nationals to work in specialized fields within the United States — and, in October 2021, began working for Kingland Systems.

In 2024, Raza sought to extend his H-1B status for another three years. Visa requests by foreign nationals are adjudicated through the Department of State’s Bureau of Consular Affairs at U.S. embassies and consulates abroad. Because of that, the lawsuit alleges, Raza traveled to Canada last year and while there attended a visa-application interview at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto on Aug. 5, 2025.

At that time, the lawsuit claims, Raza was informed that his application would be placed in “administrative processing.” In the almost 12 months since then, the lawsuit alleges, the application has remained pending with no action taken.

The lack of action has left Raza “unable to return to the United States,” which has resulted in his being placed on unpaid leave from his job in Iowa.

“Despite numerous attempts to contact the consulate about the status of his visa,” the lawsuit alleges, Raza “continues to await the defendants’ action after almost a year of delay. … (He) left the United States to travel to Toronto, attend this routine interview, and receive a visa stamp with the expectation that he would soon return and resume his job and life.”

According to the lawsuit, Raza has inquired several times about the status of his application, and that he was initially told the process would take “several months” before being told the consulate was “unable to determine when this process may be concluded.”

Through Kingland Systems, the lawsuit alleges, Raza has enlisted the assistance of three members of Congress, all of whom have only been told the application remains in administrative processing.

Raza, the lawsuit states, “has no criminal history and no immigration violations whatsoever. He received a single traffic ticket in the United States, which … would not preclude the grant of a visa or cause the present delay. (He) cannot re-enter the United States absent a visa stamp and has been on unpaid leave from his U.S.-based job since October 15, 2025. He has encountered significant emotional and financial hardship as a result of the ongoing uncertainty relating to his work status … He remains in a state of limbo.”

The situation has made it difficult for Raza to fulfill his financial commitments in both Canada and the United States and also made it impossible for him to visit his Iowa-based physician and dentist, the lawsuit alleges.

The lawsuit seeks to have the court intervene and compel the U.S. Department of State to act on Raza’s application. The department has yet to file a response to the lawsuit.

text:
Norma Bowe looked at the scene unfolding before her: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, dressed in their camo-colored tactical vests and black face coverings, pushing people with batons and yanking them into the street.

It was Memorial Day, and protesters had gathered outside Delaney Hall Detention Facility in Newark, New Jersey, as part of ongoing demonstrations demanding the release of immigrants in detention — more than 300 of whom were on a hunger and labor strike inside the facility.

Bowe is a registered nurse who has operated a mobile health clinic outside the detention center for more than a year. That Monday, as Bowe scanned the chaos, she said she could see from the corner of her eye ICE agents dragging a young woman across the asphalt. As the agents pulled her by the arms, her shirt snagged on the ground and came up and over her head, exposing her bra, Bowe told The 19th.

“Help me!” Bowe remembers the woman screaming while lying on the ground.

“I’m thinking in my head, I’ll just help her up,” she said. “ICE was so violently shoving people that I wasn’t sure if anybody was going to get to her.”

Bowe began to walk toward the woman. Then, Bowe said she went flying.

Videos of the scene captured from multiple angles appear to show Bowe landing face-first on the concrete sidewalk after being shoved by an officer. The result was a concussion, a fractured kneecap, medial meniscus tears and bruising to her left eye orbit, she said. In the nine weeks since, she has gone to the emergency room and received physical therapy and acupuncture. She’s visiting a neurologist next week for persistent headaches.

“Her story is one in a string of alleged violent incidents between ICE agents and women throughout the United States. Over the last 18 months, online videos have shown women being tackled to the ground, pulled from a car, dragged out of a workplace and fatally shot. This week, Bowe has filed a claim against the federal government. It is one of 54 claims filed by affiliates of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) in 17 states and Washington, D.C., against the federal government as a result of alleged harms by immigration authorities.

“They do whatever they want,” Bowe said, speaking about ICE. “They just harm whoever they want, whenever they want. And so, this is a step in making them accountable.”

On paper, federal law enforcement agents can be criminally prosecuted or sued in civil court for excessive violence while on the job. But in many instances, broader legal protections make it nearly impossible to win these cases.

On the civil end, a practice called qualified immunity shields government officials, including federal law enforcement, from civil lawsuits or lawsuits for money damages unless a previous court decision with similar circumstances resulted in other officials being held accountable.

A 1971 U.S. Supreme Court case established what’s called the Bivens doctrine, which has been one of the few legal avenues for people to sue a federal government official for violating their constitutional rights. But since 2017, the Supreme Court has issued rulings weakening Bivens to the point that it basically no longer exists.

That leaves the Federal Torts Claims Act, which allows individuals to sue the federal government for financial compensation as a result of harms from its employees while carrying out their official duties. In Bowe’s case, she is seeking $500,000 in money damages, according to her claim, viewed by The 19th.

Based on the law, the first step is to file administrative claims against the government, said Yasmin Cader, the ACLU’s Deputy Executive Director for Program, Strategy and Culture. The government then has six months to respond to the claim by settling with the people harmed or denying liability. If the government either ignores or denies the claim, the ACLU can elevate the claims to lawsuits.

The ACLU’s clients in these cases include a woman who was five months into a high-risk pregnancy while being held with her four children at a holding facility for approximately four weeks. “The family was held in a cell with limited access to clean running water and without any windows to the outside,” according to the ACLU press release.

“Almost half of the people are citizens,” Cader said of the ACLU’s clients. “The other half are people who are not citizens, but are nonetheless here in this country and deserving of their constitutional rights. We have racial profiling. We have abuses against people who are exercising their First Amendment rights. We have false and violent arrests. So, it is a wide array of examples of cases.”

Bowe is a grandmother who loves to stay active and kayak, and who has worked in nursing for more than 40 years. Five years ago, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, she teamed up with the Reformed Church in Highland Park, New Jersey, to set up a mobile health clinic in an RV to provide health care services for people who lacked housing or adequate health insurance and immigrants who might be fearful of using traditional health care services.

“It started off, sort of, as a COVID initiative, and it very quickly became way more than that. It’s really a social justice initiative,” Bowe said. “We’re a medical street team. I always call us the gap between the street and the emergency room.”

With support from two community health workers, local medical students and volunteers, Bowe drives her RV clinic to communities in need. They provide blood pressure, diabetes and cancer screenings, and do stroke assessments, basic first aid care, and flu and COVID testing. And, increasingly, they serve as a mental health outlet for people under duress.

Over the last year and a half in particular, Bowe told The 19th that she has seen fear take hold in her community in response to the historic expansion of immigration enforcement.

She said she’s seen how women in particular can be left vulnerable when their husbands and partners are taken into ICE detention or deported, leaving them not only without their loved one, but without the household income they once had. As part of her route, she has stopped at the Delaney Hall detention center a couple times a month to support the loved ones of detainees.

“When people come get their blood pressure, it’s just a very simple thing. It’s an act of care. But then people will talk and cry, and will tell you the story of their loved one, and so we consider that mental health screening,” Bowe said.

She is hopeful that her injuries from Memorial Day will heal and that the ACLU’s legal action will help bring more attention to instances of violence by immigration authorities and some semblance of justice for victims. But at the time of the incident with ICE, she said she could not help but think of the others — both immigrants and U.S. citizens — who have faced violence or death at the hands of federal immigration agents.

“I thought about Alex Pretti because he was a nurse. He was helping someone up off the ground that had been shoved,” Bowe said. “I really could have died. So, that was that day.”

Two days later, she returned to Delaney Hall — scrapes on her face and body — to stare down the ICE agents and continue her work.

text:
Farm workers in the US are reeling from the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigration, including increased raids and deportations, according to a new survey conducted by the United Farm Workers Foundation released on Thursday.

The survey features responses from 2,250 farm workers, many of whom are undocumented, about their experiences with immigration enforcement that has intensified under the second Trump administration.

The vast majority (92%) of farm workers said that raids and deportations have affected their employment, while 90% said they worry about family separation. Fears are widespread and have affected their everyday lives: 61% said they are shopping less and 29% say they are not seeking medical attention for fear of immigration enforcement. Another 17% said they fear having to do forced labor in immigration detention if arrested.

These fears are prevalent despite many respondents being longtime US residents, with 80% workers saying they have been in the US for more than 10 years, while 41% said they have been in the US for more than 20 years.

“When I leave to work, I’m afraid to not come home and to never see my daughters again,” said Yasmine, a farm worker, during a press conference about the survey on Thursday. A mother of two daughters who are US citizens, she said: “We only go out when it’s absolutely necessary, but if we do go out, it’s for necessities like groceries.”

Yasmine, who did not provide her last name, said she has been in the US for more than 20 years and is a Daca recipient, though she is experiencing delays getting her work permits renewed. Her husband is an undocumented immigrant.

“I’ve even had to have conversations with our daughters about what could possibly happen. They’re small and don’t really understand what’s happening, but I try to talk to them and make sure we have a plan,” she said. “The other day was our daughter’s 11th birthday and we couldn’t celebrate it out of fear of going out. Family separation worries me a lot. I don’t know what’s going to happen. I live with stress, uncertainty and fear.”

There are more than 2.6 million farm workers in the US. Most (73%) are Hispanic, 66% are noncitizen immigrants and 47% report lacking work authorization, according to data from the 2022 National Agricultural Workers Survey.

Many hope that the US government can eventually shape up its immigration system, with 76% wanting protections from deportation and detention and 53% expressing hope for a pathway to legal status and US citizenship. Many workers are also unable to visit family in their home countries because of their immigration status, with 87% saying they would be able to visit their families if Congress passed immigration reform that gave them legal status.

Yasmine emphasized having a pathway to citizenship would be life-changing for her family.

“Having a pathway to citizenship would mean a lot for me. It would change a lot for me and my family, and it would make sure that my husband and I could give a better life for our daughters,” she said. “I would finally have stability, something right now I don’t have.”

The UFW Foundation noted that gathering data from undocumented farm workers is difficult, but it drew from its farm worker database to conduct the survey.

“This is the first in-depth study to survey the concerns and fears of undocumented farm workers as well as their hopes and aspirations,” said Erica Lomeli Corcoran, the CEO of the UFW Foundation, in a statement. “We hope this survey will shine a light so those in power can understand the realities faced by those who are the most powerless. Then perhaps undocumented farm workers who produce the greatest abundance of food the world has ever seen will be seen and treated like the important human beings they are.”

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said: “Worksite enforcement remains a cornerstone of our efforts to protect public safety, national security, and economic stability while rescuing individuals who may be victims of labor trafficking or exploitation.”

authors: Peter Hall, Emily Previti, Ian Karbal

Why are these folks being put in a prison setting?” Scanlon asked in an interview Thursday.
The Moshannon Valley center is operated on behalf of ICE by a private company under a contract with Clearfield County.

text:
Nearly one year after she and other members of Pennsylvania’s congressional delegation were turned away, U.S. Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon said she was allowed Wednesday to inspect the largest U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center on the east coast.

Scanlon (D-5th District) told the Capital-Star she spent about four hours inside the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, a former federal prison with nearly 1,900 beds, near Philipsburg, Clearfield County.

The center has been the subject of criticism by immigrant rights advocates and lawmakers who say detainees are subjected to inhumane conditions, lack adequate access to health care and face retaliation for complaints. It was also the site of two deaths last year.

Scanlon said she came away from the visit frustrated that she was not generally permitted to speak to detainees, although she was able to meet with a constituent. She said she’s also concerned that the central Pennsylvania facility appears to function largely using the labor of people involuntarily held there. Detainees can earn $1 a day for working, she said.

“Why are we jailing, essentially, people who are not a danger to our communities, who are in many cases contributing members to our economy and our communities, folks who are employed and are paying taxes? Why are these folks being put in a prison setting?” Scanlon asked in an interview Thursday.

During her visit, officials told her the center housed 1,634 detainees, of whom 1,311 are “low security.” The detainees wear color-coded uniforms and lack liberty to move freely around the facility, she added.

“This is not supposed to be punitive, but it’s pretty hard to say that this is anything but,” Scanlon said.

The Moshannon Valley center is operated on behalf of ICE by a private company under a contract with Clearfield County. That allows ICE to skirt a Biden-era ban on new federal contracts with private prison companies. The county pays for-profit prison operator The GEO Group to run the center.

ICE did not respond to an email seeking comment.

The GEO Group is an international provider of correctional services that runs about 100 facilities globally, with a capacity of more than 80,000 beds. According to the American Civil Liberties Union, more than a quarter of GEO Group’s capacity is used by ICE.

Under a 2019 federal law, members of Congress are authorized to inspect ICE facilities without prior notice. At the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, the agency began turning away lawmakers at facilities across the country. Scanlon and U.S. Rep. Summer Lee (D-12th District) were prevented from inspecting the facility last August.

Since then, a group of lawmakers sued ICE over the policy, asking the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to order the Trump administration to explain how it did not violate federal law. The court issued an order in December, affirming the authority of Congress members to conduct oversight of ICE facilities.

Lee and U.S. Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-17th District) were first to visit Moshannon Valley in May.

Scanlon said Thursday that she was permitted to enter the women’s pods in the center but not the men’s, which she was able to see through glass. Scanlon said she was able to speak to a person from her suburban and south Philadelphia district but declined to discuss details to protect the person from retaliation. Other inmates were not permitted to speak to her, she said.

“It makes it difficult to … follow up on issues about food and medical care if you can’t talk to people who are impacted,” Scanlon said.

It was clear, she said, that the detainees are responsible for cleaning toilets, showers and living spaces.

“There are two janitors for the entire facility of 1,600 people, and then they showed me that they have like just a row of like five spray bottles of cleaning spray in each pod, and oh, it’s there for the detainees to use, and they like doing it,” Scanlon said. “I guess the alternative is squalor.”

She said an administrator at the center conceded that they could not run the food service or laundry without using detainee labor.

“So we have the situation where people are being jailed and then forced to work essentially for free to maintain basic sanitation, food, etc,” Scanlon said, adding “It’s inhumane. It’s traumatizing, and it’s particularly grotesque because this is then being done so private prison companies can make more profit.”

Under the contract, ICE pays Clearfield County more than $4 million a month plus additional considerations for transportation, on-call staff and $1 a day per detainee for the employee work program.

Scanlon said the oversight by Congress is important because she believes “we’re not getting straight scoop” from the Trump administration.

“The administration said they were going after the worst of the worst, and the people they are scooping up, and we’re seeing this increasingly are people on the way to work, or to school, or their court appointments to pursue their legal path,” she said.

With appropriations of $145 billion in the last two years, Scanlon said ICE is spending “outrageous amounts” detaining people who are not a threat to public safety.

“We would be much better off if we were actually spending money to create a functioning immigration system,” Scanlon said, adding, “We don’t have that now, and it’s a misdirection of money just to put out these quotas and scoop up people, many of whom have legal status.”

text:
‘Electronic shackle’ placed on released Chinese asylum seeker

Wu Shaoping released from immigration detention while he waits for his case to go before a judge.

Jordan Wilkie/WITF

As the democracy reporter for WITF, I will cover any kind of story that has to do with how we govern ourselves. That will include doing a lot of election coverage about how to access the ballot, how public officials administer elections, the technology used to run and secure elections, and the laws that govern it all.

My work will also include accountability coverage for elected officials that use their positions to then undermine democratic institutions, like the legislators that voted against the certification of the presidential election results on January 6, 2021. If that weren’t enough, I foresee covering some local government decisions, fights over public records and transparency, and some candidate coverage around the major elections. As seen in my coverage of immigrant of LGBTQ+ communities, I also report on the consequences of elections for minority groups.

Freed from immigration detention, Chinese human rights lawyer Wu Shaoping is now being tracked with an ankle monitor.

In China, Wu said, “we call it an electronic shackle.”

“I’m afraid to go outside,” he said in an interview with WITF this week, referring to the stigma of wearing the device. Wu, who does not have a criminal record, said he’s worried someone would see it and mistake him for someone who has committed a crime. He said he has a work permit, but he now needs permission to leave the state.

“I don’t want to escape,” Wu said, and pointed to his house in Lancaster County where he lives with his wife and child. Wu, 48, is in the United States to flee persecution of human rights lawyers and activists in China, according to reporting from local newspaper LNP, which has closely followed his case.

“Now, I can’t get freedom,” he said.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said entered the country on a visa which expired after six months on June 29, 2020. Wu applied for asylum.

“Pending applications do NOT confer legal status,” ICE wrote in an unattributed statement to WITF, which referred to Wu as “an illegal alien from China.”

ICE did not answer questions about why Wu was required to wear a GPS tracking device or where the policy has changed under President Donald Trump’s second administration.

Spotlight on local law enforcement cooperation

Mt. Holly Springs police pulled Wu over for a stop sign violation on July 15, according to court records. The police department signed an agreement with ICE in February that gives them “limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties,” according to ICE information.

They arrested Wu and delivered him to ICE. They detained him in the Moshannon Valley detention center for two weeks before his lawyers and pressure from an international array of advocates won his release.

“It is a single incident that’s very striking because he’s a civil rights activist from a communist authoritarian country, which we used to prioritize for immigrants,” said Perry Hazeltine.

He’s a member of Solidarity Lancaster, an activist group established after Trump’s reelection that opposes cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE. For months, the group has been organizing to persuade Lancaster’s sheriff and district attorney to end their own ICE agreements, which are ongoing.

Wu’s case was “perfect timing, in a way,” Hazeltine said.

“I hate to say it like that, but I’m sure he would be glad to have his situation make people aware of the way in which he and others are being, essentially, incarcerated,” Hazeltine said.

The case has drawn international attention from Chinese dissidents and advocacy groups who say deporting Wu could put him in danger and would violate international laws meant to protect people fleeing persecution.

text:
The woman facing the first-ever case in the Alien Terrorist Removal Court is challenging the constitutionality of the deportation tribunal, setting up a major test of the Trump administration’s decision to activate the court, which had never been used in its 30-year history.

Lawyers for Nazira Haji Zada — a legal permanent resident from Afghanistan who is accused of having ISIS sympathies and of assisting her son in a thwarted terror plot that targeted the 2024 Election — said during an initial hearing Thursday that the court’s procedure’s run afoul of several amendments of the Constitution.

“This entire scheme is in violation of due process and is unconstitutional,” said Matthew Farley, a federal public defender who has been appointed to represent Haji Zada.

Their arguments could set up months, if not years, of litigation over the court’s constitutionality, a question that could ultimately travel to the Supreme Court.

Judge Joan Ericksen, the chief judge of the court, who is presiding over the case, denied a request that Haji Zada be immediately released. But she said those constitutional issues will be briefed alongside other legal disputes that have already arisen in the novel case.

Congress created the court in 1996 as a way for the government to protect state secrets in deportation cases where the disclosure of its evidence against an alleged alien terrorist risked national security. (Alien terrorist is a term defined in immigration law).

Until the Justice Department’s decision to file the case against the woman earlier this month, however, prior administrations avoided using the court, relying instead on the procedures in normal deportation proceedings for handling classified information.

The filings that have been made public in the case against Haji Zada give a very limited view of why the government thinks she is terrorist and why it believes disclosing that evidence would imperil national security. The court’s procedures allow for the government to withhold that evidence not just from the public, but from the accused alien terrorist herself.

Farley called those procedures “woefully inadequate” and noted that the unclassified summary of the case that has been given to Haji Zada was just two paragraphs — and that one of them just described the prior convictions of her son and son-in-law for the terror plot.

Last summer, the men — Abdullah Haji Zada and Nasir Ahmad Tawhed — pleaded guilty to charges accusing them of purchasing rifles and ammunition for a plotted terrorist attack for Election Day in 2024. Prosecutors alleged in court Thursday that the alien court defendant, Nazira Haji Zada, had helped to “radicalize the family.”

Battles over secrecy

Ericksen signaled she planned to examine closely the government’s justification for keeping evidence hidden from Haji Zada and the public. The judge said a blanket explanation would not suffice, that for each piece of information that the Justice Department can’t disclose, she will want “a reason and rationale for why disclosure of that information would be detrimental to national security.”

The 45-minute hearing — the first public hearing ever before a court, after a sealed proceeding with just the Justice Department and the judge earlier this month — was aimed at explaining to the alleged alien terrorist the general allegations against her and some of the court’s procedures. Haji Zada was arrested Tuesday in Texas, where she lives. She relied on two translators, communicating mostly with head nods affirming she understood what was being said.

Beyond the constitutional claims her lawyers said they were raising, a dispute is already emerging around the sharing of classified information in the case. The law entitles Haji Zada, as a legal permanent resident, a special attorney who can view classified evidence and interrogate it on her behalf — but not share that information with her. However, Acting Deputy Assistant Attorney General Hayden O’Byrne, representing the DOJ at the hearing, said that another provision of the law allows for the government to withhold certain classified information from that special attorney as well.

Ericksen said the issue will be briefed in writing and that she would need “pretty strong” arguments from DOJ for its position.

The judge acknowledged that since this was the first case in a court that was “dormant and untested for three decades,” it was still in the “early stages of implementing an infrastructure.” Both the judge and the lawyers shuffled through paper copies of the relevant statute throughout the hearing, and some of the proceedings dealt with logistics of filing court submissions, in the absence of a digital court filing system, which is in the process of being set up.

There might be moments that appear “less elegant,” the judge said, while expressing a commitment to moving forward with the case with “fealty to the constitution.”

“A mother getting her children into car seats to go to a doctor’s appointment is just ripped away from her children,” she said.
“Why would ICE violate its own rules just to target a nursing mother who has followed all the legal steps of the immigration system?” Nora Ahmed, legal director for the ACLU of Louisiana, said in a statement.

text:
A nursing mother and Guatemalan asylum-seeker who was preparing to take her two young children to the doctor was arrested by ICE in Tennessee and is now being detained nearly 700 miles away from her family, according to advocacy groups who filed a civil rights complaint on her behalf.

The woman, who is referred to by the pseudonym Maria Perez, fled “extreme domestic violence” in Guatemala and was seeking asylum in the U.S. when she was arrested in Nashville in May, said Katie Blankenship, the founder and managing attorney of Sanctuary of the South, an immigration and LGBTQ civil rights cooperative. Perez is using a pseudonym out of fear of immigration retaliation.

Perez has a 10-month-old baby, whom she had been nursing when she was arrested, and a 2-year-old with Down syndrome. She does not have a criminal history, advocates said.

“A mother getting her children into car seats to go to a doctor’s appointment is just ripped away from her children,” she said. “It’s just living an absolute nightmare. It’s a mother’s worst fear.”

The advocacy group, along with the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition, filed a complaint calling for Perez’s immediate release with the DHS Office of the Inspector General and other agencies on Wednesday. The complaint is supported by the ACLU of Louisiana, the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and Amnesty International.

Since Perez’s detention, “her daughters have been in the care of a neighbor, as the family has no other support network in the area,” according to the complaint.

DHS did not respond to a request for comment.

The civil rights complaint said Perez was detained in violation of a policy directive that says ICE should not detain or arrest people who are known to be pregnant, postpartum or nursing unless there are exceptional circumstances, such as that they are national security risks or pose a danger.

“ICE and DHS continue to show blatant disregard not just for their own policies but for basic humanity,” Spring Miller, the senior director of legal strategy at the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition, said in a statement.

The Trump administration has not revoked the policy, but advocates have said that as arrests and detention have surged overall, they have seen an increase in the number of pregnant, nursing and postpartum women in detention facilities.

On May 19, ICE agents arrived at Perez’s home seeking the father of her children, who is separately facing federal charges, according to the complaint.

Perez “was not named in any warrant and was not the subject of the enforcement action, but was nonetheless taken into ICE custody while putting her daughters in the car and preparing to go to a medical appointment,” the complaint said.

She was taken into custody in Tennessee, before being transferred days later to the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana, a jurisdiction that does not allow bond for people who entered the country illegally, Blankenship said.

Perez’s attorneys have also filed a request for humanitarian parole and a federal habeas petition calling for her release, she said.

“Why would ICE violate its own rules just to target a nursing mother who has followed all the legal steps of the immigration system?” Nora Ahmed, legal director for the ACLU of Louisiana, said in a statement. “ICE has destroyed a family in the process and is directly responsible for putting children’s lives at risk.”

text:
For audio listeners, you can listen to our audio version of the News Digest here. You can also join our Immigration News Digest Newsletter here.

DHS Rule Allows Certain Asylum Cases to Move Directly to Immigration Court

USCIS Extends Automatic Work Authorization for Certain Burma TPS Beneficiaries

USCIS Extends TPS Work Authorization for Syria and Somalia

USCIS Extends Haiti TPS Work Authorization Through July 27

DHS Rule Allows Certain Asylum Cases to Move Directly to Immigration Court

The Department of Homeland Security has issued a final rule that allows USCIS asylum officers to bypass asylum interviews in certain cases and instead refer applicants directly to immigration court. The change is intended to streamline the asylum process by expediting cases where an officer determines an applicant is barred from asylum, is statutorily ineligible, or does not merit asylum as a matter of discretion.

Under the new rule, asylum officers will retain authority to conduct interviews in eligible cases but may forgo that step when they conclude an application cannot be approved based on the information available. Individuals whose cases are referred to immigration court will have the opportunity to present their claims before an immigration judge, who will make the final determination on eligibility for asylum and any other available forms of relief.

DHS stated that the rule is designed to improve efficiency, reduce case backlogs, and direct agency resources toward applications that require full asylum interviews. The change is part of the administration’s broader effort to accelerate immigration proceedings and increase enforcement efficiency.

Impact: The new rule may shorten processing times for some asylum cases by moving certain applications more quickly into immigration court proceedings. Employers and individuals working with asylum applicants should be aware that eligible cases could reach removal proceedings sooner, making timely legal guidance and case preparation increasingly important.

USCIS Extends Automatic Work Authorization for Certain Burma TPS Beneficiaries

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has announced a brief extension of employment authorization for certain Temporary Protected Status beneficiaries from Burma (Myanmar). Eligible Employment Authorization Documents will now remain valid through August 3, 2026, providing temporary continuity of work authorization while related litigation and court orders remain in effect.

The extension applies automatically to TPS-related EADs bearing original expiration dates of November 25, 2022, May 25, 2024, or November 25, 2025. The previous automatic extension was scheduled to expire before USCIS issued this latest notice.

The agency’s action follows ongoing litigation challenging the termination of Burma’s TPS designation and recent court decisions affecting TPS-related employment authorization. It also reflects USCIS’s obligation to comply with a July 21 federal court order concerning automatic EAD extensions for certain TPS beneficiaries who timely filed renewal applications before October 30, 2025.

USCIS has indicated that the extension is temporary, and additional guidance may be issued as court proceedings continue.

Impact: The short-term extension helps prevent immediate employment authorization interruptions for eligible Burma TPS beneficiaries and their employers. Because the extension is only in effect through August 3, 2026, employers should continue monitoring USCIS announcements and verify work authorization requirements as additional court decisions and agency guidance become available.

USCIS Extends TPS Work Authorization for Syria and Somalia

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has announced additional short-term extensions of employment authorization for certain Temporary Protected Status beneficiaries from Syria and Somalia. Eligible Employment Authorization Documents issued under the TPS designations for Syria are now valid through July 27, 2026, while eligible Somalia TPS EADs are extended through July 29, 2026.

The extensions apply automatically to qualifying beneficiaries whose EADs bear specific original expiration dates. For Syria, the extension covers EADs originally expiring on March 31, 2021; September 30, 2022; March 31, 2024; and September 30, 2025. For Somalia, eligible EADs are those with original expiration dates of March 17, 2023; September 17, 2024; and March 17, 2026.

USCIS stated that the temporary extensions are necessary while litigation involving TPS designations continues. The agency is also complying with a recent federal court order concerning automatic EAD extensions for certain TPS beneficiaries who timely filed renewal applications before October 30, 2025.

The agency has indicated these are temporary measures, and additional updates may be issued as court proceedings continue.

Impact: The brief extensions help avoid immediate disruptions in employment authorization for eligible TPS beneficiaries from Syria and Somalia. Employers should continue monitoring USCIS announcements and verify work authorization documentation, as additional court decisions or agency guidance could result in further changes over the coming weeks.

USCIS Extends Haiti TPS Work Authorization Through July 27

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has announced another short-term extension of employment authorization for certain Temporary Protected Status beneficiaries from Haiti. Eligible Employment Authorization Documents will now remain valid through July 27, 2026, providing continued work authorization while litigation surrounding the termination of Haiti’s TPS designation continues.

The extension applies automatically to eligible TPS beneficiaries whose EADs bear one of several specified original expiration dates, including July 22, 2017, January 22, 2018, July 22, 2019, January 2, 2020, January 4, 2021, October 4, 2021, December 31, 2022, February 3, 2023, June 30, 2024, August 3, 2024, August 3, 2025, and February 3, 2026.

USCIS has issued a series of brief automatic extensions following the U.S. Supreme Court’s June 25, 2026 decision permitting the Department of Homeland Security to move forward with plans to terminate TPS for Haiti and Syria. The agency stated that the temporary extensions are intended to preserve employment authorization while the courts complete the legal process following the Supreme Court’s ruling. USCIS has indicated that additional updates may be issued as litigation progresses.

Impact: The latest extension helps prevent immediate interruptions to employment authorization for eligible Haiti TPS beneficiaries and provides employers with short-term certainty while the legal process continues. Because the extension is temporary, employers and affected individuals should closely monitor future USCIS announcements for additional guidance or changes to work authorization eligibility.

Appeals Court Leaves District Court Decision Vacating $100,000 H-1B Fee in Place

A federal appeals court has declined to stay a district court ruling that invalidated the $100,000 supplemental fee previously imposed on certain H-1B petitions. The First Circuit concluded that the government had not demonstrated it was likely to succeed on appeal, allowing the lower court’s decision to remain in effect while the litigation continues.

As a result, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services is currently prohibited from collecting the $100,000 fee on affected H-1B petitions. The fee had applied to certain petitions filed for beneficiaries requiring consular notification or that otherwise could not be approved through a change or extension of status.

USCIS is expected to issue updated filing guidance and instructions reflecting the court’s decision. It remains unclear how the agency will address petitions for which the supplemental fee has already been paid, and further guidance may be issued in the coming days.

Although the fee is no longer enforceable at this time, the Trump administration is expected to continue appealing the district court’s ruling. Until the litigation is resolved, the legal status of the supplemental fee remains subject to future court decisions.

title: ICE arrests linked to airports rose under Trump - KCRA
description:
The arrests have focused on people with expired visas and have occurred in at least 15 airports, they reported.
That’s more than five times the 108 arrests linked to airports in the same time frame leading up to Trump’s second administration.

text:
WASHINGTON —

During President Donald Trump's second administration, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has ramped up operations in major cities across the country, targeting places like schools and neighborhoods. The latest enforcement operations garnering public attention have been at airports.

Earlier this week, the New York Times reported a rise in arrests at U.S. airports documented by immigration attorneys and documents the publication obtained. The arrests have focused on people with expired visas and have occurred in at least 15 airports, they reported.

The Get the Facts Data Team analyzed data from the Deportation Data Project and found an increase in arrests where the data indicated a connection with airports. That connection was an airport listed as the arrest site landmark or marked as a "current duty site."

From Trump’s inauguration day, Jan. 20, 2025, to March 10, 2026, there were 568 arrests made by ICE where the agency indicated the arrest was at or near an airport, our Data Team's analysis found. That’s more than five times the 108 arrests linked to airports in the same time frame leading up to Trump’s second administration.

The Deportation Data Project obtained and then processed the government data via a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit. The latest data was released at the end of March and included arrests through March 10 of this year.

While some arrests by ICE are linked to airports within the data, it isn't a complete or perfect snapshot. Data from Trump's inauguration through March 2026 includes just 16 airports, 10 of which had fewer than 10 arrests reported.

Chicago O'Hare International Airport was named 220 times from the time Trump took office to March of this year in the data — a large increase from five arrests it was linked to in the same time period leading up to his inauguration.

Of the 108 arrests identified that were linked to airports in the time period leading up to Trump's second administration, more than half were at the Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in Puerto Rico.

Reuters reported earlier this year that an internal document showed more than 800 people had been arrested by ICE following tips from TSA, which shared its data on over 31,000 people traveling.

On Tuesday, American Oversight, a nonprofit watchdog organization, released a document acquired via the Freedom of Information Act. The document revealed a data-sharing agreement between TSA and ICE from May 2025.

ICE did not respond to our request for comment about enforcement operations at airports.

The arrests of people with expired visas are a way for the agency to increase its arrests since they already are on the government's radar for things like having a pending application, according to Colleen Putzel-Kavanaugh, an associate policy analyst for the Migration Policy Institute.

"So it's an effort to increase arrest numbers as opposed to sort of the larger narrative that ICE is after the 'worst of the worst,'" Putzel-Kavanaugh said.

But for people with a pending application, it wasn't always an issue in the past when they were traveling domestically, Putzel-Kavanaugh said.

Immigration enforcement has ramped up under Trump's second administration. A previous analysis from the most recent data released by the Deportation Data Project through March found that the average daily number of ICE arrests has more than tripled since Trump took office in January 2025, compared to the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.

The number of arrests made by ICE has surged under Trump’s second administration, but declined following the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers during the administration’s ICE operations in Minneapolis.

title: After Biddeford shooting, Mainers turn anger toward ICE facility in Scarborough
description:
SCARBOROUGH — The eyes of the country are on Scarborough, residents warned town councilors Wednesday night.
“People who get detained in Portland are taken to the Scarborough facility,” Portland resident Lou James-Olson said.
She said she would have reconsidered living in Scarborough if she had known earlier about the ICE facility, because of the way that she looks.
But outside of Scarborough Town Hall, residents turned their anger into action, their grief into determination.
Still, many were unsure about what power the Town Council had to get ICE out of Scarborough.
text:
SCARBOROUGH — The eyes of the country are on Scarborough, residents warned town councilors Wednesday night.

In turn, councilors unanimously approved a proclamation calling on Maine’s congressional delegation to investigate the Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in town.

Scarborough is home to the state’s only ICE processing facility — which has faced increased scrutiny and protest after an ICE agent identified as David Brouillette shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford on the morning of July 13.

For many of the more than 100 residents at the council meeting, the actions of the federal agency that’s housed in their town reflect on them.

They felt ashamed and embarrassed, sad and angry, they said.

“This is not the Scarborough I grew up in,” multiple people said.

Many Scarborough residents — and the dozens of others from nearby communities who rallied in the rain outside Town Hall before the meeting with “ICE out” signs — said they knew someone whose life had been upended by ICE.

At the meeting, they spoke of coworkers who suddenly stopped coming to work out of fear of being detained or because they had been taken into custody. Children who went hungry because they relied on school for meals but were too afraid to leave home. Pregnant women whose partners were taken by ICE just weeks before they were due to give birth, and who worried what would happen to their children if they had a medical emergency. Families too scared to attend their loved one’s funeral because the cemetery wasn’t safe for them.

“Most of you can go to the beach,” said Mufalo Chitam, executive director of the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition. “They can’t.”

In Biddeford, she said immigrant children are afraid to leave home.

“Most of you have been with us since the 13th,” Chitam said, thanking the community for their support. “We haven’t slept. We haven’t slept.”

After the rally outside Town Hall, the group filtered into the meeting room at 6 p.m., their raincoats and hair dripping from the rain. The line for public comment snaked across the room, and the meeting — which was scheduled to last an hour and had only one item on the agenda — ended around 8:15 p.m.

The meeting concluded with an unusual unanimous vote. The Scarborough Town Council passed the proclamation, which called for increased transparency and accountability of federal immigration enforcement activities and the evaluation of alternative uses of the ICE building at 40 Manson Libby Road, including the discontinuation or relocation of ICE operations.

“This has brought the conversation to our front door, whether we invited it or not,” Councilor Jon Anderson said.

Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat representing Maine’s 1st Congressional District, sent the council a letter in support of the proclamation ahead of the meeting.

“The facility at 40 Manson Libby Road has become a symbol of fear, uncertainty, and intimidation for many immigrant families and their neighbors,” she wrote. “That should concern every one of us.”

But for most attendees, the proclamation wasn’t nearly enough.

A few days before, a petition began circulating online asking for the town to take three actions: pass an ordinance to limit the town’s engagement with federal immigration agents, order an investigation of the ICE facility and document ICE’s local impact. It had been signed by 375 people by Wednesday, petition organizers said.

Councilors agreed the proclamation should just be a first step.

“We’re going to pass this tonight, and we’re not going away,” Councilor Bill Donovan said. “We’re with you.”

COMMUNITY REACTION

The rally drew people from across southern Maine.

“People who get detained in Portland are taken to the Scarborough facility,” Portland resident Lou James-Olson said. “It affects our communities directly, even you don’t live in Scarborough.”

Many of the community members gathered outside wore masks or other face coverings. Fearing retaliation or doxing, they hesitated to share their names with the Portland Press Herald. One person even wore a body camera.

For Yoshimi Hooten-Ng, a new Scarborough resident, the issue is personal. She said she would have reconsidered living in Scarborough if she had known earlier about the ICE facility, because of the way that she looks.

“It’s hard not to give into despair,” Jessica Laracy said, standing next to Hooten-Ng.

In the wake of the shooting just 10 miles down Route 1 from Scarborough, many communities have grappled with feelings of helplessness and impuissance. What power does an individual or a town have against a federal agency?

But outside of Scarborough Town Hall, residents turned their anger into action, their grief into determination.

Democracy is hard work, Laracy and Hooten-Ng agreed, but it beats sitting on the couch feeling hopeless.

“Apathy got us to this point,” Rick Olson added.

Standing together, they felt power, solidarity and hope. Change begins at the local level. It begins with communities joining together, people looking out for their neighbors, constituents demanding accountability, residents said.

Still, many were unsure about what power the Town Council had to get ICE out of Scarborough.

Josh Soley, the leasing and property manager for the facility at 40 Manson Libby Road, said the U.S. General Services Administration leases the facility from owner AEY LLC, and it can choose to sublet to any agency. The lease began in 2019 and lasts 15 years.

The GSA serves as the landlord for federal government agencies, it would have to make the decision to swap tenants, Soley said.

But the residents of Scarborough aren’t letting the town off the hook.

“They should do everything in their power to make ICE feel unwelcome,” Matthew Arbor said, flying an upside down American flag.

“We appreciate the Town Council speaking through a proclamation,” the petition asking the town to take further action reads. “But a proclamation cannot be the end of Scarborough’s response.”

During the meeting’s public comment, community members poured out their fears, their rage, their sorrow.

“Our communities are under attack,” a resident said.

“This is an abomination,” another said.

The ICE facility is a danger to the town, multiple residents said. They’re worried about ICE violating their right to due process.

“Many of us are afraid because if you get shot, you don’t really get a chance to pull out your passport,” said Alex, a resident.

“This could have happened to any one of us,” another community member said. “It did happen to one of us.”

Even if Scarborough takes every lawful action it can, the town can’t guarantee it will result in ICE’s relocation, Anderson said. But Scarborough will try.

“Real accountability often comes from residents who stay involved, showing up, voting and speaking out,” Anderson said. “Tonight is just the start of a difficult conversation.”

text:
EDDYVILLE, N.Y. — Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials chased two people on Creeklocks Road who “jumped down an embankment,” town of Ulster police said on Thursday.

At 9:12 a.m., on Thursday, the town of Ulster Police Department and state troopers responded to a 911 call alerting officers of a potential injury in the case of two subjects who “jumped down an embankment while being chased by Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agents,” Ulster Police Chief Kyle Berardi said.

According to Ulster Rapid Response, an organization dedicated to tracking ICE activities in the county, at least one individual was apprehended by ICE and removed from the community.

Upon arriving at the scene, town of Ulster and state police provided scene safety and searched for injured parties, Berardi said. After failing to locate any suspects, both agencies left and returned to service, leaving federal agents to continue their investigation, both agencies said.

ICE agents along with Enforcement and Removal Operations agents, an operational directorate of ICE, were present at the scene, Ulster Rapid Response said. The organization said that four vehicles were present, a black Ford Explorer, a white Jeep, a grey Hyundai and a black Dodge Ram, all with New York plates. Ulster Rapid Response said that no further ICE activity was reported, and its members left the scene at 11 a.m.

The immigrant defense group advises anyone who suspects ICE activity to call its hotline at (845) 293-3423, according to its website.

Vehicles from Ulster County Sheriff’s Office could also be seen leaving the scene around 10 a.m. The Ulster County Sheriff’s Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Local police organizations are not allowed to collaborate with ICE. The Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, signed into law by Governor Kathy Hochul in May, bars local governments and law enforcement agencies from entering into any 287(g) agreement, a legal partnership where local governments give ICE access to manpower, information and individuals held in detention. 287(g) agreements often come with increased federal funding.

While 12 police departments statewide have continued to cooperate with ICE—a fact now facing scrutiny from the state Attorney General—all mid-Hudson law enforcement agencies comply with state law.

In photos provided to the Freeman, several masked officers can be seen alongside state trooper vehicles.

It is unclear whether the two suspects were detained by ICE, are still at large, or if they were injured.

ICE did not immediately respond to a Freeman inquiry.

In April, Ulster County’s Democratic lawmakers pushed through a policy governing interactions between county employees and ICE agents. The policy, which codifies an executive order signed by former County Executive Pat Ryan and a policy adopted by Sheriff Juan Figueroa in 2019, passed the county Legislature in a 19-4 vote.

The policy prohibits the use of county property as staging areas for federal immigration enforcement activities, prohibits county employees from sharing non-public personal information for immigration enforcement unless required by law, and directs county officials to cease asking individuals about their immigration status unless the information is required by law or necessary to determine eligibility for a service or program and requires federal authorities to present a judicial warrant signed by a federal judge to access non-public areas of county facilities.

text:
Washington, D.C. (July 30, 2026)—Today, Rep. Jamie Raskin, Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, and Rep. Pramila Jayapal, Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, sent a letter demanding that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) immediately equip all agents interacting with the public with fully functional body-worn cameras. The demand follows a disturbing pattern of deadly immigration enforcement operations carried out without basic accountability measures in place.

“We have watched in horror as Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials shot over two dozen people and killed six of them, including three U.S. citizens, during immigration enforcement operations since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025.1 In shooting after shooting, we are told that there is no body-worn camera footage of the incident and asked to accept DHS’s account of the incident. Time and again, that account turns out to be a blatant falsehood. It is time for DHS to use the $210 billion that congressional Republicans have given the agency to ensure that every DHS officer is equipped with a fully functioning body-worn camera when conducting immigration enforcement,” wrote the Ranking Members.

Despite repeated DHS promises, body-worn cameras remain absent—or nonfunctional—when they matter most. After ICE agents killed U.S. citizens Renée Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis earlier this year, DHS pledged rapid nationwide deployment. Nearly six months later, that promise remains unmet.

The consequences have been deadly. Earlier this month, ICE officers fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas without body camera footage. Days later, officers killed Johan Sebastian Guerrero in Maine while wearing cameras that were not functioning. In both cases, the public was left to rely solely on DHS’s account—despite its documented record of false and misleading statements about these incidents.

DHS has repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims about victims, including Renée Good, Alex Pretti, Ruben Ray Martinez, and Marimar Martinez—falsely alleging they attacked officers. In case after case, evidence has contradicted these claims, further eroding DHS’s credibility.

Body-worn cameras are a basic accountability tool used by state and local law enforcement nationwide. They protect officers, safeguard the public, and provide essential transparency for courts and Congress. Yet under the Trump Administration, federal immigration enforcement continues to operate without this standard safeguard.

Congress has already provided DHS with more than $210 billion for immigration enforcement in the last year and a half, including $20 million specifically for body-worn cameras. Even Republican lawmakers have urged deployment, but House Judiciary Republicans recently rejected an amendment requiring their use.

Ranking Members Raskin and Jayapal are demanding every agent who interacts with the public be equipped with fully functional body-worn cameras.

text:
Pennsylvania’s top election official, a Republican, rebuffed the Trump administration’s claim that nearly 15,000 noncitizens could be registered to vote in the commonwealth, demanding it explain how that estimate was calculated.

In a letter sent Thursday, Pennsylvania Secretary of State Al Schmidt (R) asked Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin, to show the department’s work. Without that, Schmidt said, he wouldn’t take any steps that might remove eligible voters or compromise the privacy of Pennsylvanians.

“In order to evaluate the claims in your letter and determine appropriate next steps, please provide a document explaining your methodology, which identifies the data sources you relied on (including all sources of data that connect the personal identifying information of an individual with their Pennsylvania voter record), the date you obtained any Pennsylvania voter registration records, and any other relevant information you utilized to reach your conclusions,” Schmidt wrote.

After President Donald Trump reaired debunked grievances over the 2020 election in a prime time national address earlier this month, DHS notified Pennsylvania that a “preliminary review” of publicly available registration records identified 14,576 potential noncitizens on the voter rolls.

But, as Schdmit wrote in response, “[n]otably, DHS has not identified its methodology or what data it relied on in reaching this conclusion.” Schmidt then highlighted the reasons why his office might not trust DHS’s arithmetic.

“As you know, past analyses of voter lists have relied on faulty methodologies that can lead to inaccurate results and false claims about the citizenship status of eligible voters. DHS has previously acknowledged that its SAVE database may not return accurate information about individuals whose citizenship status has not been updated in the records of the Social Security Administration,” Schmidt wrote. “An audit by SSA’s Office of Inspector General identified numerous errors in those records, and recent reporting has demonstrated that SAVE has mistakenly flagged eligible voters as noncitizens in Texas and Missouri.

“In fact, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services official who oversees SAVE has ‘acknowledged that the system can’t always find the most current citizenship information for people not born in the U.S.’” he added. “Finally, as you are aware, a federal judge has recently concluded that the establishment of the modified SAVE system was unlawful in several respects.”

After Trump’s speech, Mullin claimed that DHS identified 250,000 noncitizens registered across Pennsylvania, Nevada, California, and New Jersey. But he didn’t explain how DHS derived that total or allege that any of the people flagged had actually voted. However, Mullin did threaten states that refused to cooperate with the administration’s voter roll campaign, suggesting election officials could face fines, penalties or even prison if noncitizens cast ballots in upcoming elections.

text:
State officials are pushing back on the Department of Homeland Security’s claims that it found tens of thousands of noncitizens on their voter rolls, asking the department to explain how it arrived at its conclusion.

Ahead of President Donald Trump’s primetime speech from the White House earlier this month in which he made sweeping claims of voter fraud, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote to officials in Nevada, Pennsylvania, California and New Jersey, saying he believed the four states had more than 250,000 noncitizens on the voter rolls combined. During a news conference the day after Trump’s speech, Mullin threatened officials with potential prison time if they do not “secure their elections.”

Ahead of Mullin’s requested two-week deadline for response, officials in California, Nevada and Pennsylvania sent back letters questioning where DHS got its data. All three states have declined to share private state voter roll data that includes personal identifying information like Social Security numbers.

“The American public deserves transparency in how their private information is being used at the federal level,” Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat, said in an interview Thursday. “I don’t believe the federal government is being honest with the American people.”

“They’re gathering private information about citizens, but they’re not explaining how they’re doing it, and it may not be accurate. And to classify somebody as not able to exercise their constitutional fundamental rights is a real harm,” Aguilar added.

In separate letters to Mullin dated Wednesday, Aguilar and Pennsylvania Secretary of State Al Schmidt, a Republican, questioned how the federal government arrived at its conclusions without the unredacted voter rolls that the Justice Department has sued each state to obtain.

“How did your department match social security numbers to Nevada registrants and what data sources did you use if not the voter information provided by” the secretary of state, Aguilar wrote in his letter.

“As you know, past analyses of voter lists have relied on faulty methodologies that can lead to inaccurate results and false claims about the citizenship status of eligible voters,” Schmidt wrote. “Please provide a document explaining your methodology, which identifies the data sources you relied on.”

DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the new responses from state officials.

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, asked Mullin in a July 23 letter to share the information of anyone who gave the federal government private voter data, as it is a crime under state law.

“I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official. Indeed, state law prohibits sharing voters’ sensitive information, including social security numbers, with any person, including the federal government,” Weber wrote.

Weber asked for details on the federal government’s analysis, including data sources and whether artificial intelligence was used.

Noncitizen voting is illegal and rare. Sometimes, noncitizens do end up on states’ voter rolls, but, historically, few have attempted to cast a ballot.

Days after Trump’s speech, Gov. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey, the fourth state singled out by the Trump administration, announced that officials had uncovered a Motor Vehicle Commission error that led to around 6,600 self-identified noncitizens being registered to vote and that roughly 400 cast ballots between 2023 and 2024. The number of noncitizens that New Jersey found on its voter rolls fell short of the 35,000 that DHS claimed.

The Trump administration later asked New Jersey to hand over details on the registrants, but Sherrill said in a letter that the state would not share that information with the federal government.

“DOJ will get this information through all legal means!” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon responded in a post on X on Tuesday.

Sherrill’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

BRUSSELS | 30 July 2026 (IDN | EEPA) — The following are the situation reports on Sudan, Ethiopia, RSF troops raid towns in North Kordofan, Renewed clashes along Oromia-Sidama border and Over 117,350 migrants deported from Libya.

Situation in Sudan (per 30 July)

Rapid Support Forces (RSF) soldiers raided the towns of Um Badr, Sodari, Abu Zaima, Hamrat al-Sheikh, and El Mazroub while retreating from Um Sayala, Jabrat al-Sheikh, and Bara in North Kordofan on 29 July. The RSF also arrested citizens accusing them of working with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF).

SAF drones targeted RSF convoys in Sodari, Um Badr, and El Mazroub in North Kordofan on 29 July, supporting an advance by the SAF toward Sodari to reopen the desert route toward the Darfur region.

Numerous civilians were killed in air strikes hitting locations across North Kordofan State on 28 July.

Rights groups allege the RSF carried out widespread civilian attacks and looting in Al-Jamama, North Kordofan, leaving dozens injured, families displaced, and markets destroyed.

Boeing 727s linked to a US military contractor’s business network have been confirmed to have transported mercenaries, weapons and drones for the RSF, according to UN experts.

RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo “Hemedti” said field commanders now have autonomy to initiate offensives without central orders, and prohibited filming during military operations.

Over 23 children have been killed in North Kordofan since late May according to UNICEF.

The RSF systematically looted medical facilities in the Jabrat al-Sheikh area, transforming the main hospital into military barracks, according to the Sudanese Doctors Network.

Heavy seasonal rainfall around Ed Damazin in Blue Nile state has triggered outbreaks of disease alongside acute shortages of shelter, clean water, and medical care in camps housing displaced people. The Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative has urged UN agencies to declare an emergency response.

Over 20,000 people across South Darfur have had to flee their homes in recent weeks. The newly displaced population is in urgent need of basic survival assistance.

Monitoring teams working with the National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) have documented a systematic pattern of ethnic-based violence targeting civilians in every city under RSF control in the Darfur region, with mass executions amounting to genocide.

The NCHR also holds reliable information on mass graves in El Geneina and El Fasher, as well as close to 4,000 cases of sexual violence, of which 20% of the victims were underage.

Armed checkpoints on the highway from Khartoum toward Sennar are forcing truck drivers to pay high transit fees.

The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate says three detained women journalists in Nyala are deteriorating medically under RSF custody without formal charges, with access to hospitals barred.

Situation in Ethiopia (per 30 July)

Around 22 people have died and thousands have been displaced in clashes along the border between the East Guji Zone in Oromia and East Sidama Zone in Sidama between 26 and 29 July.

An Ethiopian national accused of “operating a brutal transnational human trafficking” has been extradited to Ethiopia from Malawi.

The World Council of Churches (WCC) has denounced the drone strike on Abbay Giyorgis St. Arsema Unity Monastery in Amhara that took place on 22 July killing 2 civilians.

International and regional situation (per 30 July)

South Sudan’s army, opposition forces, and their respective allied militias, abused civilians which led to mass displacement during fighting in 2025 in Nagero County, Western Equatoria, states a new report by Human Rights Watch (HRW), calling for the suspension of commanders credibly implicated in abuses.

SAF leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan met South Sudan security adviser Tut Gatluak in Khartoum to advance oil-transit and bilateral cooperation linked to Heglig, discuss border stabilization and potential Juba talks, and broaden economic coordination.

US senior adviser Massad Boulos has rejected claims that Washington’s Horn of Africa diplomacy is aimed at building an anti-Ethiopian alliance after Cairo meetings with Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia.

Five Kenyan security personnel were killed by al-Shabab in Mandera county near the Somali border .

Kenya launched a new specialised border crime unit, the Counter-Organised Immigration Crime Team aimed at combating human trafficking, smuggling and other forms of transnational organised crime.

Ugandan authorities declared the country to be free of Ebola on 28 July.

Ugandan MP Muhammad Muwanga Kivumbi resurfaced at Nateete police station after 19 days incommunicado, then was charged afresh with inciting violence and managing an unlawful society and remanded to Kitalya Prison, amid allegations he was tortured and denied medical care.

Migration and refugee situation (per 30 July)

At least 117,350 irregular migrants have been deported by Benghazi-based Libyan authorities, while measures to tighten migration controls have been put in place, including stricter border security and new residency regulations for foreign nationals.

Over 100,000 Sudanese migrants have registered for a voluntary return programme from Libya, with repatriation flights underway.

Five Ethiopian migrants were executed in Saudi Arabia for nonlethal drug-related offenses on 27 July.

Refugee camps hosting Sudanese refugees in eastern Chad are experiencing severe water shortages.

The Greek government aims to prevent the Libya–Crete migration route from becoming permanent, said Greece’s migration minister, Thanos Plevris, adding that Greece is increasing intelligence-sharing and surveillance with Libya.
