text:
Tampa, FL — A Cuban National was sentenced today to 30 months in prison for his role in an international alien smuggling, asylum fraud, and money laundering conspiracy.

“Enforcing our nation’s immigration laws is essential to maintaining safe and secure borders,” said U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “The conspirators in this case used sophisticated methods to violate those laws and engaged in an elaborate human smuggling scheme, for profit. The diligence demonstrated by our law enforcement partners in this case ensured that this defendant was brought to justice.”

“Ventura-Castro was part of a complex conspiracy responsible for smuggling aliens into the United States on a massive scale,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “The defendant and others recruited aliens using social media, charged thousands of dollars to bring them into the country illegally, and helped them get immigration benefits to which they were not entitled.”

“The exploitation of vulnerable people through these types of intricate schemes are egregious crimes that threaten our national security and exploit the integrity of our immigration system,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Nicholas Ingegno of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Tampa. “They knowingly orchestrated a sophisticated scheme to recruit and smuggle thousands of Cuban nationals into the United States, and unlawfully obtained immigration benefits through fraudulent applications, deliberate misrepresentations, and illicit financial transactions. Such calculated criminal conduct undermines the integrity of our immigration system and will be met with the full force of the law.”

“Today’s sentencing is evidence of our all-out war on immigration fraud,” said Director Joseph Edlow of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. “U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services is proud to have worked with our law enforcement partners to dismantle this criminal enterprise, which churned out thousands of fake asylum claims and flooded the country with illegal aliens. As Ventura-Castro and his criminal associates are being brought to justice, we will continue our mission protecting Americans from those who seek to exploit our laws and endanger our communities.”

According to court documents, Erik Ventura-Castro, 24, of Hialeah, Florida, between January of 2021 and June of 2025, conspired with others to operate an alien smuggling organization (ASO) which encouraged or induced thousands of Cuban aliens to enter the United States through the southern border and used fraudulent Electronic System for Travel Authorization (ESTA) and visa waivers. The defendants advertised their smuggling services and bogus visa services across multiple social media platforms to solicit Cuban nationals and other aliens to attempt to illegally enter the United States and fraudulently obtain lawful status in the United States. The alien smuggling organization (ASO) advertised services included assisting Cubans with making false claims of European citizenship to enter the United States on a European tourist visa waiver or ESTA and filing hundreds of fraudulent ESTA applications with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), using fake addresses and fabricated documents. To obtain admission under the ESTAs, the defendants made false representations that the applicants had not been in Cuba since 2011. The defendants knew that Cubans are not eligible for the ESTA program, and that the applicants were actually in Cuba at the time the ESTA applications were submitted.

Passports and Boarding Passes obtained as part of the scheme

Social media account advertising ASO services

Social media account using photo from human smuggling event to advertise ASO services

Ventura-Castro furthered the conspiracy by advertising trips for aliens to travel from Cuba to the United States through third-party countries and assisting the aliens in obtaining fraudulent ESTAs. The defendant submitted over 40 electronic payments to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) for fraudulent ESTA applications. As part of the conspiracy, aliens were charged between $1,500 and $40,000 for smuggling services. Co-conspirators sometimes even chartered private planes to move groups of aliens. Ventura-Castro and co-defendants conspired with each other to regularly move funds to companies operating outside of the United States and to other places outside the United States, such as by purchasing international flights for aliens to travel into the United States. Ventura-Castro transmitted over $97,000 from the United States to the Cayman Islands, Colombia and Mexico to purchase flights for aliens to unlawfully enter the United States.

Ventura-Castro pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit alien smuggling for financial gain and conspiracy to launder monetary instruments on May 7.

Twelve individuals were charged in a superseding indictment for their roles in the conspiracy. Defendants Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez, 31, Miguel Alejandro Martinez Vasconcelos, 31, Layra Libertad Treto Santos, 30, Emanuel Martinez Gonzalez, 29, and Walbis Pozo-Dutel, 31, have all pleaded guilty and are awaiting sentencing. Defendants Lazaro Alain Cabrera-Rodriguez, Luis Emmanuel Escalona-Marrero, and Gisleivy Peralta Consuegra are awaiting trial scheduled to begin on Sept. 21.

The investigation and superseding indictment were supported and prosecuted by Joint Task Force Alpha (JTFA), the Department’s lead effort in combating high-impact human smuggling and trafficking committed by cartels and Transnational Criminal Organizations (TCOs). A highly successful partnership between the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), JTFA investigates and prosecutes human smuggling and trafficking and related immigration crimes that impact public safety and border security. JTFA’s mission is to target the leaders and organizers of Cartels and TCOs involved in human smuggling and trafficking throughout the Americas. The Attorney General has elevated and expanded JTFA to target the most prolific and dangerous human smuggling and trafficking groups operating not only in Mexico and the Northern Triangle countries of Guatemala, El Salvador, and Honduras, but also in Canada, the Caribbean and the maritime border, and elsewhere. Led by the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and supported by the Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, the Office of International Affairs, and the Office of Enforcement Operations, among others, JTFA has dedicated Assistant U.S. Attorneys from the Southern District of California; District of Arizona; District of New Mexico; Western and Southern Districts of Texas; Southern District of Florida; Northern District of New York; and District of Vermont. JTFA also partners with other USAOs throughout the country and supports high-priority cases in any district. All JTFA cases rely on substantial law enforcement resources from DHS, including HSI and CBP U.S. Border Patrol and Office of Field Operations, as well as FBI and other law enforcement agencies. To date, JTFA’s work has resulted in more than 465 domestic and international arrests of leaders, organizers, and significant facilitators of alien smuggling and/or trafficking; more than 424 U.S. convictions; and more than 368 significant jail sentences imposed, and forfeitures of substantial assets.

HSI Tampa, U.S. Border Patrol Miami Sector, and USCIS’s’ Fraud Detection and National Security led U.S. investigative efforts, with substantial assistance from HSI’s Human Smuggling Unit in Washington, D.C. and CBP’s National Targeting Center International Interdiction Task Force. Authorities in the Cayman Islands provided valuable assistance.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Courtney Derry for the Middle District of Florida and Trial Attorney Amanda Brown of the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section are prosecuting the case.

text:
The Transportation Department began enforcing existing English language requirements for truckers last summer. Concerns about truck driver qualifications then took on more urgency after an August crash in Florida, when a truck driver performed an illegal U-turn that killed three people. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that driver, who is from India, should never have been licensed in the first place.

Audits conducted in every state uncovered numerous non-domiciled commercial driver's licenses that remained valid long after an immigrant's work permits had expired or were issued without properly verifying their citizenship status.

READ MORE: Supreme Court rejects Florida's bid to sue Western states over commercial driver's licenses for immigrants

Since then, about 26,000 drivers have been pulled off the road for failing to demonstrate English proficiency, and the Transportation Department said 30,000 commercial licenses were canceled because they were issued illegally. The federal government has tried to withhold millions of dollars of highway funds from California and New York for failing to comply and revoke thousands more licenses, but that has wound up in court. Several other states — including Pennsylvania, Minnesota and North Carolina — have been warned they are at risk of losing funding.

"We are removing more and more dangerous foreign drivers off our roads every day and restoring the integrity of America's trucking industry," Duffy said. "Our new Freedom Haulers campaign will help build on these successes and get the word out that there's never been a better time for America's former service members to get behind the wheel of a big rig."

The federal government has been actively enforcing CDL rules

The trucking industry has applauded the administration's effort to get unqualified drivers off the road and close down sham CDL schools, and companies praised this new effort to get more veterans behind the wheel.

"Veterans make up 15% of our workforce and bring the highest levels of leadership, discipline and technical skills that are essential to our success. We are dedicated to providing them with meaningful careers and a supportive environment where they can thrive," said Derek Leathers, who is chairman and CEO of Werner Enterprises.

Cole Stevens, who is chief strategy officer at the trucking company that bears his last name, said veterans' backgrounds make them great drivers.

"Some of the best drivers and industry leaders I've had the privilege of working with are military veterans," Stevens said. "Their integrity, accountability, and mission-first mindset make them an incredible asset."

In addition to enforcing existing restrictions, the government announced plans to restrict which immigrants can qualify for a non-domiciled commercial driver's license and require them to take the test in English, but those rules are being challenged in court.

The only immigrant drivers who can get a license under the new rules are holders of an H-2A, H-2A or E-2 visa. H-2A is for temporary agricultural workers while H-2B is for temporary nonagricultural workers, and E-2 is for people who make substantial investments in a U.S. business.

Immigrants account for about 20% of all truck drivers, but all of these non-domiciled licenses for immigrants represent only about 5% of all commercial driver's licenses, or about 200,000 drivers.

Some immigrant groups have said they believe that many drivers are being unfairly targeted. The spotlight has been on Sikh truckers because the driver in the Florida crash and the driver in another fatal crash in California in October are both Sikh.

Truck driving may appeal to veterans

The Transportation Department plans to work with the Pentagon and Departments of Veterans Affairs and Labor to promote the career field as a good job that offers independence to veterans who don't want a desk job in civilian life.

Veterans still have to study the rules and pass the written test for a commercial driver's license, but soldiers who recently drove big military vehicles over 2.5 tons (2.25 metric tons) can skip the skills test. The government said more than 40,000 veterans have already used that program, which can enable them to get on the road within a few weeks.

The Transportation Department said that truck drivers currently make an average of $70,000 a year, as the truck market has tightened up and rates have increased.

Veterans who served for at least three years can also use the money from the GI Bill program to pay for CDL training, and they might even qualify for a housing stipend.

text:
Where the attorney for a man who was ordered removed from the United States repeatedly attempted to file a motion to reopen the removal proceedings, but the immigration court prevented the filing, that defect rendered them fundamentally unfair and prejudiced the outcome of the case.

Background

After an immigration judge ordered him removed from the United States, Dwayne Burey sought to file a motion to reopen the removal proceedings. Burey’s counsel first attempted to timely file the motion electronically, but the immigration court’s electronic system prevented him from doing so. He then attempted to timely file a paper copy of the motion in person at the immigration court, but a court clerk refused to accept the paper filing.

Finally, when Burey’s counsel sent a paper copy by mail, the immigration court accepted it.

The immigration judge, or IJ, denied Burey’s motion to reopen on the ground that he missed the statutory filing deadline. Burey appealed to the Board of Immigration Appeals, or BIA, and a divided panel affirmed. Burey argues on appeal that the BIA erred in concluding that the IJ’s denial of his motion was not a Fifth Amendment due process violation.

Interest

As a threshold matter, the government contends that Burey lacks a cognizable property or liberty interest, as required to prevail on a procedural due process claim. This court disagrees. The failure to provide a statutory or regulatory procedural protection can constitute a violation of the “constitutional guarantee of due process.” A statute creates a liberty or property interest when it provides an entitlement to, not merely an expectation of, a benefit.

The government argues that Burey cannot articulate a liberty interest because he is not entitled to reopen his removal proceedings. This misapprehends Burey’s asserted statutory right. Burey does not argue that he is entitled to reopen his proceedings; merely that he has a right to file a motion to reopen them.

The Immigration and Nationality Act permits a noncitizen to “file one motion

to reopen proceedings[.]” As this court has previously recognized, this statute creates an unambiguous “right to file” such a motion. It is this right that Burey seeks to vindicate.

Due process

Burey must demonstrate that (1) a defect in his proceedings “rendered [them] fundamentally unfair” and (2) “that the defect prejudiced the outcome of the case.” Burey first asserts that, despite his best efforts, he was prevented from filing his motion on Sept. 21, 2022, first by the immigration court’s electronic filing system and then by an immigration court clerk. Burey provided evidence of both denials.

Despite this unrefuted evidence, the IJ and BIA concluded that Burey’s claim that he was prevented from filing his motion was “unsupported by the record.” The record evidence in this case, however, compels only one reasonable conclusion: the immigration court prevented Burey from filing his motion on Sept. 21, 2022. Even under this court’s deferential standard of review, the BIA’s conclusion to the contrary is clearly erroneous.

Furthermore, this court readily concludes that the immigration court’s refusal to accept Burey’s motion “rendered [the proceedings] fundamentally unfair.” An immigration court cannot prevent a petitioner from filing a motion and then penalize him for failing to do so.

The BIA also found that Burey was nonetheless unable to demonstrate prejudice for two reasons. Neither reason is availing. First, the BIA determined that Burey was unable to establish prejudice because his counsel did not return to the immigration court the following day on Sept. 22, 2022, as instructed by the clerk. The BIA, however, determined that the deadline for Burey to submit a timely motion was Sept. 21, 2022.

Whether Burey’s attorney returned to the immigration court after that date bears no relevance to the motion’s timeliness. Furthermore, Burey submitted a sworn affidavit that, though his counsel did not return to the immigration court, he continued to call the immigration court and attempted to file the motion both electronically and by mail, to no avail.

Second, the BIA found that Burey could not establish prejudice because he had not yet filed his self-petition for immigration relief with USCIS. The statute, however, does not require this precondition. In concluding that Burey could not establish that he had been prejudiced because he had not yet filed the Form 1-360 self-petition, the BIA improperly imposed a requirement not found in the statute. The evidence in this case compels one conclusion: Burey was denied due process.

Petition granted, reversed and remanded with instructions.

Burey v. Blanche, Case No. 25-1869, July 14, 2026. 4th Cir. (Berner), from Board of Immigration Appeals. Siona Sharma for Petitioner. Lisa Morinelli for Respondent. VLW 026-2-262. 10 pp.

text:
On Monday, Temporary Protected Status (TPS) protections for over 300,000 Haitian nationals living in the United States formally expired. The expiration follows a June Supreme Court ruling affirming the Trump administration’s authority to terminate the TPS designation for Haiti. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is now set to ramp up operations to arrest these former TPS beneficiaries.

Although TPS is intended only to provide temporary protections for citizens of countries affected by war, natural disaster, or other extraordinary circumstances, the program has proven anything but temporary in practice. In fact, through regular extensions and “re-designations,” the program has been consistently abused and exploited as amnesty to provide otherwise inadmissible foreign nationals with work authorizations and protections from deportation.

Haiti was first designated for TPS in 2010 following a devastating earthquake, with the Obama administration determining that Haitian nationals could not safely return home. The most recent extension and re-designation came in 2024, 14 years later, and focused on civil unrest rather than the earthquake. In 2025, the Trump administration moved to terminate TPS for Haiti, concluding that the continued presence of Haitian TPS beneficiaries was not in the U.S. national interest.

Under the Biden administration, TPS was exploited as a backdoor amnesty to protect more than two million foreign nationals from deportation, virtually all of whom were illegally in the United States. By early 2025, more than 84 percent of all eligible TPS beneficiaries – approximately 1.8 million aliens – qualified based on the Biden administration’s TPS decisions alone. That total included roughly 569,000 Haitian nationals.

Illegal immigration should never be rewarded – nor should foreign nationals be baselessly offered protections and prioritized over American citizens.

On Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a new interim final rule that would end the practice of automatically granting interviews to certain affirmative asylum applicants. The purpose of the rule is to improve the efficiency of the asylum review process by allowing U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to refer aliens with meritless or barred claims directly to removal proceedings.

Affirmative asylum is a form of humanitarian protection available to aliens physically present in the United States who demonstrate a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion in their home country. While the Trump administration has taken several measures to remedy the systemic abuse of the asylum process that occurred under the Biden administration, the rule notes that the “unprecedented crisis” facing the system remains ongoing, with 1.4 million affirmative asylum applications still pending.

Asylum officers will now be able to refer certain aliens directly to removal proceedings with the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR). In conjunction with DHS’s recent changes to work authorization for asylum applicants, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) attorneys going after asylum fraud, and the State Department cracking down, the interim final rule will help to restore integrity to our asylum system and prevent it from serving as an alternative route for economic migration.

Beyond executive actions, FAIR continues to advocate for permanent legislative fixes to our asylum laws, such as those contained in H.R. 9773, the updated version of H.R. 2, which recently advanced out of the House Judiciary Committee.

text:
A divided Ninth Circuit panel rejected the Trump administration’s asserted authority to detain noncitizens without bond hearings, the fifth federal appellate court to do so in a matter that appears destined for the US Supreme Court.

The Trump administration declared last year that millions of noncitizens living in the US without legal immigration status don’t have the right to bond hearings in immigration court, even if they’ve lived in the country for years—a legal interpretation that defied some 30 years of practice. In Thursday’s opinion, Trump-appointed Judge Daniel Bress said it makes little sense to argue that Congress gave the executive that power, “but that this change then went unnoticed and unheeded” for so long.

If Congress actually intended to require that mass detention of noncitizens, it would have used much clearer language to say so, Bress wrote. The government’s new interpretation, he said, “creates more textual and other difficulties than the traditional understanding of that provision.”

Bress cited the Supreme Court’s rejection of Trump’s tariffs in this year’s Learning Resources Inc. v. Trump, saying it casts skepticism on claims of executive power “on an uncertain statutory basis.”

Judge Margaret McKeown, a Clinton appointee, joined Bress’s opinion.

In dissent, Judge Carlos Bea said a strict read of the statute supports the government’s claims, and it wouldn’t make sense for Congress to mandate detention for noncitizens stopped at the border but not those who escaped detection and lived in the US for years.

The majority’s “underlying demand for congressional clarity” potentially “opens the door to judicial legislation, by allowing a judge to claim any text is just short of the clarity he would require,” wrote Bea, a George W. Bush appointee.

The US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit was considering the government’s appeal from a case filed in the Western District of Washington, where a district judge certified a class of detained noncitizens and found that denying them bond hearings was a violation of their rights.

Nearly all the federal appellate courts have heard arguments on the government’s assertion of mandatory detention authority. So far, the Fifth and Eighth circuits have sided with the government, while the Second, Sixth, Tenth and Eleventh have also ruled against it.

The Fifth Circuit is set to consider the issue again en banc in the coming months, this time as a matter of constitutional due process protections rather than statutory interpretation.

The government and advocates for noncitizens have separately petitioned the US Supreme Court to take up the migrant detention matter. With the deep circuit split, the justices are widely expected to decide the issue.

The Trump administration last year reinterpreted part of the Immigration and Nationality Act, claiming it gave them power to keep noncitizens in detention without bond hearings even if they have lived in the US for years. That contradicted nearly 30 years of practice, including during Trump’s first term, when noncitizens apprehended inside the country were acknowledged to have the right to argue for their release in immigration court.

Advocates describe the new policy as a powerful tool supporting Trump’s mass-deportation agenda, as those in detention are far less likely to successfully fight deportation proceedings. The switch prompted waves of litigation around the country, including a flood of individual habeas corpus petitions that have overwhelmed district courts.

The noncitizens are represented by Northwest Immigrant Rights Project and the American Civil Liberties Union Foundation.

text:
A fifth federal appeals court has rejected the Trump administration’s bid to subject millions of immigrants — most of whom have lived in the U.S. for years without criminal records — to mandatory detention without bond.

The ruling by the California-based 9th Circuit Court of Appeals is the most significant rejection yet of the Trump administration’s unprecedented mass detention policy. It will bind lower courts along a large swath of the southern border and in states where thousands of ICE detainees are housed.

The 2-1 ruling found that the Trump administration had misconstrued decades-old immigration laws to justify its expansive detention policy. The modern deportation system, adopted in 1996, was meant to require detention only for those apprehended crossing the border or soon after, the majority ruled.

Those who have resided in the U.S.for years, establishing families, livelihoods and roots, could only be detained after being afforded a bond hearing — a chance to convince an immigration judge that they can live safely in their communities while their deportation proceedings play out.

“The government’s change in policy has resulted in detained aliens filing thousands of habeas petitions in federal courts across the country, seeking bond hearings and possible release from detention,” Judge Daniel Bress , a Trump appointee, wrote for the majority. “The implication of the government’s position is that Congress in 1996 made a major change to the immigration laws by subjecting millions of unadmitted aliens present in the United States to mandatory detention, but that this change then went unnoticed and unheeded, with the Executive Branch for the next three decades … We accordingly do not think that Congress in 1996 made such a large-scale change to our established system of immigration detention in the way that the government now contends.”

The ruling follows similar decisions in the Atlanta-based 11th Circuit, the New York-based 2nd Circuit, the Colorado-based 10th Circuit and the Cincinnati-based 6th Circuit. Two appeals courts, the 5th Circuit and the 8th Circuit, have sided with the Trump administration. Rulings are pending in four other circuits. In addition to the 5-2 split among appeals courts, more than 460 federal judges have rejected the administration’s approach in more than 10,000 cases, compared to 54 judges who have backed the policy in about 1,100 cases.

The issue appears destined for Supreme Court consideration in the term. The Justice Department appealed its 6th Circuit defeat to the high court last month, and the ACLU asked the justices to overturn the 5th Circuit’s ruling shortly thereafter.

Democratic lawmakers on the House Judiciary Committee hammered U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for failing to deliver on a pledge to equip its officers with body cameras amid a rash of deadly interactions with the public.

In a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and acting ICE Director David Venturella, the Democrats noted it’s been six months since the agency pledged to adopt body cameras.

Then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem pledged to equip officers with body cameras in the wake of two killings in Minneapolis earlier this year, a promise made after Congress provided unprecedented levels of funding for ICE that included $20 million in funds earmarked for that purpose.

But in subsequent fatal shootings, including in Texas and Maine, officers have not been wearing cameras.

“In shooting after shooting, we are told that there is no body-worn camera footage of the incident and asked to accept DHS’s account of the incident. Time and again, that account turns out to be a blatant falsehood. It is time for DHS to use the $210 billion that congressional Republicans have given the agency to ensure that every DHS officer is equipped with a fully functioning body-worn camera when conducting immigration enforcement,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the top Democrat on the panel, and Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), the ranking member of an immigration focused subcommittee, wrote in the letter.

Neither ICE nor the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) responded to requests for comment.

Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS officials have shot more than two dozen people, killing six of them.

The lawmakers said the cameras can “provide a corroborating or contradictory account of what happened.”

In the shooting in Texas, which resulted in the death of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, other witnesses in the car said the DHS’s claims that he weaponized his vehicle against officers were completely false.

Instead, they said, they were scared after being trailed by unmarked vehicles that later encircled their work van on both the left and right.

And in the cases of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, the DHS also initially made claims about their deaths that appear to be false. The DHS accused Good of weaponizing her vehicle and Pretti of reaching for a gun to assault officers. Video evidence taken by bystanders contradicted both claims.

“We need these cameras now. DHS and its component agencies have consistently made false and unsubstantiated allegations about people its agents shot, including Renée Good, Alex Pretti, Ruben Ray Martinez, and Marimar Martinez. DHS initially claimed these U.S. citizens, all of whom they either killed or maimed, were attacking law enforcement officers,” Raskin and Jayapal wrote.

“In each case, evidence later emerged that definitively contradicted the government’s claims, showing that DHS made false or misleading statements. In other incidents, it was found ICE agents lied and were the aggressors, resulting in several trumped-up prosecutions against DHS’s victims being dismissed with prejudice.”

“DHS has the resources it needs to make this happen now,” they added.

text:
At the first public hearing in a never-before-used ‘alien terrorist’ deportation court, an attorney for the Afghan immigrant the Trump administration is seeking to expel complained that the court itself is unconstitutional.

Deputy U.S. Marshals led Nazira Haji Zada , 47, into a courtroom at the E. Barrett Prettyman courthouse near the Capitol on Thursday just after a court clerk opened the hearing with a cry never previously heard in public.

“The United States Alien Terrorist Removal Court is now in session!” the clerk announced to a courtroom packed with press, law clerks and others eager to get a glimpse of the historic proceeding.

Haji Zada — a diminutive mother of seven who prosecutors say can’t read or write — appeared clad in a beige patterned hijab that covered her head and shoulders as she entered through a side door and took a seat at the defense table. She looked across the courtroom and said little if anything during the 40-minute court session.

Judge Joan Ericksen wasted no time acknowledging the fledgling nature of the court, which has been on the books for three decades but has never before been presented with a case. “There may be moments that are inelegant,” Ericksen said, as she promised the court will soon deploy an electronic docketing system so both sides can more easily file documents in the case.

But Haji Zada’s lawyers quickly made clear that their concerns go far beyond the logistics involved in standing up what the judge called a “brand new” court.

“This entire scheme is a violation of due process and unconstitutional,” Assistant Federal Defender Matthew Farley told Ericksen. He said the reason the court has never been used is because its procedures are “woefully inadequate” and don’t come close to what the Constitution requires, especially when the government seeks to deport a lawful permanent resident like Haji Zada.

The Trump administration is seeking Haji Zada’s deportation based on her alleged knowledge of and involvement in a plot involving her son and son-in-law, both of whom have pleaded guilty to terrorism-related federal charges. Prosecutors said the plot to commit violence on Election Day in 2024 was in support of ISIS, the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria, which is considered a terrorist group by the U.S. The two men were arrested before the plot was carried out.

“She has openly pledged loyalty to ISIS ,” Justice Department prosecutor Hayden O’Byrne said, adding that Haji Zada had indoctrinated her children in such ideology and “radicalized the family.”

However, Farley said that if the government had solid proof Haji Zada was involved in the plot her son and son-in-law admitted to, it would have indicted her alongside them.

“This is a run-around of bringing a criminal case, to attempt to lower the standard of proof,” Farley complained, calling for his client to be freed right away due to the untested procedures of the terrorism court.

Ericksen , who was appointed to the federal district court in Minnesota by President George W. Bush and named to the terrorism court by Chief Justice John Roberts , turned down that request Thursday without explanation. However, she said she will allow both sides to file written arguments on the issue and hold a hearing aimed at assessing whether Haji Zada must remain behind bars while the deportation case proceeds.

Haji Zada was arrested at her home in Texas on Tuesday “without incident” on a warrant Ericksen signed after a closed-door hearing with government lawyers earlier this month. The judge didn’t immediately grant the warrant, but did so after demanding a follow-up submission from prosecutors.

Much of the back-and-forth at the hearing Thursday was over classified information. O’Byrne said the government’s case will rely in part on secret evidence that Haji Zada will not have access to.

Ericksen said she would start from a “presumption” that Haji Zada’s attorneys would get access to that information even if the government refused to share it with her. After O’Byrne suggested that some information might not be provided to the lawyers, the judge sounded skeptical.

“I’ll be looking for some pretty strong reasons why the information can’t be turned over to counsel,” she said.

Ericksen did not immediately set a schedule for future hearings or filings in the case, but said she intended to meet privately with the lawyers to hammer that out.

name: Policy
title: A New Trump Rule Would Lower Standards at Head Start and Exclude Immigrants From the Program
authors: smccroskey, Chris Lehmann, Bryce Covert, Eric Drooker, Mark Hertsgaard, David Vine, The Nation, Mychal Denzel Smith, www.thenation.com
description:
While the Head Start Act includes some specific requirements, most standards in the program have been delineated by this set of rules.
The proposed rule also nixes specific requirements that mandate the curriculum standards programs must adhere to.
The rule would also put the onus of verifying children’s immigration eligibility on Head Start programs, which will require extra administrative resources.
Late last year, it attempted to block certain immigrants from enrolling in Head Start, only to have the effort blocked by a federal judge.
The proposed rule, then, seems to be a new way of attempting to gut the program.
text:
The Trump administration is on the verge of publishing a proposed rule that, if finalized, will gut most of the crucial standards that ensure uniform quality of Head Start programs across the country while adding new requirements aimed at shutting out immigrants for the first time in the program’s history, according to two people with direct knowledge of the draft regulation. Head Start, the federal program that provides free preschool education and services to low-income families, was created in 1965 and currently serves more than 700,000 children, with an annual budget of $12.4 billion. In a leaked 2025 budget draft that called for eliminating Head Start entirely, President Trump said, “The federal government should not be in the business of mandating curriculum, locations, and performance standards for any form of education.”

The administration’s proposed rule, which has been drafted by the Department of Health and Human Services and sent to the Office of Management and Budget for review, would rescind the entire 133-page set of “performance standards” that currently spell out how Head Start laws must be implemented by states, counties, and programs, they said. While the Head Start Act includes some specific requirements, most standards in the program have been delineated by this set of rules. Instead, a much shorter set of standards would take its place, leaving it up to states and local governments to implement their own standards if they so choose.

“What it does is transform a program that has high quality,” one of the people said, “and create a generic early-childhood funding stream that doesn’t look like Head Start.” The Administration for Children and Families, which oversees Head Start, did not respond to a request for comment.

Currently, the Head Start guidelines place limits on class sizes and specify how many adult staff are required to supervise certain numbers of children. The new regulations would eliminate those class size and ratio requirements; instead, they would require programs to adhere to state and local laws. Some states have strict childcare ratio requirements, but others are much looser, permitting higher ratios of children to teachers than Head Start currently allows. Head Start teachers work with some of the nation’s most vulnerable children and report that since the pandemic children have presented with such significant needs that they struggle to serve children under the program’s existing ratios, the first source said. The proposed rule also nixes specific requirements that mandate the curriculum standards programs must adhere to.

The proposed rule removes guidance around the circumstances in which children can be suspended and expelled. The existing standards prohibit corporal punishment, a prohibition that will disappear in the proposed rule. It gets rid of required developmental screenings for all children and detailed regulations governing how children with disabilities must be given access to services and included in classroom instruction. Gone are guidelines around how homeless families and children in foster care should be accommodated so that they can enroll.

“If it’s not explicitly stated in [the Head Start] statute, it won’t seem to exist after this proposed rule is finalized,” the second person said. That statute was last revised nearly 20 years ago under President George W. Bush, and at that time Congress directed the Office of Head Start to keep issuing regulations to continuously improve the program. “It really turns over its authority to states and localities on how to handle almost everything.”

What the proposed rule adds is just as troubling as what is disappearing. If the rule is finalized, it will only allow children who are citizens, United States nationals, or “qualified aliens,” and with at least one parent with that status, to enroll. That will shut out a number of immigrants, and potentially children who are American citizens, for the first time ever. As of 2022, about 4.4 million American children lived with at least one undocumented parent. (Jonathan Cohn previously reported the proposal rule’s changes to immigration eligibility and to the class size ratios at The Bulwark.) The rule would also put the onus of verifying children’s immigration eligibility on Head Start programs, which will require extra administrative resources. All families, meanwhile, will face an added paperwork burden of proving their citizenship status.

The rule states that all teaching must be done in English, except for in Native American tribes, and says that if a child’s native language isn’t English, programs must prioritize teaching them in English anyway.

The rule creates a new requirement that staff must maintain records proving a family’s income, immigration, and other eligibility for a certain amount of time and provide them to HHS upon request. It says that programs have to report staff who violate eligibility requirements to HHS. The combination will create a massive increase in paperwork and the possibility that staff members will be penalized for clerical errors. “They’ve made it very high stakes,” the first person said. It’s “a very dangerous proposition to be having coworkers question their colleagues’ work at this level,” the second person added.

The current standards say programs must establish parent committees that weigh in on the program’s policies and services; the proposed rule would make those optional.

While the proposed rule would not affect Head Start’s budget, it nevertheless changes regulations that will force programs to tighten their belts. Under current regulations, programs are permitted to spend up to 15 percent of their grant funding on administration and overhead, which was already a difficult threshold for programs to meet. But the proposed rule reduces that to just 5 percent. “That’s going to be a pretty significant burden for programs,” the second person said.

The Trump administration has repeatedly claimed that removing government regulations makes public programs easier to operate. However, losing so many specific regulations may instead put a greater burden on Head Start programs, as well as the states a`nd counties that must now regulate them. Requirements will end up varying significantly from state to state or even county to county, which “gets into a really complex and confusing patchwork that just places a more significant burden on every grantee,” the second person said, while leaving parents with program quality that varies depending on where they live. Some states may fail to do anything to maintain standards at all. Many programs, meanwhile, are motivated to provide high quality, but with fewer requirements some may find it cheaper and easier to do less. “The standards are supposed to be the floor so everybody gets the same thing in Head Start,” the first person said. But “there are financial realities in these programs.” The first person also worries that the reduction in rules and regulations will open the doors for corporate behemoths to get into the space. “This is a $12.5 billion investment that comes with strings right now,” they said. “There’s a danger to exploit that if it comes with no strings.”

Ad Policy

“What we’re looking at is very much the wild, Wild West of an early childhood patchwork of programs and regulations and statutes across the country,” the second person said.

The proposed rule could change before it’s made public and may change before being finalized. Even if it is finalized in its current form, it is likely to be subject to litigation; a number of its provisions appear to contradict the Head Start statute and a 2007 reauthorization that mandates that the standards don’t eliminate or reduce quality.

But the details fit squarely with the administration’s agenda. Project 2025, the document crafted by conservative Trump allies during the Biden administration to guide the next Republican president, called for eliminating Head Start entirely. Trump’s first budget after being reelected nearly proposed doing just that: A leaked draft called for zeroing out the program’s funding. The administration has closed a number of regional Head Start offices, leaving programs with nowhere to turn to get answers, and despite Congress fully funding Head Start, last year the Trump administration sat on some of the money, refusing to dole it out, while implementing a new “defend the spend” process that held up grant disbursement. Late last year, it attempted to block certain immigrants from enrolling in Head Start, only to have the effort blocked by a federal judge. Then in May, the administration proposed rolling back the higher wage and benefit levels for Head Start teachers set by the Biden administration. “It’s one attack after the other on the very core of the program,” the second person said.

The proposed rule, then, seems to be a new way of attempting to gut the program. “This is another run at it,” the first person said.

It’s part of a “consistent approach that Head Start is not a priority for them,” the second person added. “If you can’t eliminate something, shrink it to the smallest possible degree and make it difficult to operate.” Then, when the program struggles to continue operating and providing high-quality education, it will likely be used as justification to further reduce it. “It’s a self-fulfilling prophecy,” the second person said.

text:
A fifth federal appeals court has rejected the Trump administration’s bid to subject millions of immigrants — most of whom have lived in the U.S. for years without criminal records — to mandatory detention without bond.

The ruling by the California-based 9th Circuit Court of Appeals is the most significant rejection yet of the Trump administration’s unprecedented mass detention policy. It will bind lower courts along a large swath of the southern border and in states where thousands of ICE detainees are housed.

The 2-1 ruling found that the Trump administration had misconstrued decades-old immigration laws to justify its expansive detention policy. The modern deportation system, adopted in 1996, was meant to require detention only for those apprehended crossing the border or soon after, the majority ruled.

Those who have resided in the U.S.for years, establishing families, livelihoods and roots, could only be detained after being afforded a bond hearing — a chance to convince an immigration judge that they can live safely in their communities while their deportation proceedings play out.

“The government’s change in policy has resulted in detained aliens filing thousands of habeas petitions in federal courts across the country, seeking bond hearings and possible release from detention,” Judge Daniel Bress , a Trump appointee, wrote for the majority. “The implication of the government’s position is that Congress in 1996 made a major change to the immigration laws by subjecting millions of unadmitted aliens present in the United States to mandatory detention, but that this change then went unnoticed and unheeded, with the Executive Branch for the next three decades … We accordingly do not think that Congress in 1996 made such a large-scale change to our established system of immigration detention in the way that the government now contends.”

The ruling follows similar decisions in the Atlanta-based 11th Circuit, the New York-based 2nd Circuit, the Colorado-based 10th Circuit and the Cincinnati-based 6th Circuit. Two appeals courts, the 5th Circuit and the 8th Circuit, have sided with the Trump administration. Rulings are pending in four other circuits. In addition to the 5-2 split among appeals courts, more than 460 federal judges have rejected the administration’s approach in more than 10,000 cases, compared to 54 judges who have backed the policy in about 1,100 cases.

The issue appears destined for Supreme Court consideration in the term. The Justice Department appealed its 6th Circuit defeat to the high court last month, and the ACLU asked the justices to overturn the 5th Circuit’s ruling shortly thereafter.

text:
Why It Matters

The U.S. Refugee Admissions Program has shrunk to historic lows, with a new Congressional Research Service report documenting a dramatic reversal from the prior administration's approach. The fiscal year 2026 refugee ceiling stands at 17,500, the lowest level since the U.S. refugee admissions program began in 1980, while actual admissions have lagged far behind even that constrained target.

The shift represents a fundamental recalibration of American refugee policy. In less than 18 months, the ceiling dropped from 125,000 under President Joe Biden to 17,500 under President Donald Trump, a significant reduction that has left over 128,000 fully vetted refugees stranded and unable to be admitted.

The collapse in admissions capacity raises immediate questions about how the administration interprets its legal obligations under the Refugee Act of 1980 and whether the current approach aligns with the statutory definition of who qualifies for protection. The CRS report documents not just the numerical decline, but also a shift in what is being prioritized by the administration.

The Big Picture

Soon after Trump took office, he issued Executive Order 14163, stating that entry of refugees under the program would be detrimental to U.S. interests and directed that refugee entry be suspended, subject to exceptions, until he determined that resumption was in the national interest.

President Trump initially set the FY2026 refugee ceiling at 7,500. That figure was then increased to 17,500 through an emergency presidential determination issued in May 2026, which cited "racially motivated violence" by the South African government against Afrikaners, descended from Dutch, German, and French settlers in the area.

The statutory framework gives the President broad authority to set refugee ceilings, but it also imposes procedural requirements. The Refugee Act of 1980 amended the Immigration and Nationality Act to establish the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP) and requires the President to set the ceiling before each fiscal year after "appropriate consultation" with Congress. It also authorizes emergency presidential determinations to increase the refugee ceiling during a fiscal year in the event of an unforeseen emergency refugee situation where the admission of certain refugees is justified by grave humanitarian concerns or is otherwise in the national interest.

Political Stakes

For Democrats

The collapse in admissions numbers and the prioritization of Afrikaners, a group not recognized by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees as a refugee population, represents a departure from the Biden Administration's approach. The backlog of 128,000 fully vetted refugees unable to be admitted has become a focal point for criticism.

The Bottom Line

Over 128,000 fully vetted refugees remain unable to be admitted due to the ongoing suspension, and the Trump Administration is showing little motion to address the issue.

text:
A divided Ninth Circuit panel rejected the Trump administration’s asserted authority to detain noncitizens without bond hearings, the fifth federal appellate court to do so in a matter that appears destined for the US Supreme Court.

The Trump administration declared last year that millions of noncitizens living in the US without legal immigration status don’t have the right to bond hearings in immigration court, even if they’ve lived in the country for years—a legal interpretation that defied some 30 years of practice. In Thursday’s opinion, Trump-appointed Judge Daniel Bress said it makes little sense to argue that Congress gave the executive that power, “but that this change then went unnoticed and unheeded” for so long.

If Congress actually intended to require that mass detention of noncitizens, it would have used much clearer language to say so, Bress wrote. The government’s new interpretation, he said, “creates more textual and other difficulties than the traditional understanding of that provision.”

Bress cited the Supreme Court’s rejection of Trump’s tariffs in this year’s Learning Resources Inc. v. Trump, saying it casts skepticism on claims of executive power “on an uncertain statutory basis.”

Judge Margaret McKeown, a Clinton appointee, joined Bress’s opinion.

In dissent, Judge Carlos Bea said a strict read of the statute supports the government’s claims, and it wouldn’t make sense for Congress to mandate detention for noncitizens stopped at the border but not those who escaped detection and lived in the US for years.

The majority’s “underlying demand for congressional clarity” potentially “opens the door to judicial legislation, by allowing a judge to claim any text is just short of the clarity he would require,” wrote Bea, a George W. Bush appointee.

The US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit was considering the government’s appeal from a case filed in the Western District of Washington, where a district judge certified a class of detained noncitizens and found that denying them bond hearings was a violation of their rights.

Nearly all the federal appellate courts have heard arguments on the government’s assertion of mandatory detention authority. So far, the Fifth and Eighth circuits have sided with the government, while the Second, Sixth, Tenth and Eleventh have also ruled against it.

The Fifth Circuit is set to consider the issue again en banc in the coming months, this time as a matter of constitutional due process protections rather than statutory interpretation.

The government and advocates for noncitizens have separately petitioned the US Supreme Court to take up the migrant detention matter. With the deep circuit split, the justices are widely expected to decide the issue.

The Trump administration last year reinterpreted part of the Immigration and Nationality Act, claiming it gave them power to keep noncitizens in detention without bond hearings even if they have lived in the US for years. That contradicted nearly 30 years of practice, including during Trump’s first term, when noncitizens apprehended inside the country were acknowledged to have the right to argue for their release in immigration court.

Advocates describe the new policy as a powerful tool supporting Trump’s mass-deportation agenda, as those in detention are far less likely to successfully fight deportation proceedings. The switch prompted waves of litigation around the country, including a flood of individual habeas corpus petitions that have overwhelmed district courts.

The noncitizens are represented by Northwest Immigrant Rights Project and the American Civil Liberties Union Foundation.

title: Immigration officials misused weapons hundreds of times during protests, report finds
authors: Kate Morrissey, Michelle Griffith, Ria Gupta, Claudia Boyd-Barrett, KFF Health News, Brian Martucci
description:
Human rights investigators have documented hundreds of instances of misuse of crowd-control weapons at protests of immigration enforcement since President Donald Trump returned to office.
The authors of the report called for manufacturers to stop making certain weapons that are particularly harmful and likely to be misused and urged law enforcement agencies to change their use-of-force policies.
Schell said that at most of the protests where the team documented misuse, multiple law enforcement agencies and subagencies were present.

text:
Reprinted with permission from Capital & Main.

Human rights investigators have documented hundreds of instances of misuse of crowd-control weapons at protests of immigration enforcement since President Donald Trump returned to office.

Department of Homeland Security employees and local law enforcement both committed violations of standards of use for crowd-control weapons, injuring protesters, according to a report from Physicians for Human Rights and the University of California, Berkeley’s Human Rights Center. The authors of the report called for manufacturers to stop making certain weapons that are particularly harmful and likely to be misused and urged law enforcement agencies to change their use-of-force policies.

“There’s a lack of standards across the board in the United States when it comes to the use of crowd-control weapons, and there’s a lack of standards around training, testing, figuring out what these weapons are, how they should work and how we should use them,” said Sasha Schell, supervising reporter at the Berkeley Human Rights Center, who led the open source investigative team.

The team used open source investigative techniques, including cataloguing incidents through the review of publicly available video, to determine which agencies misused which weapons. The researchers labeled an incident as a misuse of the weapon if it went against international human rights standards, manufacturer instructions or the agency’s own use-of-force policy, or if the law enforcement agency attacked a protected group such as journalists, legal observers or medics.

Because of limitations in the video that the team could find, Schell said, the report’s statistics are likely an undercount.

Immigration officials and other law enforcement have used a mix of tear gas, rubber bullets, pepper spray, pepper balls, flashbangs, batons and shields on crowds gathered to protest during large-scale immigration enforcement operations in cities including Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis.

Under international law, in order to use force on protesters, law enforcement agencies must ensure that the force is necessary and must have exhausted other options, and officials should take precautions to minimize harm caused, the authors of the report said. Force should be proportional to the threat and not excessive.

But the U.S. government does not have specific federal standards for crowd control weapons in its laws, according to the report.

Schell said that at most of the protests where the team documented misuse, multiple law enforcement agencies and subagencies were present. Each had its own use-of-force policy that didn’t necessarily align with those of other agencies.

“It becomes a real mess for holding anybody accountable when misuse does occur,” Schell said.

He gave an example of one protest where Chicago police gave protesters one set of instructions and federal officials gave protesters a different set of instructions.

“That led to a bunch of people getting shot with pepper balls,” Schell said.

Amended lawsuit alleges more unconstitutional conduct of feds in Minnesota

Department of Homeland Security employees, including officials from Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, committed the majority of the violations.

Those included spraying people directly in the face with powerful chemical irritants after they were already detained, handcuffed or pinned to the ground or even beating them over the head with the canisters, Schell said.

The most common misuse, according to the report, involved deploying crowd-control weapons at too close a range. Researchers also noted many cases in which law enforcement deployed these weapons in enclosed spaces or other situations that the protesters could not escape.

Schell said that most of the violence occurred at unplanned protests, such as responses to a particular immigration enforcement operation, rather than at planned protests like the No Kings rallies.

“In the vast majority of incidents, protests were peaceful before crowd-control weapons were deployed, and in all cases, basic standards of proportionality, precaution, and necessity were not met,” the report says.

When asked about the report’s findings, the Department of Homeland Security blamed protesters.

“The pattern is NOT of law enforcement using force,” an unnamed department spokesperson said via email. “It’s a pattern of violent agitators attacking our law enforcement.”

The department encouraged protesters and journalists to “exercise caution.”

“Being near unlawful activities in the field does come with risks — though our officers take every reasonable precaution to mitigate dangers to those exercising their protected First Amendment rights,” the spokesperson said. “However, when faced with violence or attempts to obstruct law enforcement operations, our officers will take legal and necessary steps to ensure their own safety and the public’s safety.”

The report includes 175 cases of misuse of force against journalists.

Schell said he didn’t want to discourage journalists from doing their jobs, but he encouraged them to be alert when they move through the crowd in quieter moments to conduct interviews.

“You’d have a little bit of a standoff between the protesters and law enforcement where maybe not much is happening, and then out of nowhere these guys will decide, ‘All right, we’ve got to clear this crowd,’ with very little warning,” Schell said. You’ll see a barrage of tear gas, pepper spray, these muzzle-blast weapons come in and launch. Those were the times we saw journalists being hit the most.”

Researchers found a significant number of deployments of crowd-control weapons targeted people’s heads, causing contusions, traumatic brain injuries, hearing loss and ocular injuries. Crowd-control weapons are not supposed to be deployed on someone’s head, Schell said.

The authors of the report called the number of head injuries concerning because it suggests “that law enforcement agents either intentionally or recklessly deployed force towards the head in dangerous and improper ways.”

The rate of violations worsened when Border Patrol leader Gregory Bovino was present, according to the report. Bovino was demoted and later retired shortly after the fatal shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis.

Researchers also noted that in Los Angeles, the police and Sheriff’s departments also committed a significant number of violations.

The Los Angeles Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.

The L.A. County Sheriff’s Department said via email that its staff had not yet reviewed the report’s findings and couldn’t comment on them.

“During the period referenced in the report, Los Angeles experienced unprecedented federal immigration enforcement activity that prompted some of the largest and most sustained demonstrations in the country,” the department wrote in the email without naming a speaker. “As emotions ran high, local law enforcement officers, who live and work in these same communities, often became the focus of that frustration, despite not being responsible for federal immigration enforcement actions.”

The department said its training emphasizes de-escalation.

“Each city had its tone, and each protest would have its own tone,” Schell said.

In Los Angeles, that meant Sheriff’s deputies firing flashbangs that are supposed to detonate above a crowd, Schell said. The noise and flash are supposed to scare crowds into backing up.

But, instead of firing the weapons well overhead, deputies aimed them so that they detonated on individuals’ heads, causing injuries.

“Those were pretty shocking to see,” Schell said.

The report notes that police agencies that had previously enacted use-of-force reforms related to crowd control since 2020 had far fewer incidents of misuse than agencies that have reversed or abandoned those policy changes in recent years. It noted that while the Los Angeles Police Department enacted some reforms, the Sheriff’s Department did not.

“There is limited but clear evidence that when police reforms, weapons bans, and crowd management policies are enacted and followed, use of force incidents, misuse events, and resulting injuries, go down,” the report says. “The opposite is also true: when reform is not implemented, or is reversed, incidents, misuse, and injuries go up.”

The authors of the report said piecemeal reform at individual agencies is not enough to respond to the nationwide trend of misuse of force as documented by the researchers.

They called for the U.S. government to enact broad reform to protect people exercising their First Amendment rights.

Schell, as a journalist himself, said he hopes the report and accompanying database will inspire more journalism digging deep into the questions raised in the report.

“Who is setting standards? Who is doing the training?” Schell said. “It’s quite an opaque thing.”

He said he wants more information about how weapons receive a “less lethal” designation to begin with.

“A lot of times the injuries that we see [are] not consistent with what they’ve said about how these things function,” Schell said. “Some of the injuries we saw were really gruesome.”

text:
A federal immigration agent said in newly publicized court documents that an immigration raid outside a rally hosted by Gov. Gavin Newsom last year was a “stunt,” bolstering claims Newsom has made that the raid was politically motivated.

The documents, filed in federal court in Los Angeles this week and highlighted by Newsom’s office in a press release Wednesday, include text messages and a sworn deposition from immigration agents. In the deposition, a Homeland Security Investigations special agent said the raid “seemed to be purely political.”

“They marched to a democratic governor’s press conference. It seemed to be purely political,” the agent said in sworn testimony. “It did not seem like there was a good operational basis to be doing that,” the agent said. “To me, it appeared political.”

Article continues below this ad

The documents are part of a case in which three men are challenging their arrests by immigration officers in Pasadena in June 2025. They contend that their arrests were illegal, and part of a broader “pattern and practice of flouting the Constitution and federal law in connection with ongoing immigration raids in the Los Angeles area.” Several cities across Southern California have joined the lawsuit.

The Homeland Security Investigations officer’s name is redacted in the filings, but the agent said they previously served as a Border Patrol officer in the El Centro sector.

Newsom was holding a press conference in Los Angeles last August to promote Proposition 50, his ballot measure that redrew California congressional district lines to add five Democratic-majority districts. The measure was approved in November by more than 64% of the state’s voters.

Agents led by Gregory Bovino, chief of the Border Patrol’s El Centro (Imperial County) sector, showed up at the site and made several immigration arrests.

Article continues below this ad

“We’re here making Los Angeles a safer place, since we don’t have politicians that’ll do that,” Bovino, a leading public figure in President Donald Trump’s mass arrests and deportations of immigrants, said at the time in a clip posted by Newsom’s office.

Asked about the newly disclosed documents, Trump’s Department of Homeland Security said in a statement late Wednesday that “the only publicity stunt the media should concern themselves with is an American governor in an American city holding a press conference to protect criminal illegals at the expense of Americans.”

The raid occurred at a moment of intense tension between the Newsom and Trump administrations. Trump had federalized the California National Guard earlier that summer, a move that drew outrage from Newsom and other Democrats in the state. Sen. Alex Padilla, who attended the rally, had been forced to the ground and handcuffed weeks earlier when he attempted to question DHS Secretary Kristi Noem about the deployment at a news conference. Newsom’s campaign for Prop 50, in response to efforts by Texas and other conservative-led states to redraw congressional districts to favor Republicans, had just started to pick up steam.

At the time, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told the Los Angeles Times that the raid outside the Prop 50 event was focused on enforcing the law, not on Newsom.

But the actual motive had nothing to do with safety, as shown by the agent’s observations, Newsom said Wednesday, citing the deposition and other filings in the case.

“Donald Trump’s own DHS agents admitted it UNDER OATH!” Newsom wrote in a social media post. “The president deliberately sent masked, heavily armed ICE agents to target our campaign kickoff on democracy.”

Newsom frequently cites the incident as evidence that Trump is a threat to democracy. Earlier this month, he mentioned it again during an event in Los Angeles, characterizing the raid as an effort to intimidate people from participating in his political rally.

“Folks couldn’t get into the event because there were masked men that were standing outside,” Newsom said. “It was a preview of things to come.”

One text exchange Newsom highlighted described the action as a “stunt.”

The morning after the event, the special agent texted another agent, saying, “Hopefully I can get replaced soon.”

When the lawyer questioning the HSI agent asked whether marching to the Newsom event constituted “the straw that broke the camel’s back for you,” the agent responded: “It was definitely one of them, yes.”

The agent said they were also disturbed by operations in which teams targeted Home Depot stores, which at the time violated a court order preventing agents from conducting enforcement actions at Home Depots and car washes, locations where the workers are largely Latino.

The agent said the Home Depot operations “weren’t in good faith because they weren’t solely going after just the targets,” and that he was disturbed by “being put in a position to potentially violate like a (temporary restraining order).”

Less than a month after Bovino’s appearance at the Newsom press conference, the Supreme Court overturned the temporary restraining order that had limited federal immigration officers’ enforcement actions in Los Angeles. The ruling allowed immigration officers to seize suspected illegal immigrants in Los Angeles based on how they looked, spoke or where they worked.

text:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security says it has terminated Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for people from Haiti, Syria and Yemen. The notice comes as lower district courts have still not executed a Supreme Court ruling officially ending the program.

Several notices from DHS tell employers they cannot continue to employ a person who does not have proof of an up to date work authorization. They also note that work authorization for TPS-holders from Haiti, Syria and Yemen are no longer valid.

The announcement adds to the already confusing state of TPS.

After the Supreme Court ruled that the administration could continue terminating TPS designation, the case was sent back down to the lower courts. TPS holders are still waiting for district judges to issue their final orders on whether the program will end.

The legal limbo leaves hundreds of thousands of people uncertain if they will lose the legal ability to live and work in the U.S.

title: Kids have no lawyers in immigration court, even as feds spend millions - NewsNation
description:
In a statement provided to NewsNation, Acacia accuses the federal government of demanding confidential information that it has no legal right to obtain.
The law firm also says that the federal government owes Acacia $65 million for legal services that have already been provided.
It did not specifically address a question about whether it declined a bridge contract with ORR that would extend beyond Friday.
150K unlocated migrant children found under Trump administration: Feds The 1,800 children in ORR care are down from 22,000 the agency was caring for under the Biden administration, Fabbricatore said.
Like the feud between the feds and the law firm, the search for more unaccounted-for migrant minors continues, which Fabbricatore admits remains a difficult process.
text:
(NewsNation) — The federal agency overseeing care for 1,800 migrant minors who arrive at the border unaccompanied by an adult alleges that a law firm contracted to represent those kids is, in many cases, forcing thousands of them to appear in court unaccompanied by legal representation.

The Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement tells NewsNation it became concerned when 60% of minors the federal government is legally required to represent showed up in court without a lawyer.

The federal government was fully funding the deal, paying an estimated $20 million per month to contract with a Washington, D.C.-based law firm, Acacia Center For Justice, to represent the minors in court hearings.

ORR told NewsNation that it repeatedly asked Acacia to provide documentation indicating which migrant minors received representation or what legal services were provided before the government paid the invoices turned in by the law firm. The federal agency says that despite the continued requests for the paperwork, Acacia has failed to respond.

John Fabbricatore, a senior adviser to HHS and ORR, told NewsNation Thursday that the agency began noticing discrepancies in the cases in which Acacia said it had represented migrant minors.

In some of those cases, those children were no longer in the United States, and in other cases, there were discrepancies in the age of the children receiving legal representation. He also said that in many cases, Acacia was declining to provide information that ORR had already provided and was asking for in return, raising more red flags.

“I think it’s important for the American taxpayer and for these children to make sure that with the money that we’re putting out, every child has a representative,” Fabbricatore said.

He added: “We need to really examine all of the records to determine if there was some fraud there. I don’t want to come forward and say there actually was, but that’s why it’s important to work together to ensure that the services we are paying for …are actually being provided.”

Acacia says funding doesn’t cover legal representation for all migrant minors

The current bridge contract expires Friday. ORR says it has tried three times since late 2025 to award a new contract, but each procurement has been delayed by bid protests, preventing a new award. ORR says it offered Acacia a second bridge contract requiring documentation to support future invoices, but says the organization declined the offer.

In a statement provided to NewsNation, Acacia accuses the federal government of demanding confidential information that it has no legal right to obtain. The law firm also says that the federal government owes Acacia $65 million for legal services that have already been provided.

“The Trump administration is trying to sabotage this program by challenging paperwork as a pretext to strip away legal rights for thousands of undocumented children,” Acacia told NewsNation in a prepared statement. “This issue is not about paperwork or even non-payment of the bills it owes.

“It’s about more than 20,000 vulnerable immigrant children who deserve to have someone in their corner and not be left alone without legal counsel to navigate our very complex immigration system.”

Fabbricatore told NewsNation that Acacia has acknowledged to the federal government that some of the children did not receive legal representation. In its statement to NewsNation, the law firm says it provides legal representation to as many children as possible within the constraints of the funding provided by ORR.

The firm maintains that the contract does not provide enough money for all the children it is contracted to represent to receive those services. It did not specifically address a question about whether it declined a bridge contract with ORR that would extend beyond Friday.

“We will do everything we can to protect vulnerable immigrant children and ensure they have the legal protection they deserve,” the firm’s statement said.

In response to Acacia’s claims about not being paid for services rendered, ORR told NewsNation that in the United States, services are delivered and paid for with proof. A governmental contract is no exception.

“The government has every right to know which children in its custody are receiving the legal representation that the American taxpayer is paying for,” the agency said. “Demanding basic accountability is not unreasonable, it is a minimum standard.”

Fabbricatore said the lack of representation has forced ORR to seek another contract with another firm to ensure that children are being properly represented. He said the agency has contingency plans in place, including using attorneys from other federal agencies, if a new contract cannot be secured within the next couple of days.

150K unlocated migrant children found under Trump administration: Feds

The 1,800 children in ORR care are down from 22,000 the agency was caring for under the Biden administration, Fabbricatore said.

While declining to provide specifics, Fabbricatore said ORR has raised the issue to other federal agencies that could become involved.

The dispute over legal services comes as the Trump administration says it has located 150,000 of the more than 300,000 children who went missing after arriving at the border unaccompanied without an adult after being smuggled into the United States. More than 540,000 unaccompanied children have been apprehended at the southern border since Biden took office in 2021, according to DHS data obtained via NewsNation sources.

That compares to 287,276 unaccompanied children who were taken into custody in the previous six fiscal years combined between 2015 and 2020.

Officials announced in June that 146,000 of those missing migrant minors have been located since President Donald Trump took office, blaming the Biden administration for allowing so many children to enter the country illegally between 2021 and 2024.

In many cases, those children were abused, assaulted and exploited during the process of being trafficked across the border by criminal sponsors, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said. Those criminals, working with Mexican drug cartels to move the children across the border, often sponsored multiple migrant children, Blanche said, which required them to lie to U.S. government officials, claiming they were close relatives of the children being trafficked into the country.

A woman recently pleaded guilty in El Paso for being part of a child trafficking ring where they drugged the kids with THC gummies to get them across the border. Dianne Guadian, 33, pleaded guilty in a federal court to four counts of aiding and abetting the smuggling of unauthorized migrants for financial gain, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

As the dispute continues, Fabbricatore said ORR is working to reunite children with their parents back in their home country or to find suitable care for them with foster sponsors and families who can care for them while they remain in the United States.

Like the feud between the feds and the law firm, the search for more unaccounted-for migrant minors continues, which Fabbricatore admits remains a difficult process. He says information provided by the previous administration and vetting processes used to vet potential sponsors has complicated the matter.

“It has been publicized that we’re looking so for those who know that we’re looking, they’re hiding a little bit more and it’s a little more difficult (to find them),” he told NewsNation. “So yes, we are still on this mission and we’re still looking for these children, but it’s been very difficult.”
