title: Could Trump Haitian immigrant crackdown hurt the economy? What to know - USA Today
description:
Now, they warn, the Trump administration’s sweeping crackdown on immigration is threatening that labor pool.
Immigration rights groups expect the Trump administration will also end TPS for immigrants from other countries.
Does TPS help or hurt American workers?
A group of economists told the Supreme Court in April that deporting immigrant workers does not lift wages or provide meaningful benefits to American workers.
The brief cites research that says deporting TPS recipients would reduce job opportunities for U.S. workers.
text:
For years, employers from Florida to Ohio have relied on immigrants taking part in a humanitarian program to staff hard-to-fill job openings for construction workers and home health aides.

Now, they warn, the Trump administration’s sweeping crackdown on immigration is threatening that labor pool.

More than 300,000 Haitian migrants are set to lose their Temporary Protected Status that allows them to live and work in the United States.

The Supreme Court last month cleared the way for Haitians who sought sanctuary in the United States after natural disasters and political unrest in the Caribbean island nation to lose that protection. The ruling also covers about 6,000 people from Syria, which endured a devastating civil war from 2011 to 2024.

Immigration rights groups expect the Trump administration will also end TPS for immigrants from other countries.

“The T in TPS stands for temporary,” James Percival, general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security, said last month on Fox News. “It is closing time. You don’t have to go home but you can’t stay here.”

Businesses brace for TPS impact

Trump’s reforms worry Mark Zandi. The chief economist at Moody's Analytics says immigrants are a key ingredient in the American economy’s “secret sauce.”

More workers filling jobs and spending money spurs economic expansion, creating more jobs.

“The highly restrictive immigration policies are a significant headwind to economic growth and a tailwind to the uncomfortably high inflation,” Zandi said. “Many industries are struggling to replace immigrant workers who are leaving the workforce, most notably agriculture, construction, manufacturing, transportation, leisure and hospitality and personal services. This is limiting the ability of these industries to expand and raising their costs and thus inflation.”

The potential loss of workers in key industries has set off alarm bells in the business community. Trade groups have mobilized, warning of looming economic disruptions in industries already facing chronic labor shortages.

Some 830,000 TPS recipients are part of the U.S. labor force, principally in construction, retail and wholesale, leisure and hospitality, transportation and business services, according to a recent estimate from pro-immigration think tank Fwd.us.

The sudden loss of Haitian-born workers would be “especially acute” in health care and caregiving occupations and could affect “the delivery of care and other essential services” in nursing homes and other facilities, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce warned in a July 10 letter to Senate leadership.

With 50 to 75 job openings at any one time, Goodwin Living President, an Alexandria, Virginia, nonprofit that provides health care, hospice and housing services to about 5,000 older adults, is always on the lookout for qualified workers, from nursing assistants to housekeepers.

Of Goodwin Living’s 1,500 employees, 70% hail from foreign countries. As a result of the White House’s immigration reforms, the organization has hemorrhaged seven staff members in the last couple years, according to CEO Rob Liebreich.

“When you lose people who are doing great work, it's really hard to find replacements for them. And, even when you do, those replacements don't come with the same knowledge and developed relationships that the people that have been with us had,” Liebreich said.

He says he’s living the workforce version of Jenga – the more wooden blocks you pull, the greater risk the whole structure will collapse. The loss of the existing labor pool just as demand from the nation’s aging population is rising will make it harder for seniors to get care and will drive up the cost of that care, Liebreich said.

“At a time where we actually need more hands, we're pulling away these pieces and taking away parts which would give us more hands,” he said. “Every American has a vested interest in having more capable hands available.”

Rebecca Shi, CEO of the American Business Immigration Coalition, said fewer immigrant workers will weaken industries like Liebreich’s already struggling to keep pace with demand. TPS recipients account for 15% of noncitizen healthcare workers.

“If our goal is to strengthen the U.S. economy, we should be keeping vetted, work-authorized people on the job, not creating chaos for employers, workers and the communities that depend on them,” Shi said.

Does TPS help or hurt American workers?

Established by Congress in 1990, TPS gives temporary protection to people who don’t feel safe returning to countries plagued by disaster or armed conflict such as El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua.

President Barack Obama granted this status to Haitians in 2010 after an earthquake devastated their island. Trump unsuccessfully tried to end TPS during his first term; it was then extended under the Biden administration.

When Trump returned to office last year, he moved to end the TPS status of about 1.3 million immigrants from 17 countries legally living in the United States under the program as part of his immigration reforms that he says are critical to securing the livelihood of U.S.-born workers. The White House said in a recent economic report that "record flows of illegal immigrants depressed wages for Americans, inflated the demand for housing and drained the welfare system."

Critics argue a program offering short-term amnesty in emergency situations has expanded beyond its original intent. Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Missouri, recently called TPS a “one-way racket towards permanent mass migration” on the Senate floor.

That resulting migration is a drain on public resources and on taxpayers, they say. “The Trump administration is right to let these overused TPS programs expire as originally intended,” Daniel West, director of government relations for Heritage Action, the lobbying arm of the Heritage Foundation, said in a statement.

Some Republicans don’t agree. Mike DeWine, the Republican governor of Ohio, told CBS that deporting Haitian migrants – thousands of whom live in his state – is a “mistake” that will kill jobs and damage the local economy.

"These are people who have helped Springfield really come back," DeWine said of Haitians who have filled jobs and opened businesses in his hometown. "The Haitians who are living there and employed there, they came there to work and they came there because there were jobs that were not being filled by other people."

Economic ripples from ending Temporary Protected Status

Broadly speaking, economists say they don’t anticipate widespread economic reverberations including labor shortages.

“The truth is even with all the TPS termination and deportations, we are talking about fewer than a million people losing work authorization or being deported from inside the U.S. cumulatively since the start of the Trump administration. This is out of a labor force of nearly 170 million people,” said Daniel Di Martino, a fellow at the Manhattan Institute who researches immigration. “So any labor market impact of immigration is very limited and only concentrated in more affected industries that employ illegal immigrants in specific areas such as the Miami metro area.”

How limited and how concentrated is a matter of some debate.

A group of economists told the Supreme Court in April that deporting immigrant workers does not lift wages or provide meaningful benefits to American workers. In fact, they said, eliminating the TPS program could result in the loss of more than 600,000 American jobs in four years.

TPS recipients are homeowners and taxpayers who “are overwhelmingly employed, pay billions annually in taxes and fill essential roles in healthcare, construction, transportation and food production,” the amicus brief read.

The brief cites research that says deporting TPS recipients would reduce job opportunities for U.S. workers. In fact, a recent study showed that a large and sudden increase in deportations causes a "substantial reduction” in the employment of American workers because fewer new businesses open and more existing businesses close, these economists said.

The construction industry has seen the largest drop in employment, according to Elizabeth Cox, a University of Colorado Boulder professional research assistant in the economics department. Service sector jobs in auto repair shops, commercial machinery repair shops, nail salons and dry cleaning businesses have also recorded substantial declines.

“We see that there has been a decline in employment for both immigrants – authorized and unauthorized – and U.S.-born workers in response to the heightened ICE activity from 2025. Importantly, there's also no evidence that wages have increased in response to immigration enforcement for either of these groups,” Cox told USA TODAY. “This is largely counter to the narrative we often see in the media, that deportations will create better job opportunities for U.S.-born workers. The evidence instead suggests that enforcement has hurt the labor market by decreasing employment with no change to wages.”

Communities with large TPS populations will feel the effects most sharply, from higher prices and longer waits for home repairs and remodels to scarcer care options for young children or aging parents, said Stan Veuger, an economist with the American Enterprise Institute.

A recent study from economists at the University of Utah’s Eccles School of Business found that increased deportations caused nearly 2,000 fewer homes to be built per state per year, resulting in an 18% increase in new home prices.

“When you suddenly reduce immigration a lot or you suddenly deport a lot of people, it doesn’t make people's lives enormously better,” Veuger said. “It really is not an economic boom for the workers who remain.”

text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WKRN) — A nursing mother seeking asylum is being held nearly 700 miles away from her two young children after federal immigration agents detained her outside her Antioch home, according to her attorneys, who argue the arrest violated both the U.S. Constitution and Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s own policies.

The woman, identified in court filings by the pseudonym “Maria Perez” because of concerns for her safety, was detained as she prepared to take her children to a medical appointment, her attorneys said. She is now being held at an immigration detention facility in Louisiana while her 10-month-old infant and 2-year-old son with Down syndrome remain in Tennessee.

Attorneys representing Perez said her son’s medical care has already been disrupted.

“She was standing by her car, taking care of her children, and they ripped her away,” said Katie Blankenship, an attorney with Sanctuary of the South.

Blankenship contends ICE agents arrested Perez without a judicial warrant or legal justification.

“There is no search warrant. There is no probable cause. There is no basis at all to speaking to her, much less arresting her,” Blankenship said.

According to her attorneys, Perez fled domestic violence in Guatemala and has lived in the United States since 2022 while pursuing an asylum claim. They said she has no criminal history, is diabetic, and was forced to abruptly stop breastfeeding while being taken into custody.

Amy Fischer with Amnesty International USA criticized Perez’s transfer to Louisiana.

“Louisiana is known as the black hole of immigration detention,” Fischer said. “Detention facilities are particularly known to be cruel and particularly known to be difficult to access for attorneys.”

Perez’s legal team argues her detention also conflicts with ICE’s own policy, which generally discourages the detention of pregnant, postpartum, or nursing mothers unless extraordinary circumstances exist.

“They are not supposed to be ripping mothers from their own babies,” Blankenship said. “The only way they can justify that is if they can somehow claim Maria is a threat to our national security.”

During an immigration hearing Wednesday, a judge denied Perez’s request for bond and declined to expedite her asylum proceedings, according to her attorneys, ruling the court lacked jurisdiction over that request.

Perez’s attorneys said they now plan to file a federal habeas petition in Louisiana and pursue additional constitutional claims challenging her detention.

The Department of Homeland Security told News 2 it planned to provide a statement. ICE did not respond to multiple requests for comment before publication.

title: Don't call them ICE detention centers. Call them camps | John Washington | The Guardian
description:
We don’t have concentration camps today in the United States, but we have something close.
Concentration camps under the Third Reich began not with the extermination camps of Auschwitz or Treblinka, but as holding centers that incarcerated alleged subversives.
This is the history that we must invoke to help us understand, and ultimately close, today’s immigration camps.
A definitional aspect of detention camps is that they strip people of, or at least diminish, their legal personhood.
In immigration camps, along with concentration camps, people are locked up because of who they are or where they are from.
text:
We don’t have concentration camps today in the United States, but we have something close. More than 65,000 people are currently confined in demeaning, often dangerous, sometimes torturous and increasingly deadly conditions not because they have committed a crime, but because they have committed the civil infraction of being on the wrong side of a border. They are ripped from their homes, their families, their jobs and are shipped hundreds of miles away where they languish in squalid, freezing cold and punishing conditions with limited and sometimes no access to lawyers, loved ones, nutritious food, sunlight or medical care. At least 52 people have died in ICE custody since the second Trump administration came into office. Tens of thousands have been held in solitary confinement.

Oversight mechanisms of these facilities have been gutted, members of Congress have been turned away, and ICE has stopped reporting basic and legally mandated data about who is inside and what happens to them. The rapid expansion of the detention system, the inherent inhumanity of policing human mobility, and lack of oversight is partly why a woman in Arizona, who has been detained for 16 months without proper medical care to treat her leukemia, has reportedly lost more than 70lb and is regularly vomiting blood. It’s why people in a now shuttered camp in Florida were allegedly subjected to a two-by-two-foot outdoor punishment cage. The stories that leak out of these camps should terrify not only the migrants directly targeted, but should alarm the conscience of us all.

Calling such facilities “detention centers” sanitizes their brutal and increasingly deadly reality. Calling them “Alligator Alcatraz” or the “Cornhole Clink” sensationalizes them.

As a journalist who has spent a decade reporting on immigration and border enforcement, I’ve dedicated much of my career to trying to expose a reality glossed over and concealed by whitewashing official designations. Which is why I’ve started to call them camps, not only because of the accurate historical resonance of the term, but as a warning. The word camp best captures the political function they serve: concentrating, immobilizing and excluding populations deemed unwanted.

Concentration camps under the Third Reich began not with the extermination camps of Auschwitz or Treblinka, but as holding centers that incarcerated alleged subversives. They followed a model first developed in Cuba and South Africa by the Spanish and British respectively at the end of the 19th century, and later mirrored in the United States with Japanese American “internment camps”. This is the history that we must invoke to help us understand, and ultimately close, today’s immigration camps. The Italian philosopher Giorgio Agamben calls the variations of camps a “progression”, suggesting that there is slippage among them.

A definitional aspect of detention camps is that they strip people of, or at least diminish, their legal personhood. And while people held in immigration camps are not completely outside the sphere of law, they are mocked by the law. As the scholar Dan Stone writes of people held in immigration camps: “They are very close to falling into [philosopher Hannah] Arendt’s category of the superfluous stateless person from whom the ‘right to have rights’ has been removed.”

A concentration camp, in its most basic definition, is a place where a targeted civilian population, not necessarily accused of a crime, is detained and at least some of their basic rights are suspended. That’s precisely what’s happening in the United States today. We don’t need to stretch history or force an analogy to see how the term applies to immigration detention: US officials have long used the term themselves. FDR called for concentration camps to detain Japanese Americans even before the second world war, and then built them to lock away more than 120,000 people during the war. In a 1981 memo, released as the Reagan administration began caging tens of thousands of Cuban and Haitian refugees, an immigration taskforce worried that “the appearance of ‘concentration camps’ which, at the present time, would be filled largely by blacks, may be publicly unacceptable”. They used scare quotes, but successive administrations have only expanded the immigration camp system in the United States.

While the prison system is also rife with suffering and injustice, there is at least a semblance of court regulation and due process. People suffering inside prisons or jails are there, the logic goes, because of something they allegedly did. In immigration camps, along with concentration camps, people are locked up because of who they are or where they are from. That is an even more penetrating attack on their personhood.

Not only is the current administration spending billions to try to rapidly grow the camp system, they are trying to make it more painful and permanent. Last fall, the Board of Immigration Appeals ruled that no undocumented migrants who entered the country without inspection would be eligible for release on bond. The camp became mandatory: indefinite detention without the benefit of trial by jury. And while the fifth circuit recently ruled that people held under that mandatory detention statute must get a bond hearing within 90 days, that ruling merely claws back a modicum of rule of law. Nobody gets released because of the ruling. They just, for now, get to make their case for freedom every 90 days instead of never. An appeal from the government is expected.

Meanwhile, despite some rollbacks of the spectacular violence seen in the streets of Minneapolis and elsewhere, more immigrants than ever before are being arrested in this country, and tens of thousands of them – abducted off the streets – will suffer for weeks, months, or longer in the camps. Recent reporting detailed just how cramped some of these facilities can be, with 86 people at one point held in a small room – a “closet of humanity that smelled of sweat, urine and feces”. In one notoriously abusive Texas camp, one person said he was told: “You’re only getting out deported or dead.”

Immigration camps in the United States today disappear people politically before, all too frequently, they disappear them physically. To combat the suffering we should use language that reveals the inhumanity rather than conceals it. The word camp does just that.

title: At least 11 Bay Area residents have been detained in ICE airport crackdown
authors: Sara DiNatale, Ko Lyn Cheang, Staff Writers
description:
At least 11 Bay Area residents have been ensnared in the crackdown in the last three weeks, according to immigration attorneys, relatives and witnesses.
Before the most recent detentions, ICE agents in airports mainly targeted those with judge-issued removal orders or administrative warrants.
Another Oakland woman was waiting for a connecting flight in Phoenix when ICE agents detained her.
She is representing the three friends who flew out of SFO for vacation, only to be immediately met by ICE agents after landing in Los Angeles.

text:
A newlywed on her way home after celebrating her marriage to her American husband with friends.

A professional athlete who’d previously been granted a visa for sportsmen with extraordinary abilities. A student about to start a master’s degree. Three friends who planned a short trip to Southern California are now sitting in detention centers.

All of them were flying to or from the San Francisco International Airport when they were detained by immigration agents, as part of a new front in the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign. At least 11 Bay Area residents have been ensnared in the crackdown in the last three weeks, according to immigration attorneys, relatives and witnesses.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Bay Area politicians, immigration attorneys and civil rights activists are now warning immigrants with unresolved immigration issues to avoid traveling through airports if possible.

“Ask any immigration attorney, whether they’ve been practicing for five years or 40 years, the types of actions that we’re seeing at airports across the countries is essentially unheard of,” said Ghassan Shamieh, a San Francisco-based immigration attorney who represents the newlywed and professional athlete, who both declined to be interviewed.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is now targeting foreign citizens with expired travel visas for detention, even when they have U.S. spouses, no criminal records, no removal order against them and have pending applications for legal immigration statuses — a group that federal immigration agents have not historically focused on detaining.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to provide the number of airport arrests it has performed over the last two weeks. An agency spokesperson said the Trump administration reversed a “horrendous Biden-era policy” and was now ensuring “aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.” But even during the first Trump administration, ICE agents weren’t targeting airport travelers with ongoing immigration cases.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Shamieh said that he believes there are two reasons for ICE stepping up airport arrests. First, it is “low-hanging fruit,” he said, in the sense that when someone books a flight, they must share sensitive personal information that the Transportation Security Administration can share with ICE. Second, he said, given the backlash that ICE agents have faced after large-scale enforcement operations in cities like Minnesota, making arrests at airports, behind the closed doors of security lines, provides ICE agents with relatively less public exposure and scrutiny.

“The manner in which ICE has detained them is what we find problematic,” Shamieh said. “That they’ve done this without a pre-deprivation hearing.”

Five of his clients have been detained at airports in Los Angeles, San Francisco and Phoenix in the past two weeks. Four of those had pending asylum applications, which generally provides individuals temporary legal authorization to remain in the country and protection from deportation until a decision is made. The fifth had pending visa applications, he said. None had criminal records, he said.

“Because of this expansion, it’s not safe for people with uncertain immigration status to fly right now, including for anyone currently in the process of changing their status,” state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, said in a statement Wednesday. “People with uncertain immigration status may want to consult with an immigration attorney before deciding whether to fly.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The New York Times reported Tuesday that immigration agents in plain clothes have been picking up people with expired visas across 15 airports, including San Francisco. At least 27 arrests across nine states, including California, targeted those with expired visas, ABC News reported. Before the most recent detentions, ICE agents in airports mainly targeted those with judge-issued removal orders or administrative warrants.

On July 20, agents picked up one Oakland woman from Ecuador while she tried to board a flight in Denver. Another Oakland woman was waiting for a connecting flight in Phoenix when ICE agents detained her. A Richmond City Council member filmed a photographer and cafe worker, a woman from the Ukraine, being detained by ICE at San Francisco Airport as she was returning from a trip to Portland.

Rep. Kevin Mullin, D-San Mateo, whose district includes SFO, told the Chronicle in a statement that he’s “concerned about reports of ICE operations at Bay Area airports.”

“Trump’s chaotic ICE deployments across the U.S. have been incredibly unsafe for communities, including for citizens and non-citizens who are in this country legally,” Mullin said in a statement. “Airports should not become an ICE enforcement zone to round people up.”

San Francisco-based immigration attorney Kyra Lilien said her firm is advising clients to avoid air travel if they have an ongoing asylum case, pending green card application or any other non-permanent status that may be in transition or pending approval.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Lilien, a former immigration judge who lost her job under Trump, said ICE agents’ recent actions are worrisome for anyone with a nonpermanent status, including those who have valid work visas.

She is representing the three friends who flew out of SFO for vacation, only to be immediately met by ICE agents after landing in Los Angeles. The friends all came to the Bay Area on student visas and have since applied for asylum, she said. Another client, a green card applicant from Southern California, was planning to visit a Bay Area friend but was detained as soon as they landed at SFO.

“These are people who are complying with the process, who have done everything asked of them,” Lilien said. “They have no criminal histories and they’re not a threat to anybody.”

ICE agents in March arrested a mother at SFO, but in that case the family had an outstanding removal order from 2019.

People with expired visas span a broad category that covers hundreds of thousands of people, including those married to U.S. citizens, skilled workers and people with valid work permits issued by the federal government while awaiting green cards or visa extensions. They lack permanent legal status but, in most cases, are actively trying to obtain it.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Many of the recent airport arrests involved asylum-seekers who were awaiting interviews with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, their attorneys said. The Trump administration earlier this week announced plans to bypass that interview process to cut down on backlongs and put pending cases before judges sooner. Lilien said ICE’s airport crackdown dovetails with that policy shift because it’s another way to “pluck” people from the process of applying for citizenship and, instead, drop them into courtrooms and detention centers.

The recent arrests suggest ICE is using flight passenger information to locate non-citizens for arrest, the American Civil Liberties Union is warning on its website. Attorneys with the San Francisco-based Asian Law Caucus also believe the Transportation Security Administration, which handles airport security, is sharing passenger information with ICE. TSA did not respond when asked if the agency was sharing passenger information with immigration officials.

Abraham Sanchez, the husband of the Oakland woman detained in Phoenix, wrote in a GoFundMe plea seeking donations to help cover his wife’s legal fees that an officer approached the couple with a photo of his wife, Mabel, on his phone.

“(He) asked her to confirm her name, and took her away,” Sanchez said on the fundraising website. “She spent the first night detained near the airport, and the next day was taken to Eloy Detention Center.”

Sanchez said his wife has a pending asylum claim and a work permit.

Chantal Rojas, the Oakland woman detained in Denver, entered the country legally in 2023 on a J-1, or exchange visa, as an au pair, her attorney Lauren Lichter said in a statement.

“She followed the rules of her program and, before it ended, timely filed an application with U.S. immigration authorities that allowed her to remain in the country while her case has been pending,” Lichter said.

A woman detained at San Francisco International Airport last week, 38-year-old Iryna Gorb, had lived in the city for over a decade. Wiener said he is troubled that ICE wants to deport her back to war-torn Ukraine.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security called Gorb an “illegal alien” with an expired visa. The video of her detention, filmed by Richmond City Council Member Doria Robinson, spread quickly online last week.

In the recording, Gorb can be heard screaming for help. She’s now being held at an ICE detention center in California City. One of Lilien’s Bay Area clients is now at a detention center in Texas.

Immigration attorneys have been challenging many of the arrests, seeking to get their clients released from detention.

A judge ordered the release of Shamieh’s professional athlete client on Wednesday.

A separate judge recently ruled that another one of Shamieh’s clients could be released on $35,000 bond, an “exorbitant” amount he said is almost unheard of. The Department of Homeland Security has 30 days to appeal, after which she may be released.

text:
Since the start of last year, ICE and Border Patrol, encouraged by the Administration’s mass deportation agenda, have committed countless unlawful abuses against immigrants and U.S. citizens, with no end in sight. Earlier this month, ICE agents fatally shot Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Colombian national Joan Sebastian Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine. Salgado Araujo had lived in the U.S. for 35 years and was in the process of obtaining legal status while Guerrero was not even the target of the ICE operation that took his life and the reason he was stopped is still unclear. ICE agents in both these shootings were not wearing body cameras. Congress has further greenlighted these repeated abuses that have caused serious injuries and preventable deaths by providing nearly $250 billion in extra funding that mostly goes to ICE and Border Patrol since last year.

Across the country, AILA members have been in the trenches responding to the crisis-level needs of their clients, forcefully defending them in immigration courts, filing emergency habeas petitions in federal court to demand their clients’ release, and more. In these trying times, these efforts constitute a last line of defense to uphold the rule of law and ensure that no one’s rights are trampled.

Since the onslaught of unlawful government abuse began, AILA members have also fought back in the halls of Congress. More than 1,600 AILA members have urged their elected officials to block more funding for ICE and Border Patrol by sending over 5,300 messages this year. While we lost that fight in June with Congress giving DHS another $70 billion in reconciliation funding, we are starting to win the war in public opinion which has shifted dramatically against the administration’s agenda.

During this year’s appropriations and reconciliation fights, AILA has focused its legislative asks on specific, actionable demands to make American communities safer and ensure the rule of law is followed. These demands include enforceable consequences for unlawful ICE actions as well as prohibiting racial and other forms of profiling. AILA has also called for requiring probable cause and warrants before any arrests or entry onto private property, banning immigration enforcement at sensitive locations, and reallocating funds away from immigration detention and toward helping the American people deal with the ongoing affordability crisis.

AILA’s advocacy, along with pressure from partner organizations, helped secure a modest legislative victory in March when the FY2026 DHS appropriations bill passed without additional funding for ICE or Border Patrol enforcement operations.

Throughout this process, AILA issued statements and vote recommendations warning about the harmful and violent impact this funding would have on American communities. Regrettably, ICE and Border Patrol continued to perpetrate abuses against immigrants and U.S. citizens alike, including multiple serious incidents over just the past two months.

In addition to the two fatal shootings mentioned above, ICE arrested and briefly detained a Nigerian nun, who is also a registered nurse, as she was walking to Mass in Texas and arrested a student on a community college campus in Washington. According to the college president, the ICE agents failed to provide their names, badges, or a warrant when asked. U.S. citizens have not been immune from unlawful ICE actions, like when a Spanish-speaking U.S. citizen was stopped, handcuffed, and interrogated for hours in Louisiana even after showing a valid state ID and valid Social Security card. She was only able to be released after a lawyer intervened. These incidents, and many others, are in large part the result of the failure to implement reforms, like the ones in AILA’s legislative asks, that pave the way for accountability, oversight, and reform in ICE and Border Patrol enforcement operations.

To address the urgent need for reform, last month AILA released its Principles for America’s Future, a comprehensive, forward-looking vision for immigration reform, including immigration enforcement. To stop continued ICE and Border Patrol abuses, AILA urges Congress to create a robust, independent oversight body with the power to stop continued ICE and Border Patrol abuses. Immigration agents should also be required to undergo extensive law enforcement training, use body-worn cameras, and identify themselves during enforcement operations, with enforceable consequences for violations of these requirements. In addition, immigration enforcement should prioritize violent criminals instead of relying on indiscriminate detentions, and immigration enforcement activities should be prohibited at sensitive locations.

text:
The ACLU of Washington filed its intent to sue the Department of Homeland Security on Tuesday, July 28, on behalf of a family held for nearly a month at the Blaine Border Patrol Station in 2025.

The civil rights organization claims U.S. Customs and Border Protection violated its own policies when it held the family of six asylum seekers, one of whom was five months pregnant with a high-risk pregnancy, in a single “unbearably hot and filthy” cell, according to the legal filing.

The family, which includes mother Josefina, father Jose, and four children, ages 13, 10, 5 and 11 months, arrived in the United States in 2024, seeking asylum after Jose was persecuted for being a member of an opposition political party.

A year later, in April 2025, an immigration judge denied the family’s request for more time to prove their asylum claim and found the family to be deportable, according to the ACLU.

With few options, the family fled to Canada to request asylum there. However, they were detained at the border by immigration agents.

Typically, immigrants who are deemed to be deportable and are detained are transferred to a detainment facility, such as the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, within hours and for up to 72 hours. But in the case of Josefina and Jose, they were made to stay inside a single windowless cell at the Blaine border station for a month, according to the ACLU.

“My children were confused and scared about why they were trapped in this cell, why they could not go outside and why they had no toys to play with,” Josefina said in a news release. “They cried all the time. I wanted to comfort them but had no answers to give them.”

While detained in Blaine, Josefina experienced multiple medical episodes related to her pregnancy and diabetes diagnosis, two of which required hospitalization. Doctors told Customs and Border Protection staff the conditions Josefina was being held in were unsafe.

After the second hospitalization, federal agents allowed the family out of the cell once a week to sanitize the cell. The family was released from custody after four weeks and continues to reside within Washington state.

“Months after their cruel incarceration, our clients’ mental and emotional scars remain,” said David Montes, an ACLU Washington staff attorney, in a news release.

Recently, the 13-year-old said he didn’t want to go to an upcoming immigration hearing out of fear the family would be arrested and returned to the Blaine cell, according to the legal claim.

The ACLU alleges the agency knew holding the family, including a pregnant woman and children, would be harmful to their health and well-being. The group also alleges the agency should not have held the family in Blaine for four weeks, rather that the family should have been transferred to a separate facility within 72 hours.

The ACLU intends to seek $15 million in damages for the family. The intent to sue over the Blaine incident is just one of 54 claims brought by the ACLU in recent days against federal law enforcement in July.

The Department of Homeland Security has six months to respond to the claims. It did not immediately respond to comment from Cascadia Daily News.

text:
The Justice Department is proposing a new rule to empower federal immigration judges to hold attorneys, their clients and witnesses in contempt if they violate court orders, in a move that departs from historical practice and which legal experts warn could be unconstitutional.

The regulatory proposal by the Executive Office for Immigration Review, an office of the DOJ that runs the immigration court system, would allow immigration judges for the very first time to impose fines ranging from $1,000 up to as much as $3,500 if an attorney or other individual continues to defy court orders.

"It is crucial for immigration judges to have every tool available—including the authority to impose civil money penalties—to control the proceedings before them," the Justice Department wrote in its proposal.

The proposal notably exempts federal government employees, such as Department of Homeland Security attorneys, from being subject to any contempt order by an immigration judge — in what critics say represents a lopsided and unfair scenario that would allow potential government misconduct to go unchecked.

In federal district courts, by contrast, Article III judges have the power to hold all attorneys who appear before the court in criminal or civil contempt, if warranted. In its proposal, the Justice Department argues that giving immigration judges the power to sanction government lawyers is not necessary because DHS attorneys can be disciplined by the Office of the Inspector General or the Office of Professional Responsibility.

"By proposing a completely skewed regulation that empowers judges to hold in contempt only the attorneys for immigrants but not ICE attorneys, the Administration has revealed that its goal has nothing to do with the just and balanced rule of law. Instead, this rule is another effort to target immigration attorneys that falls in line with the President's intimidation tactics," said Gregory Chen, senior director of government relations at the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

The new proposal marks the latest in a series of efforts by the Trump administration to more readily crack down on immigration and carry out President Trump's mass deportation policies.

At the Executive Office for Immigration Review, hundreds of longtime federal immigration judges have left since last year, many of whom were fired abruptly without warning or cause. In 2025, EOIR lost 370 attorneys, according to government data analyzed and published by a former FBI analyst.

At the same time it has lost so many judges, the immigration court system is facing a current backlog of more than 3.5 million cases, according to the proposed rule.

Many former immigration judges have spoken publicly about pressures they faced to expedite deportations or detain people without bond. In ads seeking to hire replacement judges, the DOJ has referred to the role as being that of a "deportation judge."

The new proposal that would allow immigration judges to hold noncitizens or their lawyers in contempt "ties into the culture of fear," said Karen Donoso Stevens, a former longtime immigration judge. "First, scare the judges. Then the judges will scare the attorneys."

The proposed rule, published in the Federal Register, states immigration judges would be allowed to sanction lawyers or their clients for a variety of offenses, from repeatedly failing to appear on time or failing to follow orders, up to disorderly conduct or making false statements.

Several legal experts who spoke with CBS News said the proposal is potentially unlawful because immigration courts are part of the executive branch and fall under Article II of the Constitution, which states that the executive branch has no contempt authority. That power belongs exclusively to the judicial and legislative branches.

The proposal is "constitutionally flawed," Chen said.

The public will have 60 days to review the proposal and submit comments.

text:
Friends, family and a U.S. congressman say a Louisvillian from Uganda is currently in a medical “crisis” after federal immigration officers detained her a week ago.

Democratic Rep. Morgan McGarvey told reporters Wednesday that Immigration Customs and Enforcement officers detained Sarafinah Bukirwa on July 22 at the Muhammad Ali International Airport. Her family said she suffers from sickle cell anemia, runs a nonprofit to treat the disease and was on her way to a sickle cell conference when she was detained.

Public records show she was taken to the Grayson County Detention Center that day and charged with an unclear immigration offense.

Previous reporting by the Kentucky Center for Investigative Reporting found that the jail is a common holding facility for women detained by ICE in Kentucky.

Since her detainment, her brother, Isaac Kabunga told Kentucky Public Radio he’s spoken with Bukirwa and visited her at the Grayson County Detention Center in Leitchfield, Kentucky. Bukirwa told him there were days in detention where she didn’t receive medication, or, would receive medicine mixed into water so she wasn’t sure what she was taking.

“This morning I received another phone call again from her, and she was telling me she really needs a hospital,” Kabunga said. “She's never experienced something like this before, and at this point, what I care about is her medical attention.”

McGarvey described the situation as "nauseating" and said he’s working with Kabunga and others to advocate for her proper medical care.

“She is sick, it is a complex medical condition,” McGarvey said at a Wednesday afternoon press conference. “She needs care. We want to make sure she's getting that care.”

McGarvey also said there were “disturbing reports” about how she was detained. In a letter to federal immigration officials, he described reports of officers hitting Bukirwa and stripping her in front of male officers.

In written statements from Bukirwa to her lawyer, she describes mocking comments from jail guards and difficulty getting blankets.

McGarvey is giving ICE officials a week to supply more information about her detention such as body camera footage and schedules for feeding and medication.

“Sarafinah shouldn’t be there in the first place,” McGarvey said. “This woman has done nothing wrong. She’s never been charged with so much as a speeding ticket.”

Bukirwa is originally from Uganda and entered the country in April 2024. Kabunga said she originally entered with a two-year tourist visa and had since applied for asylum.

Kabunga said Bukirwa was on her way to a conference in California for sickle-cell “warriors.” Online event programs show a Sickle Cell Community Consortium was held in Los Angeles beginning on July 22. Bukirwa is listed as the director of a nonprofit registered in Kentucky called “Sarafinah Sickle Cell Society / SASCELLS Inc.”

McGarvey’s office reviewed federal records and said she has a valid work authorization, a pending asylum case and has never been charged with a crime.

title: Scarborough calls on Congress to investigate activities at local ICE facility
description:
Several new laws took effect Wednesday that limit local cooperation with federal immigration agencies.
ICE in Maine Unlike many other states, Maine does not have a standalone ICE detention center.
The Scarborough processing facility is an administrative building for routine check-ins with three small, short-term holding cells.
The U.S. General Services Administration, which manages federal real estate, leased the facility from owner AEY, LLC.
Since ICE arrived at the site, local community members have regularly protested outside the facility, and hundreds demonstrated in Scarborough the day after Guerrero was killed.
text:
Members of the Scarborough Town Council voted Wednesday to pass a proclamation calling on Maine’s congressional delegation to look into the operations of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility in the town after a federal agent shot and killed a man in Biddeford earlier this month.

But residents who spoke at the town council meeting said the proclamation doesn’t go far enough.

“We’re not in charge of federal immigration policy, but all eyes in Maine are on us as the only town that hosts a facility,” said Mary Ellen Galante, a Scarborough resident and retired nurse midwife, who objected to the proclamation because it “places all of the responsibility for action on our federal delegation and not on our town.”

Galante was among the roughly 70 people who attended the packed meeting, while more than 50 others braved the rain outside holding signs calling to get ICE out of Maine.

New restrictions on state involvement in immigration enforcement take effect Wednesday

The killing of 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 has renewed scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement in Maine and many residents have called for local and state leaders to do more to protect communities in the state.

The question of how much power a community has to challenge federal activities within its jurisdiction is one that has wracked the state since President Donald Trump’s administration launched its enhanced enforcement operation in January. Several new laws took effect Wednesday that limit local cooperation with federal immigration agencies.

ICE in Maine

Unlike many other states, Maine does not have a standalone ICE detention center. The Scarborough processing facility is an administrative building for routine check-ins with three small, short-term holding cells. Detainees have historically been held in local jails or transferred to detention centers in Massachusetts or New Hampshire, or as far as Texas.

But during the meeting, several speakers raised concerns that ICE was misrepresenting what was occurring at that location.

“I think there are legitimate questions about whether the ordinances and the plans that have been put into place are consistent with what is happening in practice there,” Maine Rep. Sophie Warren, a Democrat who represents Scarborough, told Maine Morning Star. Warren presented a petition signed by more than 370 Mainers, 175 of which are Scarborough residents, calling on the council to take specific actions, including formally investigating the operations at the ICE facility and enforcing local laws and other municipal tools to rein in unlawful activities, which she said has precedence in Oregon.

The U.S. General Services Administration, which manages federal real estate, leased the facility from owner AEY, LLC. According to the agency’s lease inventory, the current 15-year lease began in 2021.

Since ICE arrived at the site, local community members have regularly protested outside the facility, and hundreds demonstrated in Scarborough the day after Guerrero was killed.

U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts made an unannounced visit to the facility on July 17, during which he said he confirmed that is where the officer who shot Guerrero works.

In December, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree also visited the building on Manson Libby Rd. after concerns were raised about attorneys not being permitted to accompany their clients to routine check-ins.

Josh Soley, the leasing and property manager for the building, said the GSA has the authority to subleaseto whichever agency they choose and that neither the state nor landlord has a say in who occupies the building.

Soley said he’s in support of the protests but believes the facility has nothing to do with what happened in Biddeford. He said people are “trying to find a place to put their voice, but I think it needs to be better targeted.”

But Scarborough councilmember Jon Anderson said that he believes Soley “must be part of this conversation.” Anderson said residents should know whether the company intends to extend the lease when it expires, and said Soley should also explore whether there’s a “mutually agreeable path” to end the lease arrangement with GSA early, “given the tragedy that occurred from the ICE agent employed at that facility.”

GSA declined to comment on the proclamation or the terms of the current lease agreement.

“I have a 20-page lease that I need to re-sign every single year and it asks me not to do unlawful activity,” Scarborough resident Sarah Lunt told the council. She added, “I would assume that that includes murdering someone in cold blood.”

Proclamation details

The proclamation asks Maine’s congressional delegation to engage with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and other agencies to review the facility and evaluate alternatives, “including the relocation or discontinuation of such operations at that location.”

It further asks for transparency and community engagement regarding federal immigration enforcement activities and for the delegation to “ensure that federal actions conducted within Maine respect human dignity, civil rights, public trust, due process, and community safety and commit to raising concerns with federal officials should evidence emerge that these standards are not being upheld.”

The town notes the proclamation should not be interpreted as opposition to lawful immigration enforcement but rather, the “expectation that such enforcement be conducted in a manner consistent with the values of safety, transparency, accountability, and respect for all people.”

While a handful of residents expressed concern that the resolution was beyond the purview of the council and would open the town to lawsuits from the federal government, the vast majority who spoke said they supported the proclamation as a first step for the town to take.

Congressional support

Ahead of the meeting, Pingree, who represents the southern Maine district that includes Biddeford and Scarborough, told the Scarborough council that the town “has every right to ask whether continuing to host this facility serves the interests of the community.”

“In my view, that question deserves serious consideration from the Department of Homeland Security,” Pingree wrote in a letter. “When a federal facility reaches the point where its very presence undermines the public confidence and leaves residents feeling less safe, the federal government has a responsibility to reconsider if that facility belongs there at all.”

Pingree added that she’s “exploring every available avenue to address enforcement operations and the continued presence of ICE in Scarborough.”

U.S. Sens. Angus King and Susan Collins, and U.S. Rep. Jared Golden did not comment on the proclamation. They previously sent a joint letter to the DHS Inspector General calling for a full, transparent investigation into the shooting and King has called for a review of ICE protocol.

title: Ohio Haitians lose jobs, face terror — and impossible choices
authors: Marty Schladen, Siddarth Sivaraman, Megan Henry
description:
With Ohio’s Haitian refugees losing their protected status Monday, Springfield’s large population has begun being terminated from their jobs, a pastor who works with the community said on Tuesday.
Early last year, Ohio’s then-Attorney General Dave Yost and 27 other Republican state AGs wrote a letter to the Trump administration stressing the word “temporary” in temporary protected status.
They claimed without evidence that it was safe for some with protected status to return to those home countries and urged a review.
Lawyers for the Haitians sued, arguing that Noem had failed to follow the 1990 law creating temporary protected status.
But for Haitians in Ohio, that might seem a thin reed on which to lean.
text:
With Ohio’s Haitian refugees losing their protected status Monday, Springfield’s large population has begun being terminated from their jobs, a pastor who works with the community said on Tuesday.

Without legal status, their work permits become invalid. They also face being forced to return to a nation that the International Rescue Committee says is “in the grip of an overwhelming humanitarian crisis.”

Right now, gangs control Haiti. Kidnapping, murder, and rape are rampant. And the pastor, Carl Ruby, said one Springfield 12-year-old faces having to return to a place where he saw animals feeding on murdered corpses when he was just five.

‘Thousands of people are now going to die violent deaths,’ says attorney for Ohio Haitian community

“They’re just terrified for their physical safety,” Ruby said during a virtual press conference. “Many of them have already been traumatized… Some of them have been in prison. Some of them have been tortured. Some have been beaten. Some had been raped. Nearly all of them have seen friends or family members killed.”

And some of those families — those who have had children since coming to the United States — face an excruciating choice: whether to take their children with them into the violent chaos that is Haiti or leave them behind in a relatively peaceful, prosperous place where their children’s citizenship gives them the right to stay.

More than 330,000 Haitians have received temporary-protected status since an earthquake devastated the impoverished Caribbean country in 2010. Once in the United States, their status has been renewed as conditions in Haiti continued to deteriorate.

Early last year, Ohio’s then-Attorney General Dave Yost and 27 other Republican state AGs wrote a letter to the Trump administration stressing the word “temporary” in temporary protected status.

They claimed without evidence that it was safe for some with protected status to return to those home countries and urged a review.

Then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in November announced that she was terminating protected status for Haitians who had qualified, including about 45,000 in Ohio and roughly 15,000 in Springfield.

Lawyers for the Haitians sued, arguing that Noem had failed to follow the 1990 law creating temporary protected status. It requires that the government conduct a mandatory review of conditions in a group’s home country to certify that it’s safe to return before forcing them to go.

Lower courts blocked the termination.

But in June, in a 6-3 ruling the U.S. Supreme Court reversed them, ruling that the TPS law itself barred most court challenges to the way its provisions were or were not applied.

Attempt to halt imminent deportations of Haitians and Syrians blocked in US Senate

The court didn’t bar constitutional challenges, however, and SCOTUS Blog on Tuesday reported that some of those are in the works.

But for Haitians in Ohio, that might seem a thin reed on which to lean. They and many others are bracing for a mass-deportation such as those conducted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in other regions.

Ruby, the Springfield pastor, said no such operation has happened yet.

“It could happen as soon as this week,” he said. “What we’re hearing from other reporting is that they’re planning on deporting them directly back to Haiti. There have been cases in the community where they have been picked up one day. Sent to a detention center the next day. And on the third or the fourth day they’re back in Haiti. It’s obviously not safe for them to go there.”

The pastor added that jobs and support services are almost nonexistent when deportees get to Haiti.

In addition to terror over what might happen in Haiti are worries about what’s next for Springfield.

Ruby said that he and his colleagues have been working for the past 18 months to build “a very large coalition of faith leaders not only here in Springfield, but across the state of Ohio and across the nation who will stand with us if we have anything like what took place in Minneapolis.”

He was referring to a mass-enforcement operation last winter in which masked ICE officers shot and killed two protestors, both of them citizens. Analysis of videos taken at the scene showed that neither protester posed the threat that Trump administration officials claimed after the shootings.

Ruby stressed that he and other faith leaders want any protests of ICE enforcement actions to be peaceful, and that protesters have to be ready for the possible consequences of civil disobedience, such as going to jail.

Gov. Mike DeWine has criticized some of his Republican colleagues for falsely demonizing Springfield’s Haitian immigrants.

On Tuesday, his spokesman reiterated a statement DeWine issued last month when the U.S. Supreme Court issued its ruling that effectively revoked their protected status.

“Today’s decision is a legal decision,” DeWine said. “As I have stated in the past, the policy to remove these individuals from this country is a mistake.”

DeWine later added, “The situation in Haiti could hardly be much worse. The violent gangs run most of the country. The government barely functions. And, the economy is in shambles.”

Lynn Tramonte, founder of the Ohio Immigrant Alliance, questioned whether DeWine would instruct the Ohio Highway Patrol not to assist ICE in enforcement operations.

In the past, the Highway Patrol has worked with U.S. Border Patrol to apprehend undocumented immigrants, the American Immigration Council reports.

Dan Tierney, DeWine’s press secretary, didn’t answer directly when asked if the Highway Patrol would assist ICE with enforcement operations in Springfield.

Tramonte said DeWine could do more to help Haitians who suddenly find themselves without status.

“The governor might claim he is powerless to do anything in the face of federal agents invading our state to take our people, but here are two things he can do,” Tramonte said in a text message.

“He can instruct the Highway Patrol not to assist ICE in the enforcement of civil immigration laws. That’s not their job and they shouldn’t have to get involved. He can also underscore the same point for local police who often seem to think they should be on the hunt for immigrants instead of focusing on crime.”

authors: Emily Scolnick, Emily Previti, Ian Karbal

text:
Emily Scolnick is a 2026 Dow Jones News Fund intern at the Pennsylvania Capital-Star.

Immigration advocates from across Pennsylvania called on Gov. Josh Shapiro to shut down a youth detention center in Berks County and end state collaboration with Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Wednesday.

Over 100 people from 15 Pennsylvania counties joined a rally on the Capitol steps, urging Shapiro to protect immigrant communities, limit the enforcement of ICE detainers, and prevent ICE from accessing state databases and information from PennDOT that could lead to enforcement efforts.

“Imagine waking up every day and knowing that going to work could separate you from your family,” said Vincent Nguyen, a youth leader with the Woori Center and intern with the Pennsylvania Immigration Coalition (PIC), at a press conference Wednesday. “My generation is inheriting Pennsylvania, the United States, that today’s leaders are shaping. I want to inherit a commonwealth where every family can … live without fear.”

The Shapiro administration said it is currently reviewing how ICE, Customs and Border Protection, and other federal agencies can access state systems. Pennsylvania State Police officers are also not permitted to detain individuals due to their immigration status.

Several attendees said Shapiro’s response moving forward — or lack thereof — could determine how they vote in November’s election, where he is running for a second term against Republican and current state Treasurer Stacy Garrity.

“You want our vote, you earn our vote,” Jasmine Rivera, PIC’s executive director, said at the rally. “You are not getting a dime of our money until you finally do something.”

Nguyen told the Capital-Star that he and many other young people “aren’t just voting for the party anymore. They’re voting for the person.”

“I think it’s time that Josh Shapiro and many other politicians realize that they won’t get our support just because we may sort of agree with them on some things,” he said.

Tammy Murphy, the public policy and advocacy manager for Make the Road PA, said politicians can’t hide from the immigration issue going into this year’s elections. She added that while she won’t vote for Garrity, that doesn’t mean Shapiro will get her vote if he does not act.

“I’m an immigrant myself, formerly undocumented,” said Miguel Andrade, who is the communications director for PIC, but shared his personal views. “It’s a personal issue for me, and it does make me think about who are the elected officials I’m going to be supporting moving forward.”

“I would not vote for Shapiro in this moment,” he added.

Calls to close Abraxas

Many rally attendees displayed signs calling for Shapiro to issue an Emergency Removal Order to close Abraxas Academy, a youth detention center in Berks County that has faced several lawsuits alleging sexual abuse within the facility this year.

“A society is measured by how we treat our most vulnerable members, especially those who are in prison and children,” said David Wesley Cornish, an attorney representing multiple Abraxas victims. “Children are to be protected and cared for. They are to be nurtured. They are not to be harmed.”

Rosie Lapowsky, a spokesperson for Shapiro, wrote in a statement that Pennsylvania’s Department of Human Services currently performs weekly unannounced visits to Abraxas to inspect living conditions and assess treatment of its youth.

“The Shapiro Administration has zero tolerance for any neglect, abuse or mistreatment of children in facilities it licenses,” she wrote. “Our priority is keeping these children safe — and we are mindful that if an Emergency Removal Order were to be issued for Abraxas Academy, non-citizen youth would be transferred back into the custody of the Trump Administration, at which point Pennsylvania would no longer have the oversight authority to ensure they are being cared for.”

In November 2025, DHS revoked Abraxas’ license for its Secure Detention Unit — one of three licenses the facility maintains — for failure to report alleged instances of abuse. Lapowsky said there has been no new evidence that has prompted additional investigation.

The other two licenses continue to be subject to increased monitoring from DHS, which has no role in placing non-citizen children, according to the Shapiro administration.

“Every leader, every lawmaker, every citizen of Pennsylvania should be demanding the immediate release of these youth and the immediate closure of the Abraxas facility,” said Leslie Mamas, a reverend at the United Church of Christ in Montgomery County. “This isn’t a political issue. It is a moral one.”

Following the rally, Rivera led a group of organizers to Shapiro’s office to deliver a letter signed by immigrant rights advocates. The contents have not been released publicly.

She said up to this point, there have been no direct conversations with the governor about the coalition’s demands, “and it’s not for lack of asking.”

“There’s been many, many, many conversations and research and reports sent over to his staff,” she added.

title: Can the UN's Refugee Convention survive? - Al Jazeera

text:
At the end of World War II, great swaths of Europe lay in ruins and millions had been forcibly displaced.

The humanitarian disaster prompted the United Nations to agree on a comprehensive legal framework outlining states’ obligations to protect refugees. This became the 1951 Refugee Convention, which initially applied to Europeans but was subsequently amended in 1967 to apply to all those fleeing persecution. Today, 149 nations are parties to the convention and no country has ever withdrawn from it.

At least, not yet.

Nearly eight decades later, the world is struggling. The Syrian civil war triggered an enormous influx of refugees into Europe. Now, millions of refugees have fled Sudan’s brutal civil war, state collapse in Venezuela has caused mass migration, and the Russian invasion of Ukraine and many other conflicts around the world are in full swing, again causing mass displacements.

The UN currently records more than 41 million refugees worldwide.

The UN convention defines a refugee as a person who is outside their country of origin with a “well-founded fear of being persecuted for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion”. The principle of non-refoulement – the stipulation that a refugee should not be returned to a country where they could be harmed – is a cornerstone of the treaty.

In recent years, some of the world’s richest countries have begun to roll out increasingly punitive policies towards refugees as populist, anti-immigration sentiment has taken hold.

Last month the Supreme Court ruled in favour of allowing the Trump administration to turn back asylum seekers at the border and remove temporary protected status (TPS) from Haitians and Syrians. This year refugee admissions to the US have been almost exclusively white South Africans.

Refugees attempting to reach Australia by boat are now either turned back at sea or sent to offshore detention facilities, leading to strong criticism from human rights organisations on the Pacific island of Nauru.

Denmark, which was the first country to sign the convention three-quarters of a century ago, has stripped Syrian refugees of legal status and threatened them with deportation after deeming those from Damascus and surrounding regions safe, despite the country still being under the control of the Assad regime at the time. It passed a sweeping package of reforms in 2019.

A decade on from the refugee crisis, fuelled by the Syrian war and which saw more than one million people flee to Europe, border guards in several European Union states now routinely conduct violent pushbacks. Greece turns back boats while Poland forces them over the border into Belarus.

‘Share, not shift, responsibilities’

For campaigners, new European policies fly in the face of the convention’s principles, such as the right to territorial asylum and the principle of non-refoulement.

Adriana Tidona, migration researcher at Amnesty International, told Al Jazeera: “The new Migration and Asylum Pact will make it easier for EU countries to reject asylum applications without review, and send people to so-called ‘safe third countries’ to which they have no connection and where they have never even set foot.”

The 75th anniversary of the convention, Tidona said, is “an urgent reminder of the need to re-centre international cooperation in refugee protection and to share, not shift, responsibilities.

In the United States, the Trump administration is reportedly mulling withdrawing support from the UN refugee agency UNHCR, amid accusations that it pursues “a mass migration agenda”. It has also recently removed “protected status” for Syrian and Haitian nationals.

But for proponents of refugee rights, the Refugee Convention has its own limitations anyway.

While tens of millions have benefitted from its protection from persecution since 1951, others who are escaping different kinds of hardship such as poverty, climate change, natural disasters or gang violence, do not necessarily qualify under the criteria.

Without any specific court or treaty which can oversee and punish breaches, governments tend to interpret the convention according to their interests or even flout it altogether, experts say. According to Jeff Crisp at the Oxford University Refugee Studies Centre, who is also former head of policy development and evaluation at UNHCR, this is by design.

“The convention wouldn’t have been set up if there was enforcement,” he told Al Jazeera. “And the lack of it has become evident as the atmosphere around refugee protection has become more toxic.”

In recent years, Western governments have gone further than enacting anti-refugee policies; they have actively deported people to third countries to which they have no connection.

The former Conservative government in the United Kingdom sought to send asylum seekers to Rwanda, until the policy was overturned by the new Labour government in 2024. Italy has set up detention facilities in Albania and the US has sent deportees from multiple nationalities to countries including Iran, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Several EU countries, including Germany, Austria and the Netherlands, are now exploring the establishment of “return hubs” in Asian and African countries to process asylum seekers who cannot be returned to their home countries.

As states increasingly reinterpret or even flout the convention’s principles, Susan Fratzke, senior policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, said an update could address some of the existing gaps.

“A new protocol would avoid reopening some of the fundamental parts of the convention like the definition of a refugee and the principle of non-refoulement,” she told Al Jazeera.

“But by providing states with a sound legal basis for implementing more restrictive policies like safe third country or returns policies, you could also open up more protections for refugees like integration and the right to work.”

Removing safe routes

While the convention states that they should not be punished for entering countries irregularly to claim asylum, European governments from Greece to the UK have been detaining refugees under anti-smuggling laws in recent years.

At the same time, many of the same countries have removed or restricted safe routes for refugees such as family reunion pathways or resettlement schemes.

In 2025, only 37,000 refugees were resettled by UNHCR, down from 116,000 in 2024. With legal avenues disappearing and while people are required to be physically present in a country to access its asylum system, they are therefore increasingly reliant on smugglers to facilitate their movement.

About 65 percent of the world’s refugees have fled to neighbouring countries, meaning that the responsibility of hosting displaced populations primarily falls on the shoulders of low or middle-income countries.

Findings this month by polling company Ipsos, which questioned 21,000 people in 29 countries, suggest that public attitudes towards refugees may not be as hostile as politicians and media often claim, though it is still a mixed picture.

While two-thirds of Ipsos respondents said they support giving refuge to those fleeing war and persecution, a similar proportion questioned whether those claiming to be in need are indeed genuine. On whether borders should be closed to refugees, 49 percent agreed while 41 percent disagreed.

Ultimately, according to Crisp from Oxford University, there is no “big bang solution” for reform.

“We may have to accept the fact that the convention or a variant of it will remain, though not respected in practice, and governments will continue to take unilateral actions.”

And, Crisp warns, while Western countries may wish to reduce refugee protections, there may not be international consensus.

“So far the whole debate has been on the Global North’s terms, but the Global South may be resistant to making major changes, especially externalisation and containment policies that lead to a greater proportion of refugees remaining in their region.”
