text:
Flawed and racialised models that underpin the AI-powered age-detection systems to be introduced by the British government will endanger children, rights groups and children’s charities have warned.

Urging ministers to reverse plans to introduce facial age-estimation technology to screen migrants, critics have warned that black children arriving from conflict zones are at risk of being of thrust into the adult system.

Maddie Harris, of the Humans for Rights Network, said the charity had worked with hundreds of children who were already being wrongly filtered into the adult system during age assessments at borders carried out by immigration officers.

In May, the Helen Bamber Foundation revealed that 755 children in 2025 were incorrectly identified as adults on arrival to the UK, according to Home Office figures.

Harris said the introduction of AI was a “cheap process” that would not improve these numbers. “This is not about protecting children – this is about shoring up the decisions that [the authorities] are making,” she said.

The government has admitted that even the best systems can have a 30-month margin of error.

Harris said this is particularly risky for children, especially those from countries such as Sudan and Somalia, who she said were already “adultified” by the system.

“As soon as a child is treated as an adult, they are susceptible to – or exposed, rather – to any of the egregious consequences that the Home Office is applying to adults, such as detention and removal,” she said.

Unaccompanied children would be forced into accommodation alongside adults, exposing them to risk and to the violence threatened by the rise in protests targeting accommodation for asylum seekers, she said.

In May, the government announced a contract to use facial age-estimation technology developed by Cognitec, a German firm that calls itself “the face-recognition company”.

That system showed bias against sub-Saharan Africans, tending to overpredict the ages of minors, according to an investigation by Lighthouse Reports in June.

The UK-based tech monitor Foxglove has said these systems relied on “racist bias” and said the government should not use children to test experimental technology.

The Refugee and Migrant Children’s Consortium has raised concerns about the technology’s ability to assess children who have undergone difficult journeys. It noted that trauma can “age” a child’s appearance.

The Home Office plans to use the technology alongside checks by immigration officers. A spokesperson said: “Age assessments are a vital tool in maintaining border security. As part of our work to make this process more robust and consistent, we are exploring cutting-edge AI technology to verify migrants’ ages.”

Petra Molnar, who co-founded the advocacy group Migration and Tech Monitor, said this was the latest in a series of failed attempts across Europe to implement tech and AI into border policy.

She said previous attempts in Europe to implement AI-powered lie-detection systems for screening refugees had proven to be “snake oil” and did not progress beyond pilot schemes.

She likened the use of facial age-estimation technology to “the study of skulls and skull shapes” by colonial-era scientists to categorise different ethnic groups, saying that like the discredited 19th-century pseudoscience of phrenology, these systems similarly relied on categorising physical features to determine age.

“The context really matters here,” said Molnar. “We know that trauma ages you. We know that malnutrition, dehydration, torture – even just the journey itself – has physical impacts on your face, on your body.

“It’s effectively ‘neo-phrenology’ by categorising people based on physical features,” she said. “Relying on these kind of imperfect tools is not the solution.”

title: The professor facing prison in 'antifa' case: 'They want to scare all who oppose ICE'
description:
He was arrested on the spot on charges of being part of a “conspiracy” to “impede or injure” Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers.
He is not accused of violent acts, taking any specific actions at protests nor having any encounters with ICE agents.
To support the alleged “antifa” connection, the Department of Justice has highlighted a photo showing one of the defendants wearing an “I’m Antifa!” sweatshirt.
I’ve seen people pad out papers when they’ve got nothing to say.” Facing 26 years in prison Among the Minnesota protesters facing the most severe charges is Natasha Rakotz.
Like Davis, Rakotz faces conspiracy charges.
text:
Erik Davis was driving to a medical appointment in St Paul, Minnesota, on 16 June when federal agents surrounded his car.

“They hauled me out … and put me in a belly chain,” recalled the 53-year-old. He was arrested on the spot on charges of being part of a “conspiracy” to “impede or injure” Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers.

Davis, a college professor and father of two, was one of thousands of Minnesotans who had rallied earlier this year when the Trump administration launched an aggressive crackdown on immigrants in the Twin Cities.

Now the government alleged that he and 14 others used “force, intimidation, and threats” to prevent officers from carrying out their duties.

In its 94-page indictment, the government has argued that Direct Action Minnesota, the loose coalition of organizers that Davis was connected with, conspired to obstruct federal law enforcement and had “ties” to “antifa”. The prosecution follows a pattern seen in other cases against demonstrators this year, with the government highlighting the comments and actions of some activists in the coalition to paint all 15 defendants as agitators pursuing violence against ICE.

One such case in Chicago spectacularly collapsed last month. Demonstrators in Texas were recently convicted of terrorism charges and sentenced to decades behind bars, though in that case one protester shot and injured an officer. Prosecutors have not alleged any specific injuries to officers in Minnesota.

Civil rights advocates have said these prosecutions, even when unsuccessful, are part of an effort to criminalize lawful community organizing, weaken movements opposing deportations and turn the lives of activists upside down.

Davis, the government says, has attended and facilitated meetings about protests and discussed his “anti-authoritarian” ideology with other activists. He is not accused of violent acts, taking any specific actions at protests nor having any encounters with ICE agents.

He is facing six years in prison.

“It’s petty revenge,” Davis said. “They’re trying to portray being part of a community as an illegal conspiratorial act.”

Davis, and other defendants interviewed by the Guardian, are confident that the case against them will collapse. But the government is trying to send a signal, he said: “This isn’t just about us. It’s about trying to scare everybody who opposes ICE.”

‘Everybody wanted to do something’

Davis is a Buddhist studies scholar at Macalester College in St Paul and has long been part of labor organizing and activism against police violence in the region. When federal agents flooded the Twin Cities in January in a massive effort to round up immigrants, he felt compelled to step up, he said: “It was a federal invasion and terror campaign on our streets. The behavior of these masked thugs was horrific … they were ripping human beings out of families.”

Outrage and local organizing efforts swelled following the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. There were rapid response and mutual aid networks, groups documenting ICE sightings, know-your-rights training sessions, food donations for immigrant families trapped at home. And many joined Signal groups with strangers to get plugged in.

“It was astonishing. The overwhelming sense was that almost everybody was opposed and angry and scared, and almost everybody wanted to do something,” said Davis, who joined hyper-local group chats with neighbors.

The indictment does not describe Davis orchestrating any specific protest plans, giving detailed directions to other activists or conducting any violence. It does allege that on 11 January, four days after Good’s killing, Davis helped facilitate an “emergency meeting” for residents interested in “resistance to ICE” that featured discussions of protest tactics, like civil disobedience, marches and “blockades” to stop ICE officers.

Prosecutors also cite a post by Davis in a Signal group six days later in which he shared information about upcoming protests and encouraged people to be at a federal immigration building. The indictment further notes Davis suggested people delete the group while on the ground during demonstrations, and that he participated in two additional meetings and a rally.

The indictment accuses other defendants of more serious offenses: eight of the other defendants are said to have participated in an action at a federal building on 1 March where demonstrators held shields and blocked vehicles from entering or leaving a federal building. Prosecutors say “individuals threw projectiles” at local sheriffs during the protest, but did not specify if any defendants were involved in that.

Four defendants face charges for separate incidents. One is accused of telling people to get guns in January. One is accused of following an agent in May to Wisconsin, just across the state border. And one is accused of assault and destruction of government property after allegedly knocking paperwork out of an agent’s hand and kicking an officer’s car in May. The indictment doesn’t allege Davis was involved in any of the incidents in March or May.

Across the indictment, there are no allegations of injuries to specific ICE officers, or charges of serious violence like there were in the recent federal prosecution of protesters in Prairieland, Texas, in which one protester shot and injured an officer.

Daniel Rosen, the Minnesota US attorney, said whether the Minneapolis protesters caused physical harm was not the measure of criminality in this case.

Vague ‘antifa’ claims

The broader suggestion of the indictment is that Davis’s statements in Signal chats and meetings, alongside the statements and actions of others, show the groups collectively were conspiring to oppose the US government’s authority and interfere with ICE – and that they were connected to “Antifa groups” that “blend anarchist and communist views”.

At a press conference announcing the charges, Rosen said the prosecution supported the mission of Donald Trump’s executive order last year that designated “antifa” a “domestic terrorist organization” responsible for “riots” against ICE. Antifa is not a formal entity, but an umbrella term for a wide array of anti-fascist activism.

To support the alleged “antifa” connection, the Department of Justice has highlighted a photo showing one of the defendants wearing an “I’m Antifa!” sweatshirt. Prosecutors also quoted another defendant’s post on Facebook: “YOU WILL NEVER WIN WITH NON-VIOLENCE ALONE.”

The indictment does not cite any comments by Davis about antifa. The charges don’t define the relationships of the protesters to one another, nor does it provide evidence that defendants like Davis endorsed the more radical statements or actions of others facing charges.

Authorities say Davis referred to his ideologies as “anarchist”, “broadly anti-authoritarian” and “broadly anti-capitalist” and praised the “revolutionary potential of our organizations” and “militancy” in a Signal message.

Spokespeople for the Department of Justice in Minnesota declined to comment. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson declined to answer questions about the case, pointing to an earlier statement saying people who “lay a hand on law enforcement … will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law”.

Davis said his own political beliefs are focused on expanding equality and people’s freedoms and opposing state violence and authoritarianism – far removed, he said, from the stereotype of a violent “anarchist” extremist.

Davis said the meeting he helped facilitate involved more than a hundred participants with a wide range of ideologies – a space for people to come together after Good’s killing. “I’m not sure I’m described as doing anything illegal, which makes sense, because I didn’t.” He noted it was common for people to delete Signal chats at protests due to concerns about officers accessing phones during arrests.

“It’s bewildering. It seemed weird and laughable,” Davis said of the indictment. “It felt like the length of the indictment was a cover for how thin it actually was. I’m a professor. I’ve seen people pad out papers when they’ve got nothing to say.”

Facing 26 years in prison

Among the Minnesota protesters facing the most severe charges is Natasha Rakotz.

Rakotz, a 45-year-old home health aide, said it took her a while to get involved in organizing efforts after ICE arrived in the city. She said she wasn’t connected to any activist groups and didn’t know where to start. But she felt morally obligated: “People say, if it was 1935 Germany, what would I do? I couldn’t do nothing. I couldn’t sit by and wait for them to kill somebody else. I couldn’t sit in my privileged white existence and allow the government to absolutely ravage people that need protecting … It felt like nobody was going to save us.”

Rakotz eventually linked up with groups monitoring ICE and threw herself into the work. Like Davis, Rakotz faces conspiracy charges. The government says she participated in a Signal chat focused on observing ICE vehicles, talking about what times she would be observing and how she takes photos of license plates. She asked others what they had observed and said she was interested in learning more about civil disobedience.

But in addition, the justice department says that on 18 May, Rakotz followed a federal immigration officer’s vehicle, “brake checked” and “side swiped” the car, “causing a collision”. The indictment does not provide further details.

Rakotz has denied the allegation. State records show local officers called to the scene of the collision cited her for a misdemeanor of allegedly violating her “duty to drive with due care”, a minor offense. A court report said she told an officer she was not following the federal agent and the collision was an accident. She was not arrested at that time.

Eventually, state prosecutors dropped the misdemeanor, saying federal prosecutors were filing charges covering the incident. The US attorney’s office has since accused Rakotz of assault on an officer, with a charge alleging “physical contact” and “injury”, though the indictment doesn’t identify a victim nor specify the injuries the collision may have caused, and it doesn’t detail any damage to the government’s car. That charge could carry a 20-year sentence on top of six years for conspiracy.

“I really believe these charges are going to get dropped because they’re unfounded and ridiculous,” said Rakotz. “But I feel like the process is the punishment.”

‘They’re trying to ruin us’

A trial date has not been set and complicated cases like this can drag on for months.

In the meantime, the consequences of the case have been far-reaching for the defendants. “They are trying to ruin our lives … I try not to remind myself all the time that the consequence of this bureaucracy is my freedom,” said Davis.

Davis worries about impacts on his career. He said he has long strived to keep his academic work and activism separate, but now thrust into the spotlight as an alleged “conspirator”, he wonders if his scholarship could be affected.

He has struggled to sleep, and the case has taken a toll on his personal relationships, he said. The 15 defendants are under a strict “no contact” order with each other, which has meant he has been cut off from several close friends, who are also defendants in the case.

He has worked hard to not dwell on the possibility of being locked up for six years: “I suspect I’m going to be afraid at some point and will have to process that … but I’ve been able to be unafraid because of the support and solidarity we’ve received.”

Both Davis and Rakotz said they didn’t want the case to discourage others from organizing against ICE and hoped people would stay focused on immigrant communities subjected to ICE enforcement and violence.

“Far more important than anything that happens to us is continuing to organize against the armed masked people in our streets,” Davis said.

Rakotz said she, too, had tried not to think about what a conviction would mean. “I am free right now and I refuse to let this stop me from enjoying life and doing what I can to positively impact the community.”

She paused. “And if I have to go to prison because I did what I could for the greater good, I’m ready and willing to do that.”

text:
Reform UK’s deputy leader in Scotland has reported one of the country’s most high-profile lawyers to police over a speech he made at a protest in Glasgow last weekend.

Thomas Kerr revealed in a post on social media site X that he has asked officers to investigate a speech made by Aamer Anwar during a counter-protest to anti-immigration demonstrators on Saturday.

Rejecting Mr Kerr’s claims, Mr Anwar accused the Glasgow MSP of wasting police time and described him as a “wannabe tartan Tommy Robinson”.

Mr Kerr told his social media followers that Mr Anwar’s comments “go beyond robust political debate and, I believe, have the effect of encouraging hostility towards a section of Scots based on their political views, nationality, ethnicity and cultural identity”.

He described the remarks as “abhorrent”, claiming Mr Anwar had described political campaigners as “terrorists” and had spoken about questioning “their culture and religion”.

“His words, I have no doubt, will contribute to increased hostility and community tensions, and I hope Police Scotland investigate the matter fully,” he added.

During his speech, Mr Anwar said “racist thugs” had sought to hold Muslims and non-white people collectively responsible for the actions of “one madman in Belfast”, in reference to the alleged attempted murder in the city in June which sparked riots.

The human rights lawyer compared the incident to the alleged anti-Muslim knife attack in Edinburgh later that month.

He told anti-racism protesters in Glasgow: “I wonder what would have happened if, in response to the knife rampage in Leith, Muslims or members of the non-white community had masked up and organised pogroms against the white community, had set fire to white people’s homes with children running for their lives.

“Would there have been sympathy for their cause? Would the mob have been called campaigners with legitimate concerns? Or would we be calling them exactly what they are: terrorists?

“We would be questioning their culture, we would be questioning their religion, we would be asking which one of their community leaders was responsible for radicalising them – starting at the top with Nigel Farage and Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.”

Responding to Mr Kerr’s report to police, Mr Anwar said he was a “wannabe tartan Tommy Robinson” and he “should know police are busy tracing those masked thugs responsible for inciting and taking part in Saturday’s race hate, attacks on police officers and innocent people of colour.”

He said while Mr Kerr claims to have called out Saturday’s violence, “several of his Reform members stood next to the thugs, many of whom were masked, whilst racist abuse, threats of violence and Nazi salutes took place”.

He went on: “I doubt Reform has handed over a single name or video of these thugs to the major investigation team at Police Scotland.

“Any decent person would be calling out the pogroms in Belfast and knife attacks in Leith, yet this great defender of free speech, Mr Kerr’s reaction to my words is to waste police time, by labelling it as hate speech.”

He added: “Will he now suspend those Reform politicians that attended the ‘Unite the Klans’ event on Saturday and assist police with their inquiries?”

Glasgow Reform councillor Audrey Dempsey has admitted to speaking at the Unite the Clans rally.

Other speakers at the event spoke of their love of being white and claimed white people in the UK were being replaced.

Police Scotland said around 1,700 people took part in demonstrations in the city on Saturday, with groups engaging in violence, disorder and hate-motivated offending.

Fifteen people have since been arrested and officers have vowed that more will come.

Police said groups engaged in violence, disorder, intimidation and hate-motivated offences, including a large group of around 100 people who made their way into the city centre.

Demonstrators were seen performing what appeared to be Nazi salutes while videos on social media appeared to show a non-white delivery driver being attacked by a group shouting “get them out”.

Chief constable Jo Farrell described the violent scenes as “disgraceful” and said Police Scotland would take further action on those who caused disorder.

First Minister John Swinney branded the protest a “demonstration of far-right hatred”, describing the disorder as “completely and utterly unacceptable”.

A video of the anti-migrant group rushing towards an anti-fascist group was shared and supported by far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.

The protest was the latest in a series of anti-migrant demonstrations in Glasgow amid heightened tensions.

Police Scotland has been approached for comment.

text:
A Kean University nursing professor suffered a fractured kneecap, torn meniscus, and head injury after federal immigration agents threw her to the ground during protests outside of a Newark immigration detention center in May, the American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey alleged in a court document.

Dr. Norma Bowe, a registered nurse, grandmother, and professor of public health, alleges she was assaulted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents on May 25 while trying to help a woman who was being dragged across the pavement by agents outside the jail, Delaney Hall. Two months later, she still suffers from headaches, trouble sleeping, and mental distractions, and her injuries have limited her ability to do things she enjoys, according to the eight-page document.

“I was violently attacked by ICE agents while I was trying to provide medical care for people visiting their loved ones in Delaney Hall,” Bowe said in a statement. “ICE agents are acting like they have impunity and are inflicting harm however and wherever they want; without accountability, more people will get hurt and die. ICE must be held responsible.”

Scenes from outside Newark migrant jail Delaney Hall

The document is a notice of claim, a precursor to the filing of a lawsuit. The claim is one of 54 filed by ACLU chapters in 17 states and Washington, D.C., as part of an effort to seek compensation for what the organization says is a pattern of unlawful violence by immigration enforcement agents under the Trump administration.

“As the Trump administration continues to enable ICE agents to brutalize communities, it’s important we use every tool available to seek justice,” said Jeanne LoCicero, legal director for the ACLU of New Jersey. “Dr. Bowe’s experience is one more example of how ICE is acting lawlessly and poses a danger to everyone in our communities. ICE must be held to account through all legal means available.”

Bowe has spent the past year running a mobile health clinic out of an RV parked near Delaney Hall, providing health screenings, first aid, food, water, baby formula, and blankets to family members visiting loved ones, according to the claim.

The incident in question happened on Memorial Day, three days after roughly 300 detainees at Delaney Hall said they launched a hunger strike over conditions inside the Newark detention center. Federal agents and protestors clashed outside the 1,000-bed facility, with agents firing rubber bullets and deploying pepper spray on the crowd.

Bowe, wearing a red stethoscope around her neck, walked toward the gate and saw a large group of ICE agents gathered near an armed personnel carrier, along with protestors. The agents wore paramilitary-style gear, had masks covering their faces, and held pepper spray, batons, and firearms, according to the claim.

As she looked for injured people, Bowe spotted agents dragging a young woman across the ground, pulling off her shirt in the process, and Bowe moved to help her, the claim states. That’s when she said two masked agents assaulted her.

Two agents wearing gear marked “POLICE” and “ICE” shoved her with enough force that she “flew through the air and crashed to the ground, bouncing once before landing with her head on the concrete sidewalk and her lower body on the asphalt of the parking lot,” the claim states. She landed on her face and knee, hurting her hand that tried to break her fall.

ICE officials did not respond for comment.

text:
New this week from Solitary Watch:

Solitary Watch Director Jean Casella published a commentary reflecting on how Norway humanely houses Anders Breivik, the far-right terrorist who killed 77 people in 2011, in a purpose-built two-story suite at Ringerrike Prison, despite his continued white supremacist views. Casella toured the unit as part of a U.S. delegation studying Norway’s rehabilitation-focused system, where officials argue that restriction of liberty alone is punishment enough. She contrasts this with U.S. prisons, where solitary confinement, abuse, and suicide are endemic and 77% of people released are rearrested within 5 years. The Nation

This week’s pick of news and commentary about solitary confinement:

One hundred twenty immigrants detained at Eloy Detention Center signed a letter alleging “human rights abuses”at the Arizona facility. The letter, written by 29-year-old Venezuelan migrant Andres David Torres Chirino, describes “appalling and utterly deplorable” conditions and staff who are “unfit for their jobs because, having a degree of authority over us, they abuse the power through malpractice and policies that harm the detainees.” Chirino, who was placed in solitary after threatening to report an abusive guard, claims staff often conduct nine head counts per day to increase the amount of time detainees are locked in their cells. “Physically, it interferes with your ability to prepare your immigration case,” he told reporters. “It’s also psychological pressure designed to wear you down until you give up your case.” Arizona Daily Star

Five incarcerated people are suing the Oregon Department of Corrections for violating the state’s constitution by practicing prolonged solitary confinement and denying “medical, mental health, and disability accommodations.” Plaintiff Orlando Pouncey, 40, spent 11 years—a third of his life—in solitary, where he was let out of his cell for just 30 minutes every five days. He says isolation worsened his vision under constant overhead lighting, prevented him from using an audio player needed to complete rehabilitative programming, and denied him access to mental health treatment. Pouncey, diagnosed with depression and PTSD, began hallucinating and talking to himself in isolation: “I’ve seen people go crazy. I’ve seen people take their lives.” The lawsuit follows Oregon’s $2.3 million settlement with the family of a 22-year old man who died by suicide in 2023 while in solitary at Oregon State Correctional Institution. As of July 1, 2026, roughly 363 adults remained in disciplinary segregation under solitary conditions. Statesman Journal | As Oregon temperatures climb above 100 degrees, several state prisons lack central air conditioning, relying instead on fans and swamp coolers. Advocates say the Department of Corrections isn’t doing enough for the more than 480 people in solitary confinement, who face heightened risks without cooling. Unlike those in general population, people in solitary can’t relocate to cooler areas and lack ways to cool down, access to clean hydration, and personal fans. Oregon Capital Chronicle

At Northlake Processing Center, the largest Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in the Midwest, Iraqi immigrant Sanan Atou, 43, was held in a freezing solitary confinement cell for three weeks after taking food from the kitchen for detainees without commissary money. “I felt like I was going to freeze to death. I didn’t know if I was going to wake up,” stated Atou. As immigration detention has expanded under the Trump administration, so has ICE’s use of solitary confinement. MLive reports that over 14,000 immigrants have been held in solidarity since January 2025. Physicians for Human Rights found ICE’s use of solitary in the administration’s first four months was double the rate from 2018-2023 and six times higher than under the Biden administration. Since ICE detention is civil, not criminal and 70% of detained immigrants had no criminal record as of April 2026, researchers argue its use as punishment violates federal guidelines. Mlive.com

The Washington State Supreme Court heard arguments in June on whether Amber Kim, a transgender woman, should be transferred back to a women’s prison. After 15 years in men’s facilities, Kim was moved to the Washington Corrections Center for Women in 2021. In 2024, she received a disciplinary ticket and was placed in segregation for three months before being transferred to Monroe Correctional Complex’s intensive management unit, where she is isolated for 23 hours a day. Kim has spent over two years in solitary confinement and the ACLU of Washington argues her transfer and prolonged isolation violates the state constitution’s ban on cruel punishment. Truthout

New Jersey Republican lawmakers dismissed witness testimony of mistreatment at Delaney Hall, an ICE detention center run by the private company GEO Group, titling the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Oversight’s hearing “False Narratives Surrounding Conditions at the Delaney Hall ICE Detention Center.” The ACLU of New Jersey’s Amol Sinha testified that hundreds of detainees who staged hunger and labor strikes over medical neglect, starvation, overcrowding, and abuse were met with pepper spray, solitary confinement, and punitive transfers. One detainee, John Wilson Brutus, died after just one day at the facility. No ICE, Department of Homeland Security, or GEO Group representatives testified, and the three witnesses called by Republicans had no firsthand knowledge of conditions at Delaney Hall. Vindicator

Advocates and Department of Corrections (DOC) officials clashed over solitary confinement at a Madison protest against Wisconsin’s prison conditions. Talib Akbar displayed a replica solitary cell based on his own experience, and Crystal Keller described how her incarcerated daughter is limited to one 15-minute call every nine to ten days while in solitary. Advocates who solitary survivors describe it as traumatizing and say people are placed in isolation for minor infractions. A DOC-commissioned report found out-of-cell time “very limited,” recommending at least two hours daily and noting that solitary increases the likelihood of self-harm and suicide. Wisconsin Examiner

The Maryland Supreme Court upheld a law that lets judges fine the state’s health department when it delays psychiatric care for pretrial defendants ruled incompetent or dangerous. As of June 2026, 236 people were incarcerated pretrial awaiting placement at one of Maryland’s five psychiatric hospitals. While they wait, defendants are held in solitary confinement without access to proper care. “They get worse and worse,” said Luciene Parsley of Disability Rights Maryland. The health department is legally required to find placements within 10 business days, but says overcrowding and funding constraints make compliance “impossible.” The Daily Record

Izzy Aly, released in June after six months at Pennsylvania’s Moshannon Valley Processing Center, described how ICE uses solitary confinement to quarantine sick detainees rather than provide care. Diagnosed with chronic kidney disease during detention, Aly said respiratory illnesses, like COVID-19, spread rapidly through crowded pods, and he was told by nursing staff that the facility’s “quarantine” area was the Special Housing Unit—solitary confinement. ICE’s own records show the facility ranks among the highest nationwide for solitary use. In Aly’s words, “anybody that fears COVID infections gets threatened with solitary,” which discourages detainees from reporting symptoms, allowing infections to spread unchecked. Truthout

title: Immigration officials misused weapons hundreds of times during protests, report finds
description:
Human rights investigators have documented hundreds of instances of misuse of crowd-control weapons at protests of immigration enforcement since President Donald Trump returned to office.
The authors of the report called for manufacturers to stop making certain weapons that are particularly harmful and likely to be misused and urged law enforcement agencies to change their use-of-force policies.
Immigration officials and other law enforcement have used a mix of tear gas, rubber bullets, pepper spray, pepper balls, flashbangs, batons and shields on crowds gathered to protest during large-scale immigration enforcement operations in cities including Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis.
Schell said that at most of the protests where the team documented misuse, multiple law enforcement agencies and subagencies were present.
Researchers also noted many cases in which law enforcement deployed these weapons in enclosed spaces or other situations that the protesters could not escape.
text:
This article was produced by the nonprofit journalism publication Capital and Main. It is co-published here with permission.

Human rights investigators have documented hundreds of instances of misuse of crowd-control weapons at protests of immigration enforcement since President Donald Trump returned to office.

Department of Homeland Security employees and local law enforcement both committed violations of standards of use for crowd-control weapons, injuring protesters, according to a report from Physicians for Human Rights and the University of California, Berkeley’s Human Rights Center. The authors of the report called for manufacturers to stop making certain weapons that are particularly harmful and likely to be misused and urged law enforcement agencies to change their use-of-force policies.

“There’s a lack of standards across the board in the United States when it comes to the use of crowd-control weapons, and there’s a lack of standards around training, testing, figuring out what these weapons are, how they should work and how we should use them,” said Sasha Schell, supervising reporter at the Berkeley Human Rights Center, who led the open source investigative team.

The team used open source investigative techniques, including cataloguing incidents through the review of publicly available video, to determine which agencies misused which weapons. The researchers labeled an incident as a misuse of the weapon if it went against international human rights standards, manufacturer instructions or the agency’s own use-of-force policy, or if the law enforcement agency attacked a protected group such as journalists, legal observers or medics.

Because of limitations in the video that the team could find, Schell said, the report’s statistics are likely an undercount.

Immigration officials and other law enforcement have used a mix of tear gas, rubber bullets, pepper spray, pepper balls, flashbangs, batons and shields on crowds gathered to protest during large-scale immigration enforcement operations in cities including Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis.

Under international law, in order to use force on protesters, law enforcement agencies must ensure that the force is necessary and must have exhausted other options, and officials should take precautions to minimize harm caused, the authors of the report said. Force should be proportional to the threat and not excessive.

But the U.S. government does not have specific federal standards for crowd control weapons in its laws, according to the report.

Schell said that at most of the protests where the team documented misuse, multiple law enforcement agencies and subagencies were present. Each had its own use-of-force policy that didn’t necessarily align with those of other agencies.

“It becomes a real mess for holding anybody accountable when misuse does occur,” Schell said.

He gave an example of one protest where Chicago police gave protesters one set of instructions and federal officials gave protesters a different set of instructions.

“That led to a bunch of people getting shot with pepper balls,” Schell said.

Department of Homeland Security employees, including officials from Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, committed the majority of the violations.

Those included spraying people directly in the face with powerful chemical irritants after they were already detained, handcuffed or pinned to the ground or even beating them over the head with the canisters, Schell said.

The most common misuse, according to the report, involved deploying crowd-control weapons at too close a range. Researchers also noted many cases in which law enforcement deployed these weapons in enclosed spaces or other situations that the protesters could not escape.

Schell said that most of the violence occurred at unplanned protests, such as responses to a particular immigration enforcement operation, rather than at planned protests like the No Kings rallies.

“In the vast majority of incidents, protests were peaceful before crowd-control weapons were deployed, and in all cases, basic standards of proportionality, precaution, and necessity were not met,” the report says.

When asked about the report’s findings, the Department of Homeland Security blamed protesters.

“The pattern is NOT of law enforcement using force,” an unnamed department spokesperson said via email. “It’s a pattern of violent agitators attacking our law enforcement.”

The department encouraged protesters and journalists to “exercise caution.”

“Being near unlawful activities in the field does come with risks — though our officers take every reasonable precaution to mitigate dangers to those exercising their protected First Amendment rights,” the spokesperson said. “However, when faced with violence or attempts to obstruct law enforcement operations, our officers will take legal and necessary steps to ensure their own safety and the public’s safety.”

The report includes 175 cases of misuse of force against journalists.

Schell said he didn’t want to discourage journalists from doing their jobs, but he encouraged them to be alert when they move through the crowd in quieter moments to conduct interviews.

“You’d have a little bit of a standoff between the protesters and law enforcement where maybe not much is happening, and then out of nowhere these guys will decide, ‘All right, we’ve got to clear this crowd,’ with very little warning,” Schell said. You’ll see a barrage of tear gas, pepper spray, these muzzle-blast weapons come in and launch. Those were the times we saw journalists being hit the most.”

Researchers found a significant number of deployments of crowd-control weapons targeted people’s heads, causing contusions, traumatic brain injuries, hearing loss and ocular injuries. Crowd-control weapons are not supposed to be deployed on someone’s head, Schell said.

The authors of the report called the number of head injuries concerning because it suggests “that law enforcement agents either intentionally or recklessly deployed force towards the head in dangerous and improper ways.”

The rate of violations worsened when Border Patrol leader Gregory Bovino was present, according to the report. Bovino was demoted and later retired shortly after the fatal shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis.

Researchers also noted that in Los Angeles, the police and Sheriff’s departments also committed a significant number of violations.

The Los Angeles Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.

The L.A. County Sheriff’s Department said via email that its staff had not yet reviewed the report’s findings and couldn’t comment on them.

“During the period referenced in the report, Los Angeles experienced unprecedented federal immigration enforcement activity that prompted some of the largest and most sustained demonstrations in the country,” the department wrote in the email without naming a speaker. “As emotions ran high, local law enforcement officers, who live and work in these same communities, often became the focus of that frustration, despite not being responsible for federal immigration enforcement actions.”

The department said its training emphasizes de-escalation.

“Each city had its tone, and each protest would have its own tone,” Schell said.

In Los Angeles, that meant Sheriff’s deputies firing flashbangs that are supposed to detonate above a crowd, Schell said. The noise and flash are supposed to scare crowds into backing up.

But, instead of firing the weapons well overhead, deputies aimed them so that they detonated on individuals’ heads, causing injuries.

“Those were pretty shocking to see,” Schell said.

The report notes that police agencies that had previously enacted use-of-force reforms related to crowd control since 2020 had far fewer incidents of misuse than agencies that have reversed or abandoned those policy changes in recent years. It noted that while the Los Angeles Police Department enacted some reforms, the Sheriff’s Department did not.

“There is limited but clear evidence that when police reforms, weapons bans, and crowd management policies are enacted and followed, use of force incidents, misuse events, and resulting injuries, go down,” the report says. “The opposite is also true: when reform is not implemented, or is reversed, incidents, misuse, and injuries go up.”

The authors of the report said piecemeal reform at individual agencies is not enough to respond to the nationwide trend of misuse of force as documented by the researchers.

They called for the U.S. government to enact broad reform to protect people exercising their First Amendment rights.

Schell, as a journalist himself, said he hopes the report and accompanying database will inspire more journalism digging deep into the questions raised in the report.

“Who is setting standards? Who is doing the training?” Schell said. “It’s quite an opaque thing.”

He said he wants more information about how weapons receive a “less lethal” designation to begin with.

“A lot of times the injuries that we see [are] not consistent with what they’ve said about how these things function,” Schell said. “Some of the injuries we saw were really gruesome.”

text:
In total, DHS arrested more than 900 suspects and rescued more than 180 victims

WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) celebrates the resounding success of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) in cracking down on human trafficking operations during the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

In total, HSI and the DHS Center for Countering Human Trafficking (CCHT), along with federal, state, and local partners, arrested 905 suspects and rescued 180 victims – 150 adults and 30 juveniles.

In one operation on July 24, HSI Dallas executed 8 federal arrest warrants related to an adult bookstore in Dallas that had operated as an illicit and covert brothel for more than 20 years. The investigation, which was started by HSI Dallas in 2023, determined that thousands of adults and minors were sold for commercial sex through the illicit business, with dozens of victims being identified. One victim was murdered in 2024, for which a defendant was convicted and sentenced to life in prison. The targets of the arrest warrants were indicted on multiple counts, including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking, sex trafficking through force, fraud, and coercion, and conspiracy to launder monetary instruments. The investigation is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Northern District of Texas.

In another operation on June 23, HSI San Francisco, along with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the San Francisco Police Department, conducted an operation that identified two female minor victims of human trafficking and rescued them. One of the two victims was reported missing out of Bakersfield, California in November of 2025 and had not been seen since.

“While Americans and international visitors were enjoying the FIFA World Cup, the men and women of ICE law enforcement were hard at work cracking down on human trafficking operations in FIFA host cities across the country,” said Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis. “Federal law enforcement arrested more than 900 suspects and rescued nearly 200 victims. Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, we are dismantling human trafficking networks.”

The human trafficking arrests are just one aspect of the many accomplishments by DHS and its components during the World Cup. Other achievements include:

Combined, DHS and FBI seized more than 700 unauthorized drones.

CBP’s Air and Marine Operations flew 50+ air missions over stadiums and host cities.

CBP completed more than 19,000 inspections of vehicles headed into stadiums and fan festivals.

CBP seized more than 473,000 counterfeit FIFA World Cup merchandise items, with an estimated genuine retail value totaling more than $33 million.

HSI intellectual property rights (IPR) enforcement efforts resulted in 48 arrests and 164 seizures related to FIFA World Cup counterfeit goods, which included over 530,000 items worth over $85 million MSRP.

text:
DENVER — The ACLU of Colorado filed three claims today, July 29, 2026, against the federal government on behalf of Fernando Jaramillo Solano and his two children, ages 15 and 12. The family was stopped and unlawfully arrested and then incarcerated by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers on their way to school in Durango, Colorado, in October 2025. The filing is part of a coordinated nationwide effort by the ACLU and its affiliates to hold ICE accountable involving 53 claims across 17 states and Washington, D.C.

Fernando Jaramillo Solano was driving his two children to school on the morning of October 27, 2025, when he noticed an unmarked car behind him with emergency lights flashing. When Jaramillo Solano pulled over to the side of the road, he was joined by other unmarked vehicles. Armed ICE officers with masks covering their faces approached his car and ordered him to provide identification and exit the vehicle. Officers reached through a cracked window, opened the car door without his permission, and grabbed his arm. ICE officers grabbed his passport out of his hands, and Jaramillo Solano then provided additional paperwork for his pending asylum case and pending work authorization. Despite this, ICE officers handcuffed him and put him in an unmarked vehicle.

While handcuffed in the unmarked vehicle, Jaramillo Solano witnessed agents grabbing his children. He saw ICE agents push and handcuff his 15-year-old son before placing him in another vehicle. He also saw an ICE agent get into the backseat of his car and push his 12-year-old daughter to the passenger side of their vehicle where an ICE agent outside of the car pulled her out. She was placed in the same unmarked car as Jaramillo Solano. When locked in the car together, his daughter told Jaramillo Solano that the agent who pushed her also sexually assaulted her.

Jaramillo Solano and his two children were detained for approximately thirty hours in an ICE holding facility in Durango. The facility had no windows. The lights remained on the entire night. There was a single cement bed and seat the three of them shared. The only food they each received was a cold hamburger and a cold soup. Jaramillo Solano and his son were forced to use the open-air toilet in the holding cell. All the while, the officers repeatedly denigrated the family. ICE then drove Jaramillo Solano and his family to New Mexico, in violation of a previous court order. ICE transferred the family again to a Texas detention facility and began removal proceedings against them. In the face of deplorable detention conditions, Jaramillo Solano decided to return to Colombia with his family, despite the risks of returning to their country of origin.

“Our client and his two young children were unlawfully arrested and abused by ICE on their way to school, without warrants and no probable cause, all when ICE mistakenly thought our client was someone else. Even after recognizing their mistake, and knowing that our clients had pending asylum applications, ICE agents decided to arrest and jail them to meet arbitrary quotas. These actions were unjustified and illegal. ICE must be held accountable,” said Tim Macdonald, ACLU of Colorado legal director. “The Trump administration has repeatedly encouraged this type of violence in our communities as part of its unlawful and inhumane immigration enforcement. The ACLU and more than a dozen of its affiliates are fighting back against these injustices with the more than 50 legal claims filed in 17 states. We must work together to defend and protect the civil rights of everyone in Colorado and across our nation and we will not back down.”

The ACLU of Colorado’s filing alleges that ICE officers committed assault, battery, engaged in a false imprisonment, were negligent in their actions, received negligent training and supervision, and both intentionally and negligently inflicted emotional distress. It also states that Jaramillo Solano and his two children continue to experience significant mental health symptoms, including extreme anxiety, sleep disturbances, and more. The document details that Jaramillo Solano’s daughter is even afraid of wearing certain clothes in public for fear of being sexually assaulted.

Jaramillo Solano’s experience is not uncommon. Since the beginning of President Trump’s second term, federal law enforcement agents have terrorized communities and people in their custody with a blatant disregard for the law. The consequences have been deadly. Conditions in ICE facilities are so inhumane that the rate of deaths in ICE custody has more than doubled since Trump’s term began, reaching its highest level in over a decade. In early July, reporting revealed that, after the White House pushed to increase arrest rates, ICE officials detained more than 10,000 people in five days. Only days later, ICE agents in unmarked vehicles shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas while he was on his way to work. The following week, a federal agent shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine.

Across the country, ACLU affiliates are challenging the Trump administration’s illegal conduct by filing claims under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA), one of the few legal tools available to seek financial compensation for wrongdoing by federal government employees. Through this coordinated effort, ACLU affiliates are representing dozens of people and families who are seeking justice for the harm they experienced at the hands of federal immigration agents. The claims reveal a widespread pattern of civil rights violations and abuse carried out by officials nationwide, affecting people who are immigrants, U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, families, workers, and people exercising their constitutional rights.

text:
SAN JOSE, CALIFORNIA — On Wednesday, Speaker of the Assembly Robert Rivas stood alongside federal, state and local elected officials, community advocates, faith leaders and residents to denounce plans for a proposed ICE detention center near the Santa Clara County City of Gilroy, reaffirming the state’s commitment to stopping the project and protecting California communities from the Trump administration’s unlawful and dangerous immigration enforcement campaign.

"This fight is about far more than one detention center. It's about whether we will allow fear to replace our values as Californians. We will continue to speak out, and we will continue to fight this ICE detention center until it is defeated. Because years from now, no one will remember the politics of this moment — but they will remember whether we had the courage to defend the values that define us. Let history record that when our community was tested, California did not look away. Here in Santa Clara County, in the Central Coast, we did not look away. We stood up together on the side of justice."

— Speaker of the Assembly Robert Rivas said at Wednesday’s press conference

The potential detention center is planned in unincorporated Santa Clara County, right outside Gilroy in Speaker Rivas’ district. Since plans for the project surfaced in May, local residents, elected officials and community organizations have mobilized in opposition, arguing the detention center would bring fear and disruption to communities that have long welcomed immigrant families.

California has already taken legal action to stop the project. Last month, the California Department of Justice filed a lawsuit with Santa Clara County to block the development of the facility, due to federal officials unlawfully advancing the project in secret without complying with state environmental laws or notifying state and local governments. Construction has since been paused while the case moves forward.

This effort to block the detention center builds on the Assembly’s broader efforts to defend California communities from federal overreach and hold the Trump administration accountable for violent and indiscriminate immigration enforcement.

Over the past two years, the Assembly has enacted landmark protections prohibiting ICE enforcement at schools, hospitals, child care facilities and voting centers, while requiring federal immigration agents operating in California to clearly identify themselves during enforcement actions.

This year, the Assembly is advancing 22 additional measures to strengthen oversight of ICE operations, protect immigrant workers, expand legal protections for families and increase accountability for abuses by immigration agents and in detention facilities — so all Californians can go to work and access essential services without fear.

The Assembly also secured hundreds of millions of dollars in the new state budget to expand support programs for immigrant communities, including help for workers, parents, students and families to access legal representation, navigate the immigration system and connect with critical resources in their communities.

Speaker Rivas has also personally convened community meetings and discussions across California — including multiple events in the Central Coast — to bring community advocates and leaders together and ensure immigrants know their rights and that their Speaker has their back.

Wednesday’s press conference was organized by San Jose Nikkei Resisters and the Neighbors Not Enemies Coalition of San Jose Japantown. Drawing on the Japanese American community’s history of incarceration during World War II, organizers warned that expanding immigration detention repeats some of the darkest chapters of American history and stood alongside leaders at every level of government to reject the proposed facility.

The Central Coast has made itself clear: This detention center is not welcome here. Speaker Rivas and the Assembly will continue using every tool available to stop this facility and defend California families.

text:
We have received notice of an increase in immigration enforcement at U.S. airports, specifically the expanded collaboration between ICE and TSA that includes the detention of individuals who are eligible to remain in the United States during a period of authorized stay but lack valid visa status. These are foreign nationals who are lawful in the U.S. pending an administrative process to finalize either an extension or change of visa status or permanent residency.

Lawful Status and the Increased Importance of Maintaining It

The distinction between “lawful status” and a “period of authorized stay” hinges upon the specific actions and circumstances of an individual within the administrative process. Following the expiration of lawful status, select individuals are permitted to remain in the United States beyond the expiration of a nonimmigrant visa. In fact, regulations permit these foreign nationals in the U.S. to stay beyond the physical visa stamp in their passports. The controlling record is the I-94 Status Entry Record issued by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), a separate agency. The visa stamp is only part of the total record on any individual. In extension of status cases, individuals are lawfully permitted up to 240 days with automatic legal status extensions and employment authorization, if timely filed.

Examples of such permission include individuals with a pending, timely-filed AOS application. Employment-based AOS applicants may be exempt from certain adjustment bars even if they fell out of valid nonimmigrant status after filing, so long as the period of unauthorized stay does not exceed 180 days. This provision provides significant relief for employers to continue to employ workers whose nonimmigrant status lapses during the permanent residency process.

In addition, individuals with pending permanent residency applications may apply for a travel document called an ”Advance Parole” to travel internationally. Returning on a pre-approved Advance Parole document allows resumption of AOS processing, but does not guarantee admission; Customs and Border Protection makes the final admissibility determination at the port of entry, and a pending application does not override CBP’s board authority.

For employment-based applicants, it is now more important than ever to maintain underlying H-1B, L-1, or other nonimmigrant status, even after receiving an Employment Authorization Document (EAD) and/or Advance Parole while a permanent residency case is pending. If an AOS application is denied or withdrawn, an applicant who abandoned their nonimmigrant classification would be left without lawful status. Moreover, absent lawful status, individuals may experience heightened risk with respect to international and domestic travel.

ICE Enforcement

The recent uptick in immigration enforcement is a continuation of the expanded ICE presence at airports implemented in late 2025, when TSA began sharing information about air travelers believed to be subject to deportation orders with ICE, thereby facilitating arrests by ICE at airports. Since that period, ICE enforcement at ports of entry, including airports, has increased significantly.

Presently, ICE activity at airports includes the following: identity verification, immigration database review, and detention of individuals with an expired visa stamp, despite pending immigration matters, outstanding removal orders, or perceived status violations.

Such arrests and detentions of individuals by ICE have occurred notwithstanding pending applications for immigration benefits, including requests for asylum, lawful permanent residence (a green card), or other forms of permanent protection. On July 14, ICE detained a Southwest Airlines flight attendant in Nashville over a visa expiration issue, underscoring that enforcement actions are reaching individuals previously considered to be a low priority.

Reflecting broader enforcement trends, as of July 11, ICE held 65,765 individuals in detention, with approximately 70% of those detained lacking any criminal conviction. Such data indicates the enforcement efforts are no longer limited to undocumented immigrants; lawful permanent residents with decades of U.S. residence have been detained at airports upon return from international travel. Accordingly, non-citizens considering domestic or international travel during the pendency of a matter before USCIS should prepare for additional scrutiny at airports and ports of entry.

Practical Guidance

Given the rapidly evolving immigration enforcement landscape, employers should engage with counsel to review a list of non-citizen employees with pending adjustment of status applications, expired nonimmigrant visas, or upcoming USCIS interviews and discuss individualized risk assessments and develop proactive strategies. In addition, affected employees should take the following steps:

Notify immigration counsel before any domestic or international travel to conduct a case-specific risk assessment.

Carry the following documents at all times during domestic or international travel: receipt notices (I-797) for all pending applications; Employment Authorization Documents (EADs); valid advance parole documents; valid passport; prior visa stamps; evidence of current employment; and evidence of family ties and community connections in the United States.

Maintain underlying nonimmigrant status by not abandoning H-1B, L-1, or other nonimmigrant classification prematurely upon receipt of an EAD.

Develop an Emergency Legal Plan with family, friends, a trusted individual, or counsel to contact immediately if the individual is detained.

Consider deferring non-essential business travel pending further legal clarity.

authors: Eesha Pendharkar, Emma Davis, Kaitlyn Budion

text:
The American Civil Liberties Union of Maine is seeking a total of more than $5 million from the federal government on behalf of three Maine residents it says were wrongfully detained.

The five administrative claims filed by the local affiliate Wednesday are among 54 others filed in 17 states and Washington, D.C., under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows people to seek financial compensation for harm caused by federal employees. The claims were filed with the U.S. Department of Justice, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The Maine claims stem from the large-scale immigration enforcement operation in January known as Operation Catch of the Day, during which roughly 200 people — the vast majority of whom were lawfully present in the U.S. — were detained.

“We’re participating in this … in part to get accountability for all of those individuals, but also to shed light on the widespread abuses that ICE is doing all over the country,” said Samuel Crankshaw, spokesperson for the Maine ACLU. “And not just during big surges like Operation Catch of the Day, but happening on a daily basis, pretty much everywhere.”

The Maine ACLU filed five claims arising from three arrests during the operation. Three of the claims involve members of the same family, while the other two involve individual immigrants. All three people have since been released from federal detention, though the ACLU said they continue to live with the effects of the incident.

Whether the claims will result in compensation remains unclear. Federal agencies have six months to investigate an administrative claim and may choose to settle it or claimants can file a civil suit in federal court.

“The long-term trends are that the intent of that process under the law has not worked as well as it should,” Crankshaw said. “No matter what the outcome of the administrative complaint may be, it’s a required first step to get any kind of accountability.”

What the claims say

The first case involved an asylum seeker, who the ACLU identified as Mr. Diallo,who was detained while driving home with his family. The ACLU filed three separate claims on behalf of everyone in the car, Crankshaw said.

Years prior, Diallo had been detained and released. Despite complying with all conditions of release, ICE agents this winter stopped his car and detained him without a warrant, the ACLU said. During the stop, agents broke the driver’s side window, spraying broken glass over the entire family, including a baby, the claim reports. Diallo was detained for three weeks until he was able to obtain an attorney, who filed a successful challenge to his detention.

Another of the claims is on behalf of an immigrant who on Jan. 22 was dragged from his car after agents smashed his window. The civil rights organization did not disclose the identity of this person.

The third case involves Elias Tesfaye, who was taken from his home by masked agents on Jan. 20. Tesfaye had previously been in ICE custody but was released in 2013 and has been living and working in Maine for over a decade, where according to the ACLU he complied with all the terms of his release. Tesfaye was held in a detention facility for a month, during which he developed PTSD, had a panic attack, and was prescribed Prozac that he is still taking. After Tesfaye secured a lawyer, the government did not attempt to justify his arrest, releasing Tesfaye without responding to the legal challenge, the civil rights agency said.

A separate lawsuit filed by the ACLU on behalf of a Portland man in U.S. District Court rests on protections in the Maine Civil Rights Act — another approach the organization is taking to seek justice for wrongfully detained immigrants. The ACLU couldn’t confirm or deny if the same person was involved in one of the tort claims.

New laws limit ICE enforcement

Even after the end of the January enforcement surge, federal immigration agents have maintained a presence in Maine. Two weeks ago, 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was killed by federal immigration agents in Biddeford, prompting renewed calls to investigate ICE operations, demand accountability and place additional limits on how and where agents can operate.

Several new Maine laws took effect Wednesday that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. One restricts local law enforcement from coordinating with federal immigration authorities, another prohibits landlords from sharing certain tenant information, and a third allows employees at certain schools and healthcare facilities to deny immigration agents access to nonpublic areas without a judicial warrant.

“These laws and the claims we’re bringing demonstrate our commitment to do everything possible to stop the ICE violence and chaos that led to the shocking killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero this month in Biddeford,” said ACLU of Maine Executive Director Molly Curren Rowles in a statement.

“Congress has refused to rein in ICE, but if the federal government won’t protect people in Maine, then Mainers will continue to take action and protect one another – just as we always have.”

text:
CHICAGO — Two United States citizens attacked by federal officers while at work caring for the grounds of a suburban Forest Park cemetery last year have filed claims against the federal government. The filings are part of a coordinated nationwide effort by the ACLU and affiliates in 17 states and Washington, D.C. In all, 54 separate claims have been filed.

Since the beginning of President Trump’s second term, federal law enforcement agents have terrorized communities and people in their custody with a blatant disregard for the law. The consequences have been deadly. Conditions in ICE facilities are so inhumane that the rate of deaths in ICE custody has more than doubled since Trump’s term began, reaching its highest level in over a decade. Recent reporting revealed that, after the White House pushed to increase arrest rates, ICE officials detained more than 10,000 people in five days. Only days later, ICE agents in unmarked vehicles shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas while he was on his way to work. The following week, a federal agent shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine.

The Illinois actions are on behalf of Darren Eichler and Daniel Greer. On October 7, 2025, Eichler and Greer were at work along the Des Plaines River when they noticed a man in the water. Along with their colleagues, Eichler and Greer called out to the man to check on his health. Almost immediately, they were met with voices from on the other side of the water (voices that were unseen behind some brush) who told them to mind their own business, or they would be charged with a crime. Suspecting that the voices belonged to federal officers, Eichler and Greer joined told the officers to leave the area and stop harassing people.

Within minutes, a group of approximately seven officers crossed the river over a pedestrian bridge and approached the gated area where Eichler and Greer were working. The federal officers – masked and heavily-armed –demanded the workers unlock a gate that shielded off a private area where they were working. Additional masked, armed federal agents arrived in vehicles through the cemetery’s driveway and mustered outside the locked, gated private area. The workers refused to open the gate, saying they would need supervisory approval. Without waiting, a federal officer retrieved a set of bolt clippers from a vehicle and cut the lock.

The agents burst through the now open gate, spraying Eichler and Greer with mace and throwing them to the ground. Eichler immediately experienced intense pain – including chest palpitations – and had difficulty breathing. He repeatedly requested medical attention, a request that was ignored by federal officers for more than an hour. When he was finally taken to Rush Oak Park Hospital, Eichler was kept in handcuffs and was accompanied by federal officers – including by the one that used chemical agents – who refused to give him any privacy.

When the federal officers finally left the hospital – without any charges against Eichler – they failed to remove his handcuffs until a thoughtful nurse chased after them and called them back to remove the restraints. The federal officers did not return Eichler’s phone, wallet and other personal belongings until the next day – some of which he was never able to retrieve.

“My story is not just about what happened to me,” said Darren Eichler in a statement accompanying release of the charges. “It’s about the kind of country we choose to be. No one should lose their dignity the moment they come face to face with those who hold power.”

After Greer was sprayed with the chemical agent, he was pushed to the ground and his hands were zip-tied behind his back. He then was forced to sit in an uncomfortable position before his legs were shackled and he was tossed into a van and taken to a DHS facility. Agents never read his rights, never told him why he was detained and offered no medical assistance as the chemical agents burned his face.

After being held in a cell at the DHS center, he and other colleagues were released without any charges and no explanation as to why they had been treated so cruelly.

“As the agents escalated their attack on us, I kept thinking that they would stop and recognize their behavior was not right,” said Danny Greer. “At every step, they escalated violence and treated us like dirt.”

Across the country, ACLU affiliates are fighting back against the Trump administration’s illegal conduct by filing claims under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA), one of the few legal tools available to seek financial compensation for wrongdoing by federal government employees. Through this coordinated effort, ACLU affiliates are representing dozens of people and families who are seeking justice for the harm they experienced at the hands of federal immigration agents.

“No one – not even ICE officers under this Administration – has the right to recklessly and violently careen through our neighborhoods and act with impunity toward people – no matter their immigration status,” said Alexandra Block, Director of the Criminal Legal System and Policing Project at the ACLU of Illinois who represents Eichler and Green. “These filings– in this matter and across the country – are an important step toward accountability and justice for all those victimized by the permission structure created by this White House and their enablers.”
